en: In the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha* compiled by the Bhikṣu Saṅgharakṣa:
When the Bodhisattva first set out upon his practice, he resolved to enter the Path out of compassion for the world; because he had left the household life, he practiced patience;
because he was free from worldly attachments, his mind was in samādhi; and because he had severed ignorance, he practiced [wisdom].
Vajra-wisdom; because it eliminates and abandons playful conduct by means of the true reality, it discards the defilements of the mind;
it is for the sake of upright conduct and for the sake of ascetic practice.
Out of compassion and filial piety toward one's parents, the mind remains firm and steadfast, never abandoning one's vows;
because of detachment from desire, one listens extensively and constantly reflects upon repaying their kindness;
and because of seeking liberation, one wears the kāṣāya.
Because he wishes to dwell in seclusion within the forest, he does not observe [external] practices;
because he seeks to know his kin, he knows that his own body is bound;
because his verbal conduct is free from deception, there is no conceptualization in the mind—the root of all suffering—and thus he does not abandon existence.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices wisdom, it is called "wisdom" because of what is known therein. If, within that practice and regarding sentient beings, they repeatedly fail to understand the profound meaning, the bodhisattva must for a long night exhort, distinguish, and resolve through wisdom: "This is deep, this is shallow; this is pure, this is beneficial; this is evil, this is ugly. By drawing near to virtuous friends, those dharmas will not be confused; they are immeasurable, limitless, and without increase or decrease, just as whatever is cut by a sword or halberd is severed completely—the same is true for that wisdom.

Because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is manifested, there is the shared illumination of wisdom; because the darkness of the mind has been closed off, that light of vision is opened and made to correspond with that [wisdom]. Because of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the gates of the faculties (*indriya-mukha*) are fully perfected; because there is no timidity, its majestic power (*vibhūti*) is manifested. To sever unwholesome karmic wealth, it manifests the possession of karmic wealth; because precious jewels are otherwise unobtainable, it thus manifests as precious jewels.

By severing the life-span, he manifests his own longevity; because he has severed all fetters and proclivities, this power observes distant events and distinguishes them for others, causing all to reach definitive understanding so as to save their fragile lives. Because they are burdened by sorrow and anxiety, he arouses in them a heart of joy; by calming the mind so that it does not arise [in affliction], they depart from unwholesome dharmas and achieve wholesome dharmas.
Abandoning the heterodox and adhering to the orthodox, one thereby perfects the power of wisdom.

Because of the cycle of birth and death, one desires to sever all cravings and reach the place of ultimate liberation; yet, because one still walks within the mundane world, one traverses all realms of experience to ultimately realize the source of all-knowledge and arrive at the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Abiding well and immovable, free from the fear of birth and death,
they immediately attain the stage of non-returning and extinguish the destinies of the triple world.
Having cultivated practices for a hundred kalpas, they desire to purify the classes of sentient beings.
Having no conception of the three periods of time, you are thus able to be without longing.

When this bodhisattva practices the truth, that which is called "truth" is a mind free from falsehood and speech free from duality; he constantly delights therein, and there is neither self nor other.
He repeatedly delighted in that state; whether awake or asleep, he never engaged in frivolous play nor spoke falsely.

Furthermore, it is heard that in the past there was a king named Sūdamana, born into the royal palace, who ruled over the four quarters and whose Dharma-drum resounded far and wide, such that among his ministers and the people, there were none who did not hear it.
When such a virtuous person was born, he went to the pond to bathe and, mounting a chariot made of precious feathers, was about to exit the city gate.
At that time, there was a brahmin of handsome appearance, brilliant and wise, who came wishing to beg for jewels.
The brahmin immediately addressed the king, announcing his own name and raising his hand to beg for words.
At that moment, upon hearing the sound of the brahmin’s plea, the king felt great joy and replied:
"Stop, stop, O Venerable One!"
"When I have returned to my kingdom, I shall provide you with relief.
Since the word of a king is never double, he immediately went to that pond to bathe; having finished his bath, he was about to return to his kingdom.
At that time, there was a winged demon named Karmasapara who manifested a terrifying form and seized the king by the body.
Thereupon, the king immediately shed tears.
At that time, the ghost observed the king’s thoughts and asked:
"Great King, why do you weep? Why do you harbor such a heart of sorrow and anxiety?
Then the Bodhisattva replied:
"I have no such notion of 'self' regarding this body; it is only for the sake of the Brahmin’s wealth that I feel sorrow.
At that time, the ghost replied to the king:

"I have never heard of such a thing—so marvelous and extraordinary, rare even to hear of in the world. I came to test you for the sake of those people. If you were to release me now and let me go, would I return?"
At that time, the king was filled with great joy.
Then, that ghost, whose body possessed two wings, flew into the air; upon hearing what had been said, he immediately released him and let him go.
At that time, the Bodhisattva returned to his kingdom and joyfully gave wealth to that brahmin; there was no falsehood in his giving, he felt no regret, and he spoke these words of solemn truth.
At that time, the king went to the place where the ghost was, announced his own name, and declared, "I have now arrived here.
When the ghost saw the king’s appearance, he was immediately struck with terror; yet such were the king's truthful words that the king’s countenance did not change.
Having removed his anger and harboring no intent to kill, he spoke these words:
"How extraordinary, how marvelous! This is something I have never heard before.
Then he uttered this verse:
"I would rather drink deadly poison, have molten copper poured into my mouth,
or have my body cut by sharp blades— who would dare harm the Dharma King?
Born into the royal lineage through past merit, his virtues are beyond compare."
Your valor is indeed not in vain; you are worthy to be the sovereign of this land.

I shall now show you respect; following the King, I shall no longer kill, but shall reform my past ways and cultivate virtuous conduct, so that all sentient beings may follow according to their inclinations.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva practices gentleness, his mind becomes gentle and acquires this reputation: his speech is not impulsive or violent; because he seeks the Dharma, he constantly guards the minds of others; he never gives rise to resentment or malice, nor does he harbor expectations; he does not utter evil words from his mouth; for the sake of those who are deluded, he manifests wisdom; to remove the defilements of the mind, he is praised by all; he is free from any notion of a self or "mine," and he does not follow illusions.

Protected by all Buddhas, one attains such virtues as these; being free from guile and deceit, one entirely avoids such defilements. Within this state, one attains a mind of gentleness and flexibility, becomes fully endowed with the roots of goodness, is cherished and remembered by others, does not begrudge even body or life, and is praised and extolled by divine seers (*ṛṣi*).
Thus, with gentle composure, he contemplates the retribution of good and evil; his wisdom and merit are fully endowed as described.
For those who lack the roots of goodness and suffer from poverty, he bestows gold, silver, and precious jewels to eliminate all defilements.

When the lifespan is ten years, one encounters calamities and hardships; yet, with mastery over one's desires and refraining from killing, one performs wholesome deeds of body, acquires wealth through the mind, transmits teachings through speech, and carries out actions of conduct, thereby removing that which is covered by defilements and evils.

At that time, the bhikṣus, having found rest from the existence of the body in the world and having completely exhausted all that is not-self without remainder—being thus fully exhausted—for this reason they should depart from and abandon attachment.
"Regarding what was created in previous lives, that has already been exhausted and will not be created again; its root has been severed, and suffering has come to rest, ceased, and been destroyed.

Having spoken thus, one abides in this Dharma within this profound and wondrous teaching, like a hand grasping a wheel for six months without slackening; all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, fully perceive and fully accomplish this.
Thereupon, he spoke these verses:
"Do not harbor a mind of flattery; Recognize the karma of false dharmas.
Originally, you did not create this either; You should contemplate in this way."
"With a courageous mind like the ocean, gentle and not coarse or wild, I bow my head in prostration to the World-Honored One, who is free from attachment and rare in the world.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva was filial toward his parents, his nature was one of gratitude, reverence, and service; he stayed far from evil and approached the good, providing for them according to the needs of the moment. Rising early and retiring late, he attended to his parents' wishes, leaving no task unaccomplished, and never failed to follow their instructions or admonitions.
Because there is such a gentle and pliant mind, such things come to pass; one should constantly observe within the practice of the mind: "What task is to be accomplished?"

Upon hearing instructions and admonitions, they understand them immediately; they always harbor joy and are loved and respected by all. They keep in mind the full extent of their parents' hearts, constantly thinking of how to repay their kindness, and never uttering coarse or harsh words—there is no such place for them.

Furthermore, it is heard that in the past, before he had yet become a bodhisattva, he was a king of great elephants, peerless in his physical perfection. His head, eyes, skin, and hair were all exquisitely beautiful; one could never tire of beholding him. His ears were fully developed and complete among all elephants; his tusks and claws were square and majestic, inspiring a sense of delight. His lips and teeth were pure red, and his head and ears were perfectly formed. His body was square and round, exceedingly large, tall, and broad, like a lofty mountain. His gait was measured and dignified, with the seven parts of his body fully developed like a blue lotus. Walking with such composed steps, he was free from all impediments. Born of a dragon female, he roamed through mountains and marshes, his color like pure snow, until he was captured by a hunter.

When he was about to depart, at that time the trees of the mountains and wilds all bent and stretched themselves; the waters surged and boiled of their own accord as he approached his destination, yet he refused to partake of the various kinds of sweet food and drink offered to him.
At that time, the elephant trainer knelt before him with palms joined and addressed the elephant, speaking this verse:
"I have cultivated roots of goodness in the past, And thus this divine elephant has come to me.
Why do you refuse to eat?"
"As if harboring a heart of resentment.
At that time, the divine elephant replied with a verse:
"My mother has no eyes; emaciated and filled with sorrow, she dwells in distress."
"Recalling that they were unable to eat, I therefore pray that you will forgive me.

In those deep mountains, not eating, they would surely have perished from hunger and thirst; it would have been a most painful and bitter agony, and we would all have had to part. Because of this grief and anxiety, I was neither able to eat nor drink water."
"If there is no fruit or gourd for my mother, both of us shall die.
Having spoken these bitter and sorrowful words, the hunter was moved to joy and released them to go.

In that kingdom of Kosala, there was a secluded dwelling where a recluse named Śyāmaka resided; he was fully endowed with the practice of the ten wholesome deeds and was carrying a water jar to fetch water.
At that time, the King of Kosala went out on a hunting expedition; pursuing a deer, he shot it with an arrow in the mountains. Struck, the deer cried out:

"I am now distressed for my parents, like a bird that has lost both its wings. My parents are old and blind, seeing nothing; now, having been struck by a poisoned arrow, they too shall surely die. Yet my parents have cultivated the four immeasurable minds."
He then spoke this verse:
"My parents alone are old; their eyes are dim and they see nothing.
When my parents gave birth to me, they desired to receive the benefit of my strength."
Awakening oneself and awakening others, all things share the same nature as oneself;
just as those who hear the sounds of forms, the wise bring their own minds to rest.
The Most Victorious One takes pity on all living beings, leading them all to that place of enlightenment.
"Arising is the exhaustion of extinction; this is the most wondrous meaning in the world.
One who first gives rise to the aspiration is called a Bodhisattva, and such are their manifold practices.
To eliminate the various veils of ignorance, one brings all ignorance to the state of clarity; there is nothing that can remove ignorance.
One should practice with the wisdom that manifests clarity, thereby removing whatever is perceived by that [ignorance].
When the bodhisattva observes in this way, he practices great loving-kindness toward all classes of sentient beings.

Out of compassion for the world, he sets out upon the path; yet, because of his attachment [to conventional reality], he does not rely on his own power or authority, except for that which has been realized through his awakening.
When the bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the multitude of sentient beings.
Sentient beings are bound by form and fettered by the craving for desire; none among them are able to liberate themselves from form, except for those who possess wisdom.
When the bodhisattva observes in this way, he then gives rise to great compassion for the class of sentient beings.
Sentient beings are bound by the two thoughts of the aggregates (*skandha*) and aversion; none are able to awaken to this, except for those who possess wisdom.
When the bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for all classes of sentient beings.
Sentient beings are burdened by the heavy load of suffering and are harmed by suffering; there is no one capable of delivering them from this burden of suffering, except for those who possess wisdom.
When the bodhisattva observes in this manner, he then gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings constantly harbor fear; though a hundred sufferings converge upon them, there is no one capable of removing their dread, save for those who possess wisdom.
When the bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the class of sentient beings.

These classes of sentient beings encounter famine and the thirst of craving that knows no satisfaction; there is no one capable of liberating them from this famine, except for those who possess wisdom.
When the bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.

These classes of sentient beings are oppressed by illness; when one ailment arises, a hundred ailments increase, and there is no one able to escape these illnesses, except for those who possess wisdom.
When the bodhisattva contemplates in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the class of sentient beings.

These sentient beings are constantly pursued by birth, old age, sickness, and death, and they weary of them; yet there is none among them who can escape this birth, old age, sickness, and death to reach the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*).
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings are cluttered and entangled by manifold affairs, clinging to the notion of permanence; yet there is none among them capable of removing this clutter and entanglement.
Except for those who possess wisdom.
When the bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion toward all classes of sentient beings.
He reflects that if sentient beings fail to accomplish their tasks, their minds become distracted and disordered, and none among them are able to bring those matters to completion.
Except for those who possess wisdom,
when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings are attached to trivial pleasures while undergoing manifold sufferings, and there is no one capable of liberating them from these afflictions.
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the class of sentient beings.
These sentient beings constantly harbor hesitation and longing; they distance themselves from what is correct and approach what is deviant, and there is no one capable of severing their doubts.
Except for those who possess wisdom,
when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion toward the classes of sentient beings.
Among these classes of sentient beings, there are various views and inclinations, yet none are able to extricate themselves from these views.
Excepting those who possess wisdom, when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he then gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings are defiled by the dust and grime of afflictions; they have not crossed to the other shore, and there is none among them who is able to cross to the other shore.
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings are scorched by the intense burning of the three fires; there is no one able to escape this state, nor can it be extinguished by the rain of the Dharma.
Excepting those who possess wisdom,
when the bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings revolve through birth and death without rest, and there is none among them who is able to reach the further shore.
Excepting those who possess wisdom, when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.

These classes of sentient beings are defiled by the stains of their conduct; they increase the roots of birth and existence, and there is none among them capable of escaping this cycle of birth and death.
Except for those who possess wisdom, when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward all classes of sentient beings.
These beings dwell in a place of great peril, clutching fragile ropes with their hands; none among them are able to escape these fragile ropes.
Except for those who possess wisdom, when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion toward the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings are like silkworms driven and oppressed by their own actions; there is no one capable of liberating them from this flow of defilements.
Except for those who possess wisdom,
when the Bodhisattva observes in this manner, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward the classes of sentient beings.

These classes of sentient beings set out upon the great cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), constantly harboring hopes and desires, and there is no one capable of causing them to turn back and cease.
Except for those who possess wisdom,
when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward all classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings set out toward evil destinies, constantly harboring thoughts of sensual desires, and none among them are able to establish themselves securely on the Right Path.
Setting aside those who are already wise, when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he then gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings have long dwelt in the darkness of ignorance; there is none capable of delivering them from this false path and establishing them in right knowledge.
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he then gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings do not perceive the ultimate; they do not see the noble truths, and there is no one who can cause them to see the noble truths.
Except for those who possess wisdom,
when the bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings have dwelt for a long night in the stagnant flow [of saṃsāra], and there is no one capable of liberating them from this stagnation.
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings have no leisure or tranquility; they are bound to various realms of existence, and none among them are able to escape these states of lack of leisure and tranquility.
Except for those who possess wisdom, when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion toward the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings are greedily attached to the fetters and remain stained by them through the long night; there is none among them capable of extinguishing these fetters.
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when a bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings encounter suffering and hardship, and their minds and natures become wild and disordered; there is no one capable of leading them to the state of liberation.
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when the bodhisattva contemplates in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the class of sentient beings.
He perceives that the class of sentient beings takes desire to be purity, yet it is an internal vessel filled with stench; there is no one capable of escaping this craving and desire.
Excepting those who possess wisdom,
the Bodhisattva observes in this way and then gives rise to great compassion for the classes of sentient beings.

These classes of sentient beings take desire to be happiness, yet they do not understand that the aggregates are suffering and affliction, nor do they comprehend the supreme meaning of reaching nirvāṇa.
Setting aside those who possess wisdom, when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion for the class of sentient beings.
These beings are attached to the notion of permanence, believing that things do not shift or change; there is no one capable of showing them the path to nirvana.
Except for those who possess wisdom.
When the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion toward the classes of sentient beings.
These classes of sentient beings cling to the notion of a self and do not understand the categories of phenomena; there is none among them capable of discerning the nature of dharmas.
Except for those who possess wisdom, when the Bodhisattva observes in this way, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward the classes of sentient beings.

These classes of sentient beings fail to find protection and instead feel aversion toward *nirvāṇa*. They are just like a large dog that constantly guards a corpse, running back and forth without rest; the behavior of the ignorant is now likewise so, no different from that dog. Lacking self-nature and conduct, they run back and forth without understanding the meaning of *nirvāṇa*, shrouded by the *skandhas* and *āvaraṇas*, unable to observe clearly.
The Bodhisattva arouses a courageous mind to reach that path,
and thereupon utters this verse:
“Many classes of sentient beings Are adrift in the abyss of birth and death.”
Observing these hardships and sufferings, one dwells securely until reaching nirvana.
Covered by dark clouds, where there is no light and all is in gloom—
the wise appear in this world to dispel the clouds and let the light shine forth.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva practices this giving, at the very outset he gives rise to the perception of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃjñā*). With food that is sweet, fragrant, and delicious, he benefits sentient beings; it accords with the proper season and accords with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). His mind is free from craving for flavor, being fulfilled and complete, having removed all fetters (*saṃyojana*), yet there is nothing from which he is separated.

Not opposing those who beg means that after giving, one has no heart of regret or change of mind; all such acts are the merit of past practices which cause others to be free from fetters and attachments.

Bearing heavy burdens for the sake of all people, one casts off all fetters and compulsions, just as with today’s giving, thereby fulfilling their aspirations and desiring that all sentient beings obtain whatever they wish for.

From childhood, he has been free from various harmful intentions and has endured all manner of defilements and afflictions. His cultivation of merit has gradually increased as he guides the people like a master mariner. He never ceases his acts of giving, always delighting in generosity; though inwardly pure, he manifests an outward appearance of impurity. "Not understanding all" refers to his removal of pride toward all sentient beings and his lack of weariness or indolence.

The mind of generosity increased accordingly; his countenance was harmonious and joyful, free from resentment. He neither praised himself nor disparaged others, cherished all sentient beings, and bestowed all that he possessed as gifts, accomplishing what is right.
Gathering together the people, he repeatedly bestowed gifts with a mind free from regret, his heart filled with joy; he praised the fruits of giving as far-reaching and profound.
He bestowed gold, silver, rare treasures, musaragalva, agate, vehicles, men and women, and even cities and towns, all without any internal stinginess or envy.

Out of love for that faithful offering, desiring to fulfill their hopes and aspirations in their entirety, desiring to make the fruits of their giving entirely firm, and desiring to enable them to cross over by means of that gift—through such giving, these purposes are fully realized.

Observing the fruits of giving, he abandons all fetters; causing sentient beings to remove their greedy attachments so that no false views remain, and eliminating stinginess and greed, he rains down the rain of the Dharma according to the time and the conditions. Therefore, I take refuge in him.
"Bestowing gold, silver, and rare treasures, carnelian, agate, and pearls—beholding these, one remains insatiable; now I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas.
Elephants, horses, and celestial gold—their color is foremost among all."
Able to bestow a harmonious countenance, I take refuge in the one who has attained liberation.
With the precious chariot as foremost, adorned with rare jewels,
his countenance is entirely serene and joyful.
A golden bowl filled with silver, or filled with fragments of gold—
giving such gifts with joy, who could surpass Vaiśravaṇa?
Giving with a harmonious and joyful mind, it is like fruit that is abundant and excellent.
Giving with joy, he fills the three worlds;
giving sons and daughters of exquisite beauty, as well as his wife’s body, head,
and eyes for the sake of the world— who could equal such a giver?
"There is no gift superior to this, which neither devas nor humans can surpass;
it is like that Superior Person, whose mind is a bottomless great ocean.

When that Bodhisattva practices the precepts, he does not regard those precepts as being without precepts. Regarding the conduct of body and speech and the nectar-like Dharma arising from the mind—just as flowers and fruits protect their roots so that fruit must inevitably arise therefrom—he attains all these through human practice.

Just as that man engages in killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and various forms of self-indulgence, the Bodhisattva does not drink alcohol; he is fully endowed with all precepts and wisdom, having eliminated all that is contrary to the precepts.
Constantly abiding in samādhi within the site of enlightenment, they remain far removed from violating the precepts and harbor no intent to kill; the nature of all things is pure.
When receiving offerings of faith, even if the flavors are frequent and rich, they commit no transgression.

Internally there is no deficiency; when departing, one does not cling to existence, nor does one scatter flowers. Relying on vision, one is neither corrupt nor defiled, and does not produce new defiled fruits. What is sown is fresh goodness; in sleep and awakening, there is no sorrow.
That sentient being’s physical form is foremost; by virtue of those merits, a fine fragrance spreads afar.

Because he accepts offerings of faith with a resolute intention, his faculties are complete and thus remain unimpaired. Because his wisdom abides without wavering, there is nothing that cannot be preserved. By taking that person as an object of focus, one gains further increase.

For the sake of those beings, one bears the burden of suffering; for the sake of wholesome dharmas, there is a place of dwelling, free from sorrow and untainted by defilement. Outward appearance necessitates clothing, and for the sake of those beings, there is wealth and treasure—boundless, immeasurable, and inexhaustible. From the first moment of generating the aspiration, one has never wavered or regretted it, let alone having achieved the precepts of a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Upward and downward, and in the four directions, All who hear the fragrance of the precepts Shall fully and equally possess it;
To distance oneself from desire is the supreme requirement.”
Associate with virtuous friends; the virtuous perform meritorious deeds.
Their excellent appearance is beyond compare; the fragrance of their precepts is the foremost blessing.
All defilements come to rest; they awaken to the self as being without a self.
"The most supreme one, the seventh and last—him I now pay homage.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices diligence, although that mind has an object of focus, the mind remains free from weariness. His renunciation cannot be obstructed or severed; he has renounced the world for the sake of sentient beings. Because he is immovable, he possesses the conditions of power; because there are various kinds of sentient beings, he possesses diligence. Because he is invincible, he possesses patience; because there is growth and benefit, he manifests in the world; and because he possesses merit, he manifests before sentient beings.

Because he governs his mind, his intention does not waver; because he acts as a helmsman, he reaches the further shore; because he possesses meditative concentration, he is not distracted; and by setting forth with purposeful strides, he achieves what must be traversed. For the sake of those sentient beings, he fulfills their aspirations; and desiring to achieve the Way, he gives away elephants, horses, jewels, and chariots.

At that time, the Bodhisattva possesses such diligence toward those sentient beings that anyone who hears the name of this diligence will set out upon the Path; the merit performed within a single lifetime would be immeasurable, let alone the merit performed by the Tathāgata over countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
When sitting upright in the place of enlightenment, you subdued the non-Buddhists; traversing birth and death, you removed all sorrow and anxiety through a mind of diligence.
Diligence is the most supreme; I take refuge in the Lord of the Dharma-Kings.
Having attained perfect self-awakening as a Buddha, I now take refuge in the Peerless One.
That Honored One is the foremost; the sound of his Dharma drum spreads afar.
Having awakened to awakening through self-awakening, he is therefore returned to as the Unattached One.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva practices patience, he is fearless, without dread, and without defilement; he does not look toward the karmic retribution thereof. Possessing power and majesty, he protects sentient beings and remains forever far removed from the ranks of evil.

With a resolute and steadfast nature, one reflects upon one's own faults; seeing that all sentient beings harbor fear, one causes them to be free from fear by demonstrating the precepts to them, and likewise subdues the coarseness and wildness of all sentient beings, removing unwholesome speech and showing compassion for all beings.

That immeasurable and limitless discourse concerning sentient beings—whatever is heard therein, including the various tracks leading to the Path and the most subtle and supreme [teachings]—is like flowers and fruits that never fail to blossom. When stirred by the wind, the fragrances, essences, various colors, and the sounds of merit from the mountain crags and caves are gathered; all classes of sentient beings delight in hearing them. It is like a king of bees gathering the nectar of various flowers to produce honey, as do the smaller bees; it is like springs overflowing everywhere, and like the incomparable bliss of the Nandana Grove.

He accomplishes whatever is required even when subjected to verbal abuse; he shows shame and remorse to those who seek out sorcery; and he acts as a protector for sentient beings practicing the Path who are beset by calamities. Thus, he is named the Rishi Kṣāntivādin (The Sage of Forbearance).
At that time, King Kalmāṣapāda went into the deep mountains to hunt deer; having entered the mountains, he saw this rishi of forbearance and approached him, kneeling and asking:
"What path do you seek here in these deep mountains?"
Kṣānti replied, “I seek patience.
At that time, the Great King, without examining himself nor examining his conduct, wishing to put [the monk] to the test, immediately spoke these words:
"I shall now cut off your hands and feet," he said,
and immediately severed the hands and feet of that seer.
He then asked this question again:
"What path do you now seek?
At that time, Kṣānti replied,
"I seek the path of patience."
He immediately praised the virtue of forbearance.
At that time, the great king’s anger redoubled and he desired to take his life.
Then, having had his hands and feet severed, the rishi made this vow:
"May I, in every lifetime, harbor no ill will and never give rise to anger;
may I understand that all phenomena are entirely empty, O Great King.
Furthermore, there was another rishi to whom a person went and asked this question:
"How is it that this immortal did not give rise to anger toward that king?
When practicing such patience, possessing the power of this great forbearance, at that time he did not conceive a thought of anger, and even when observing this color of blood, it did not change.
At that time, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings went to the dwelling place of that seer. Then, Dhṛtarāṣṭra prostrated himself before him and asked:
"I now wish to kill King Kālaṃbu; would this be permissible?"
Having spoken these words, the seer remained silent and did not respond.
Then the second Heavenly King again asked this question:
"I shall now slay those men and women, great and small, and utterly exterminate the inhabitants of the city and its suburbs."
Having spoken these words, the seer remained silent and did not respond.
Then King Vairocana asked again:
"I wish to seize all the inhabitants of that realm and territory and kill them without exception; I pray you, grant me your permission."
At that time, the rishi remained silent and did not respond.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa asked again:
"I wish to take those realms and territories and relocate them to another region; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
At that time, the seer rejoiced and praised the virtue of forbearance, and then spoke this verse:
"Though my head, eyes, hands, and feet were severed, I gave rise to no thoughts of resentment or malice;
I bestowed everything I possessed upon him— how much more so for those in this world?"
At that time, the World-Protecting Heavenly King again asked this question:
"What kind of path does the seer wish to seek? Then the seer replied:
"I wish that for the body of that king, there may be no retribution for evil deeds;
though that king is fierce and violent, I grieve for him, not for myself.

When a Bodhisattva practices samādhi, even if they enter that samādhi with a mind having an object of focus, they never forget it nor are they negligent; they concentrate their single mind. Furthermore, if they do not earnestly seek skillful means, they do not grasp at conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they understand the flavor of all dharmas without being attached to them, and within that stage (*bhūmi*), there are no fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Within that samādhi, he is pure and free from blemish; he subdues external adversaries without cowardice; with single-mindedness, he understands its flavor; his mind is without attachment; he subdues his own disposition without ever becoming weary, thereby perfecting his practice.

Having attained the root of joy through samādhi, with diligence unwavering and mindfulness undisturbed, one cultivates the factors of enlightenment for an entire kalpa; what is gained through mindfulness, tranquility, joy, and valor is all based upon reliance on wisdom, whereby one gradually attains a state of bliss.

However, when a bodhisattva practices those samādhis, they initiate the skillful practice of samādhi; having perfected the skillful practice of samādhi, whether walking or standing, they never lose it.
Because he possesses these practices, he is fully endowed with wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) and undertakes various virtuous deeds; thus, all that he seeks manifests before him.

Even if his mind should experience sorrow or distress, he gradually subdues it, ensuring that he does not forget or lose his mindfulness, but rather increases and further enhances his cultivation of the wholesome.
If the mind is heedless yet still contemplates wholesome dharmas, or if the mind is bound by the fetters of sorrow and anxiety, it is nevertheless able to contemplate that wholesome liberation.

Within his own domain, his deportment is entirely excellent; for the sake of others, he expounds upon the samādhis of distracted thoughts, impure illnesses, and other varieties, as well as the samādhi endowed with all merits. The fruit of the retribution for practicing these various samādhis is the most excellent conduct, just as green trees manifest pure liberation, and other colors—blue, yellow, white, and black—all follow that samādhi in coming and going without any obstruction.

Just as the fire-gathered radiance of the sun, through the power of samādhi, leaves nothing unilluminated, so too does he obtain the divine eye which penetrates and illuminates day and night, and likewise obtains the divine ear which hears with penetrating clarity; such is his power.

That bodhisattva attains this samādhi, which is infinite, immeasurable, and incalculable; it arises entirely through the power of samādhi, as well as through reflection, through non-laxity, through the clear knowledge of wisdom regarding how to roll up and how to unroll [the teachings], through the aspiration for samādhi, through the departure from evil signs, and through the power of samādhi in both its direct and inverse applications.

Such various conceptions are born from that samādhi; through each of those dhāraṇī-doors, one accomplishes samādhi. Wherever one goes, there is no fatigue; seeking skillful means, one practices samādhi because it is not a fixed or solid state. For the sake of all desires, one subdues the mind and thoughts, maintaining excellent protection and contemplation without confusion. One acts with sovereign mastery according to one's will, refrains from speaking of others' faults, and remains immeasurable, limitless, and inexhaustible.
In this present samādhi, one cuts off all doubts and emits various kinds of light, relying on all wholesome dharmas;
with all fetters and latent tendencies purified, one repeatedly practices samādhi, relying on all wholesome dharmas.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Having attained this mind of liberation, In samādhi there is no obstruction;
The Indus flows toward the great ocean, Its swift current difficult to restrain."
If the mind has no desires, the heart likewise does not waver;
wishing to cut off the waters of sensory objects is entirely the practice of the sense-gates.
For a hundred years, I bore my parents upon my shoulders.
It does not fulfill my wishes; yet it can repay the kindness of one's parents.
Having already obtained protection for them, it points out the way to the parents' abode.
One who can awaken to this knows what the world desires to possess.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva practices with a firm mind, he employs such skillful means to gather and withdraw from existence; possessing courageous intent, his actions are unimpeded and cannot be obstructed by others. For this reason, one should seek [this state] through skillful means.

I have heard that in the past, Ārāḍa Kālāma arose from various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Having relinquished those concentrations, he further sought the unsurpassed path of the *Samyaksaṃbuddha*. He then traveled south for half a *yojana* to a secluded place, where he engaged in various ascetic practices (*duṣkaracaryā*). He ate fruits and drank water, wore garments of pure black leather, and sat cross-legged beneath trees. At times he drank water, at times he ate fruits and melons, and at times he practiced breath-retention (*vāyubhakṣa*). Performing such austerities, he slept upon the grass or covered himself with ashes. For three nights, his complexion remained unchanged despite his devotion to those practices; for nine days, he prostrated and worshipped the sacrificial fire.

Those who were heedless followed his instructions; at times they sacrificed to the gods until their heads and eyes grew gradually emaciated and both arms became exposed, or they stood on one leg with their bodies bent and hunched, yet they did not engage in theft, finding joy in the Dharma.

In his pursuit of the Way through those ascetic practices, he abstained from food and drink; his skin and bones became joined together as his body grew increasingly emaciated day by day. His body turned black and his complexion grew withered and yellow, like a lute that is hollow within. His ribs and spine were all exposed, and his form underwent a hundred transformations such that it could no longer be looked upon. All traces of youthful appearance vanished forever; he was like an old elephant incapable of any exertion, lacking the strength to sit, lie down, walk, or even speak, though he still clung to life, unable to remain much longer in this world.
At that time, the celestial messenger arrived at his dwelling and employed various skillful means, manifesting such diverse transformations.
For the sake of the Dharma, he maintained his discipline whether waking or sleeping; thus seeking liberation, he disregarded his own body and spoke these verses:
"Even if my body were to melt away, And my human form were divided into a hundred parts..."
Furthermore, when there is no thought of malice, and sentient beings reach the state of non-differentiation,
how could one’s mind harbor greed?
Amidst countless transformations of suffering and affliction, to harbor the notion of a self— how does this differ from being asleep or dead?

At that time, when the Bodhisattva was renowned for his great learning—meaning those who heard his name proclaimed his virtue as being foremost—and was honored and waited upon by the assembly of those who had stilled their minds.

Their resolve and nature are undisturbed; they are able to retain what they have heard, and being fully endowed with this power of hearing and retention, they never forget it. They contemplate its meaning and eliminate arrogance. Possessing such karma that accords with wisdom, they now hear and know all things. Through wisdom free from indolence, they show reverence to their teachers and elders, and their aspirations become sovereign.

If there are those who are hungry and empty, he gives rise to great compassion, subdues the great non-Buddhists, and remains without obstruction or defilement; manifesting his path and practice in other buddha-fields, he is not stained by desire or attachment, and he gives rise to skillful means for the sake of the people of the world, desiring to bring them to liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva possessed such a mind of loving-kindness; all that serves as the cause for omniscience arises from skillful means.
Thereupon, he spoke these verses:
"Hearing various sounds, his countenance did not change."
Even that which is firm does not endure for long; how much less so this body of mine today?
Having first received this Dharma, I have faith in the World-Honored One;
thus great wisdom has arisen, and all fetters and afflictions have been removed.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva practices benevolence, he recognizes its merit and does not forget it; thus he possesses this wisdom, desiring to repay that kindness by performing even small meritorious deeds. He never forgets them nor does he ever exhaust them, just as planting a few grains of seed ensures they are not forgotten for a lifetime.
In the past, when the Bodhisattva was seeking the Unsurpassed Way, he was dwelling in a secluded and quiet place where there was a Bodhisattva-parrot who constantly resided in a tree.

At that time, the wind blew against the trees, causing them to rub against one another; from this friction, fire emerged. The fire gradually grew more intense until it reached the mountain crags, and all the lush green trees were completely consumed by the flames. A thick smoke arose, its color extremely brilliant and never subsiding for long, like sunlight rising together with dust and smoke. All the large and small trees were utterly burnt away without remainder, like the time when heaven and earth are molten and ruined; in an instant, those who saw or heard of it were filled with terror, and the objects being burned were exhausted as they went, until every single tree had perished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having taken the form of a parrot, reflected thus during the night:

"Just as a flying bird that perches upon this tree should have a sense of returning to it, and should give rise to a feeling of gratitude when associated with it, how much more so for us who have dwelt within it throughout the long night—could we not even extinguish this fire?"
"Now is precisely the time for me.

Displaying his majestic power, he went to the great ocean, took up water with both wings, and sprinkled it upon that fire; whether sprinkling with his wings or with his mouth, he rushed back and forth from east to west.
At that time, a deity spoke this verse:
"This fire is most fiercely blazing; Its clouds of smoke cannot be approached.
Though you possess such a virtuous mind, You still cannot extinguish it."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, in the form of a parrot, said to that deva:
"While dwelling in these mountains, I have never failed to repay their kindness;
how could I abandon them and allow fire to burn this forest?"
"Now that I possess this power, I wish to extinguish this fire;
it is not for nothing that I dwell on this mountain, for I desire to repay his kindness.
At that time, the tree deity spoke again:
"This bird is compassionate and its form is most upright;
this accords with the way of humans, a rarity in this world.
At that time, the deva, having had this thought, spoke to the Śuka Bodhisattva:
"Knowing that you possess kindness and compassion, I shall extinguish the fire for your sake;
out of pity, with such a heart, I shall quickly put out the flames.
At that time, a great cloud arose, out of pity for that parrot.
"Now I shall extinguish this fire so that his vow may bear fruit;
how much more so when he attains equal and perfect enlightenment?
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“At that time, the Tathāgata possessed such a heart of kindness and compassion;
all who gave rise to joy were honored by gods and humans.
Because he was able to reach the other shore, he remained far removed from birth, old age, and sickness.”
"Deep faith is already firm, / Governing the lands of the ten directions.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva dons the *kāṣāya*, he serves as a model for the people of the world; for the sake of all sentient beings, he transforms the mundane to pursue the Way—this is the great banner and canopy.
Thus, having renounced his kingdom, wife, and children, he left the household life to study the Way in order to cross over all doubts.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva donned the *kāṣāya*, there was such an increase in his meritorious qualities. He had previously heard that in the past, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, while wandering through gardens where flowers and fruits were in full bloom, desired to leave the household life.

Within that garden, people wander about; though a Buddha has appeared in the world, they never tire of beholding him. The populace is flourishing, yet within that garden there is no clamor of many voices.

He wore the three-colored *kāṣāya* robe with a clear and pure countenance; his ears were attuned to the sounds of liberation, which were gentle and harmonious. His lifespan was limited, yet all beings took refuge in him. For the sake of all suffering, he subdued his anger. His complexion was like that of red copper; as he breathed with all his might, smoke and wind arose. Having seen this form, he spoke thus:
"That which arises in conjunction with my mind—this state of mind is my liberation."
At that time, because there are many virtues in protecting the *kāṣāya* and abandoning those defilements, for this reason he spoke this verse:
"Nor does one recognize one's own name, Yet it corresponds with that [name];
Nor is it well-washed or cleansed, But having been subdued, it has come here."
Swiftly subdue that fruit; cut yourself away without regret.
Even if you speak kind words of instruction, they will surely bring about your own ruin.
Though you may hold such views, explain this meaning to me.
"I shall bestow [my body] upon him, and endure this karma of suffering and affliction.
Having thus cut himself and subdued his own mind, he spoke these words and uttered this verse:
"Do not harbor the distress of suffering; such stinginess and envy exist [only in the mind]."
"Though this fruit is small, its retribution for evil is limitless.

At that time, the Bodhisattva delighted in dwelling in quiet and secluded places. While observing that garden, he found it pure, free from crowds and distractions, and devoid of worldly affairs; those who traveled there all felt a sense of awe. His heart was filled with joy, as he had previously heard that there was a place where sages resided, which was supremely wondrous and beyond compare, as described in detail above.
In the dwelling place of the seer, all his possessions were completely exhausted without remainder, so he departed from this park and grove.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, who had not yet attained fixed certainty in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, took the body of a rabbit; at that moment, the rabbit lived in dependence upon the seer.
At that time, seeing the seer descending from the mountain, the hare addressed him with a verse, saying:
"The human body dwelling in this world Is most wondrous and beyond compare;
Having already attained birth among men, One ought to dwell in mountain forests and groves."
Excellent is this seer, with a countenance of noble appearance and serene presence;
free from all blemishes and evils, he has brought his own mind under control.
Regarding the arising of violence, he knows its proper limits.
One who is able to subdue their own mind has no perception of objective realms.

"Having already abandoned the objects of sensory enjoyment, for the sake of renunciation I seek the path to liberation; with a resolute mind, do not abandon the nectar [of the Dharma]. Cast off that longing for worldly things, and dwell together with those of merit in the mountain forests; such is the samādhi wherein the mind is free from all distraction."

Having already dwelt in these mountain forests, you should take delight in them; just as the moon illuminates the night and the sun shines during the day, the Muni, endowed with kindness and compassion, should dwell in these mountain forests.
“However, when you were young and strong, you dwelt here in these mountain forests; now that you have grown old, for what reason do you abandon this place and depart?
At that time, the seer spoke these words:
“I have brought my own mind under control.”
Filled with even greater joy, he spoke these words:
"If the seer were to depart, who would find delight in dwelling here?
The Bodhisattva rabbit then spoke this verse:
"I now have no such beans, nor fine rice or other grains;
yet my mind can subdue itself, and I wish to dwell here in these mountain forests.
At that time, having attained *abhisambodhi*, he remained there, illuminating the world and delighting in that secluded dwelling; for this reason, one should dwell in those mountain forests.
Then he spoke this verse:
"The realm is most orderly; Though one practices austerities in the mountain forests, Always delighting in dwelling in quietude, One should reflect upon one's own conduct."
"The merit of the body of liberation, with a mind and heart always harmonious and joyful, and wisdom that is most subtle and profound—one should draw near to the mountain forests.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, possessing such a spirit of friendship and constantly harboring a heart of loving-kindness, reflected upon his own birth as it truly occurred. Just as it was heard in the extensive discourse on the mountain forests in the Sūtras, he then thought:
"This mountain forest has no fruits; the liberation of all dharmas is liberation through the dharma of patience.
At that time, throughout the long night, the Bodhisattva possessed this mind of loving-kindness; liberated in all dharmas, he did not cause any harm or disturbance to those people.

Sitting upright there, he remained motionless in contemplation; with a bird’s nest above his head, he perceived the bird nursing its young atop him, and fearing constantly that the eggs might fall, he did not move his body.
At that time, he observes and then leaves his body to go to that place, remaining motionless; through the power of diligent effort, he gives rise to the desire to gather them in.
At that time, although the bird has already grown wings, it does not abandon its efforts until it can fly.
"Now that I have practiced this loving-kindness to its conclusion, what marvel is there? Nor do I feel any fear; such a thing has never been done by sentient beings before.
Knowing this for himself, he then spoke this verse:
"He is able to accomplish this deed, And thus he is great among men."
Nor does he disturb or afflict others; this virtue is unsurpassed.
Therefore, that World-Honored One is the foremost among deities;
thus, at the site of the Bodhimanda, his merits are spontaneously and fully perfected.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva practices compassion, he possesses the power and strength to bear a heavy burden; seeking out a place, he thinks: "I shall deliver all sentient beings and increase their merit; I shall free those who are powerless from various sufferings, removing their worldly grief and anxiety; I shall act as a protector for those without protection; I shall provide hope for those without hope; and I shall provide strength for those who lack it."
For those afflicted by various diseases, he acts as the King of Physicians; for the elderly, he manifests youthful vigor; and for the young, he manifests great strength.

It was heard that when the World-Honored One was traveling, surrounded before and behind by countless bhikṣus, a fire broke out and burned a park and its pavilions. When the bhikṣus saw the great fire and rising smoke, they each ran toward the World-Honored One; some extolled the World-Honored One and stood before the Tathāgata.
Those bhikṣus who stood before the Tathāgata as spectators then spoke this verse:
“As I am without peer, Possessing the merits of the three periods of time,
By these words of utmost sincerity, May evil be swiftly stilled.”
Having spoken these verses, the fire of that mass of flames was immediately extinguished.

At that time, the bhikṣus marveled at what they had never before experienced, saying, "All this is through the power of the World-Honored One's grace. Rejoicing in the Tathāgata, they each spoke these verses in praise, exclaiming, "It is unprecedented!"
The World-Honored One said:
"When the bhikṣus were in a secluded place amidst various objects and manifold forms, at that time I had not yet attained perfect enlightenment; at that time, I was the elephant Kuñjara."
Since his birth, he has been youthful and independent, delighting in bestowing gifts upon others and seeking subtle and wondrous practices.

At that time, the kingdom of Caṇpā was densely populated and its lands were fertile; it abounded in bamboo, reeds, and trees of great height. Then, a fire broke out with such extreme intensity that it gradually spread to the mountains and marshes; such was the transformation that occurred, as described at length in the Sūtra.

At that time, there was a flock of birds, each having recently laid eggs; their wings and feathers had not yet grown, though some had just begun to sprout. Some had fallen to the ground, and some had broken heads or tails; they were unable to fly. Others were suffering from hunger. Seeing the fire blazing fiercely, they all desired to fly away.
When I saw this fire at that time, I did not protect my own body; for throughout countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, my merit has possessed such a protective resolve.
At that moment, within that purity, I gave rise to this thought: "May these sentient beings be delivered from this great calamity."
At that time, I extinguished this fire, and the fire was immediately extinguished.
At that time, I extinguished this fire in that garden while practicing this mind of compassion; how much more so do I today achieve great compassion?
"Today the fire shall be extinguished.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Born from that which is slight, one fundamentally observes all transformations."
"All things shall utterly perish; have compassion for all living beings.
As he spoke, that fire was immediately extinguished. Not long after the fire had been put out, he used the light of wisdom to extinguish the fires of the world.

At that time, for the sake of birth and death, when the Bodhisattva was about to be born, he sought to rescue and deliver sentient beings by contemplating the root of the suffering of birth. He had previously heard that within the empty and quiet mountain forests there dwelt crows, deer, pigeons, and snakes.
In that place there was a rishi-bodhisattva who always dwelt therein, eating fruit and drinking water.
At that time, the crow went to where the rishi was, stood to one side, and spoke these words:
"What suffering is there in the world?"
At that time, the crows spoke thus:
"Hunger is the greatest suffering; by what causes and conditions does this suffering arise?
Each of us shall speak of it in turn."

The body is utterly exhausted and tormented, the faculties are unsettled, one cannot speak with the mouth nor hear with the ears, and one is constantly preoccupied with thoughts; therefore, hunger is the greatest suffering.
"This body, afflicted by suffering, is scorched by fire; because of this famine and this incurable illness, they are all interconnected, and each possesses such suffering as this.
At that time, the deer spoke these words:

"Fear is suffering. That which is called fear is when one dwells alone and constantly harbors fear upon seeing a hunter; the impurities of body and mind cause one to constantly dread the loss of this life, and furthermore, one fears the hunter’s desire to kill and harm oneself."
What stability is there in this body?
It must dwell in impermanence, rushing hither and thither.
From what does this terror arise?
They constantly maintain this thought:

"All those who possess existence have these conditioned formations; they abandon all such bodies. We, too, possess these bodies and are perpetually filled with dread, finding not a moment's peace; all of this is the suffering of decay caused by what was originally created, and thus we experience such terror."
"For this reason, agitation and fear constitute suffering.
At that time, the pigeon spoke these words:

"Sensual desire is the greatest suffering; though one may find pleasure within it and perceive its objects as pure, even when contemplating one's dwelling place, there is no escape from this affliction of desire."
This desire is like fire, and also like clarified butter placed in a vessel; when ignited, it blazes furiously and, through whatever speech there is, becomes attached to the mind.

The fire of desire is likewise: it attaches itself to the mind, consumes the physical form, and increases all fetters. For incalculable eons, one is joined with the delusions of desire, which fiercely burn the human body.
"For this reason, desire is the greatest suffering. At that time, the snake spoke these words: "Hatred is the greatest suffering.

That which is called hatred brings harm to human life regardless of noble or lowly status; it increases the roots of all sins. One's physical appearance and complexion constantly change; one is always intent on killing. With a frowning brow and bloodshot eyes, one’s teeth are long and sharp, making one loathsome to behold. Shaking the head and moving the body, one sighs deeply and spits venom. One’s flesh and skin are entirely ablaze with the fire of hatred. All people in the world dislike seeing such a person. One always lurks in empty places; one is angry when hungry and angry when full. One’s gaze is malevolent, and such are its transformations. It is like a fire burning through mountains and marshes; this fire of hatred is just the same."
"For this reason, anger is suffering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having contemplated this with profound wisdom, spoke these verses:
"All things are entirely suffering; One should attend closely to their true nature."
Birth is inevitably accompanied by suffering; listen now to what I say.
Just as this great affliction brings boundless distress, so too is everything rooted in birth; therefore, birth is not true.

If there are those who will certainly accomplish the path of a bodhisattva, they shall circulate through birth and death while protecting and pitying all sentient beings with kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; possessing swift wisdom that is free from obstruction, they maintain a courageous mind to cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) without weariness; they teach and transform others without harboring doubt, always maintaining impartial vision, and their resolve is so firm that it cannot be broken. Having attained its flavor, they do not lose their aspiration; being capable and resilient, they discern all phenomena without distortion or leakage, and they achieve great wisdom, bestowing liberation of mind without regret or change of heart.

In all forms of giving, he was like King Śibi, who constantly cultivated pure conduct without ever growing weary; in the perfection of the power of patience, he was like King Mahādeva; in the integrity of his precepts, he was like the ṛṣi Kṣānti; and in his constant delight in renunciation and his serene countenance, he was like the scholar Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.

Furthermore, if one’s mind remains free from attachment amidst affection and reverence—just as King Mahāsudassana wandered and transformed the secular world; just as King Gopīnda delighted in the Dharma; just as the young brahmin Uttara took pleasure in secluded places; just as the sound of musical instruments was pure and resonant; and just as the Bodhisattva Sujāta let out a lion’s roar amidst the great assembly—all shall attain liberation and reach the realm of Nirvāṇa. Endowed with all merits, they will surely achieve completion; their virtues on the Path will increase manifold, and they will fulfill the practices of a Bodhisattva.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Free from any intent to harm, The Bodhisattva’s merit is pure;
His will and nature are firm and steadfast, Like the sun emitting its radiance."
"Delighting in such a Dharma, a field of merit free from defilement, out of compassion for the people of the world, he thus proclaims these karmic deeds.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, harboring no fear, descended from the Tuṣita Heaven; observing that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, his mind was free from distracted thoughts. He constantly observed himself, knowing the place from which he had come, and further knew of himself that he would not again receive a womb-born existence.
There is this True Dharma; having thoroughly investigated its source, the mind is free from defilement and attachment.

Even while descending into the mother’s womb and dwelling therein, there is no distracted thought. Therein, one contemplates the violation of precepts as unwholesome conduct and the upholding of precepts as purity, yet remains entirely free from attachment.
Within the womb, he practices no impure conduct, just as a lotus flower is unstained by water.

Having frequently generated the aspiration for the Path therein, he possesses this wisdom; the sons of the gods constantly guard him, and the gods of Tuṣita come in succession to attend and protect him, manifesting sexual impurity while delighting in the cultivation of pure conduct.

Ever since the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb, the lady’s body has never known impurity. The Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts is exceedingly pure; his mind is free from any intent to harm, and he practices his vows with profound discernment and utmost sincerity. As he desires to leave the household life, the Great Honored Ones, the Wondrous Devas, and the Sons of Heaven all provide support, ensuring the purity of the womb and freedom from affliction.

When he took seven steps with his feet, he conceived the intent to leave the household life and immediately surveyed the four quarters, thinking: "Toward which direction should I now proceed so that there may be no further suffering?

At that moment, a fragrant pool appeared naturally for him to bathe; this was all brought about by the merit of his previous lives. The heavens rained down *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata, whereupon he spoke these verses:
"Through countless ages of toil and exertion, For the sake of saving those sentient beings..."
The wheel turns without measure, bringing peace and security to devas and humans.
All the celestial musicians attain hearts of joy;
the fragrant wheel turns before him, subduing all demonic adversaries.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva descended from the Tuṣita Heaven, the hosts of Brahmā deities all attended upon him as his retinue; this is the first sign when the World-Honored One is surrounded by the multitudes of humans and devas.
If a bodhisattva descends from the Tuṣita Heaven, the earth shakes greatly.
When the World-Honored One awakens, and the afflictions of sentient beings are free from defilement, this first auspicious sign is that the earth shakes greatly.
Those classes of sentient beings will never again give rise to afflictions; this supreme bliss is the first auspicious sign.

When the Bodhisattva descends from the Tuṣita Heaven, a great radiance illuminates the world-realm; this is the first auspicious sign of the mark of the light of wisdom. That all dark and obscure places become clearly visible is likewise a mark of wisdom.
When the Bodhisattva first took birth and walked seven steps with his feet raised, this was an auspicious sign of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
At that time, when the Bodhisattva surveyed the four directions, this was an auspicious sign of the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*).
At that time, when the Bodhisattva laughed loudly, he manifested the auspicious response of saving sentient beings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva saw in a dream this world as his bed and Mount Sumeru as his footstool, with his hands and feet hanging beyond the four seas; this was the auspicious response of the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma, which dispels the worldly notion of permanence.

Furthermore, he dreamed that a *tinduka* tree grew from his navel, its branches covering the three thousandfold world system; this was an auspicious omen of the site of enlightenment, revered by devas and humans alike.
He dreamed that a great multitude of flying birds surrounded him from all sides, all being of one color; this manifested as an auspicious omen of the accomplishment of the assembly.
He dreamed of insects with black heads and white bodies; this manifested as an auspicious omen of the accomplishment of the assembly of upāsakas.
Furthermore, he dreamed that he was walking upon a mountain peak, a portentous sign of his present attainment of gain and freedom from stinginess.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"A portent such as this has never occurred before; He possesses great merit."
That which arises must necessarily perish; it is the shifting of suffering and joy.
Seeing all this, one rejoices, for a Buddha will surely appear, like the sun clearing away clouds and mist, so that no further dust remains.

At that time, the Bodhisattva’s resolve was irreversible as he had declared; like the new moon rising from the darkness, revered by all people, he rose from his seat, desiring to go forth into homelessness. Then, he gave rise to this thought:
"This is my final existence; this is the third joy."
At that time, as the Bodhisattva descended from his high couch, he likewise gave rise to this thought:
"This is the most lofty and expansive of couches.
Just as when the Bodhisattva departed through the city gate, at that moment he formed this reflection:
"I shall not return until I have attained the Way.
Just as the Bodhisattva untied his jeweled necklace to give to Chandaka, he then further thought:
"This precious robe is the very last thing I possess."
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva gave the horse to Chandaka, he then formed this thought:
"This is the horse upon which I shall ride hereafter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took a sword in his right hand and shaved his own hair, and at that moment, the Bodhisattva again formed this thought:
"These are my very last remaining hair and beard.
At that time, the Bodhisattva exchanged his precious robes for deerskin to use as a *kāṣāya*. Then, the Bodhisattva again had this thought:
"This is truly the garment I ought to wear."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he then forms this thought:
"I shall not rise from this seat until I understand the full-lotus posture and have attained all-knowledge."
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Accumulating merit begins from what is small, And one shall obtain immeasurable blessings;
Just as drops of water gradually swell, They will surely become a great river.”
"Observing these various kinds of things, which are produced by conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one should consume the flavor of the nectar of immortality and eliminate all evil poisons.

When the All-Knowing One attained Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), he observed that the world is impermanent, suffering, and empty. Having attained Perfect Enlightenment, he was free from all afflictions. Regarding the causal conditions through which he attained Perfect Enlightenment, he realized that all that arises must return to cessation. He fully awakened to the knowledge that all who die are subject to rebirth.

At that time, the discerning eye-consciousness forms such an awareness: it accords with the high and low states produced by sentient beings and the nature of their objective spheres; having already accomplished this through wisdom, it is free from doubt. Regarding those objects of awareness, its fundamental causes and conditions, and so forth, its perfect awakening is without limit or boundary.

At that time, there arises a multitude of wisdom; one realizes that there is a path circulating in the world, and one realizes that this path is immovable. At that moment, one completely transcends all suffering.

Distinguishing each and every object of perception, whether for one eon, a hundred eons, or a hundred thousand eons, the flow of his mind cannot be diverted; his mind is free from attachment and remains undisturbed. His wisdom is immeasurable and he does not abandon wisdom; his mind skillfully discerns as it ranges through the realms of objects, seeking their appropriate means. His retribution is immeasurable, his wisdom is fully perfected, and there is no obstruction whatsoever.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:

"Awakening to all things, They are likewise immeasurable; Coming and going, circulating everywhere, Without any obstruction, Fully awakening to everything— This is the supreme object of contemplation."
To eliminate the suffering of the three realms and to illuminate the world—who else could discern this?
Only the Buddha can understand it.
If you seek the subtle and wondrous, you should seek the Tathāgata.
"The Tathāgata, according to the occasion, acts in accordance with them; that which is to be accomplished shall never regress.

At that time, the World-Honored One wandered alone without companion and without teacher. His merit was immeasurable as he sought to instruct sentient beings. He had fully perfected the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; having achieved the single wisdom, he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Most honored, subtle, and peerless, he awakened to and understood the fundamental source of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and everything was completely fulfilled.

With mindfulness unshakable, one discriminates all phenomena through wisdom and transcends all fetters and afflictions; being subtle and supreme, one eloquently expounds all practices; therefore, it is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā).
Having already attained omniscience, he focuses his single mind to understand all phenomena and sever all fetters and latent tendencies; therefore, it is called "the extinction of all.
Having eliminated existence and non-existence as well as craving for existence, and being without companion, he has accomplished all meritorious virtues and wisdom.

They protect all sentient beings equally, like parents loving their children; through the successive power of their merit, they achieve perfection. Because they are free from greed and arrogance, they are called "Supreme. They manifest the Eightfold Noble Path and turn the Wheel of Dharma.

This is illustrated by the analogy of a shadow: it does not exist before the sun, nor does it exist before the darkness. It is the same in this case; all fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*) do not coexist with the Path. For this reason, the Wheel of Dharma is turned.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Each and every merit is fully possessed; It is beyond all measure.
How much more so his inconceivable form, Complete with every mark."
"Just as the light of the moon illuminates the dark and hidden places, and as various jewels gather in the ocean, so too are the virtues of the Śākya clan.

Having thus contemplated dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), he attained the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) regarding the twelve links of causation. With a mind that had firmly eliminated the dust and defilements yet still gave rise to the wisdom of attachment, his thoughts roamed within his heart; or, giving rise to the wisdom of outflows (*sāsrava-jñāna*), he practiced various asceticisms and thereby attained the path of liberation. Knowing that he must extinguish all fetters (*saṃyojana*), he was free from the notions of suffering or pleasure, and possessed the notion of rest.

Wisdom gains increase through non-self; wisdom and its associated consciousness perceive the emptiness of body and mind. Wisdom seeks to subdue the impulses of youth, and when the mind becomes defiled by attachment, it gives rise to the wisdom of reliance. Through self-reflection and decisive understanding, it extinguishes all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), giving rise to the wisdom of clear insight to subdue those fetters. It gives rise to the wisdom of rising and ceasing to cross over to the other shore, and thus gives rise to the wisdom of lightness and elevation to realize the awakening of one's own body.

Sentient beings, through the thorough examination of the truths, give rise to the knowledge of cessation; by taking those truths as their object of contemplation, they attain various subtle dhyānas. Because of that contemplation, they give rise to the knowledge that crosses to the other shore. Their minds attain aspiration, and others likewise attain aspiration; all share the same track, and with the mind resting upon its object, they reach the wisdom of the four great elements in their state of cessation.

Contemplating that which accords with its characteristics, one reaches the further shore; attaining the wisdom of the divine ear, one transcends those realms. Having attained uniformity in that single practice, one reaches the further shore of equality. Attaining the wisdom of the divine nose, one relies upon that consciousness to possess discerning wisdom; through the wisdom of knowing the minds of others, one knows their thoughts. All being pure, there is that which is practiced; desiring to transform sentient beings, one thereby attains the wisdom of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). For the sake of those virtuous forms, one displays the four great elements and thereby attains the wisdom of the divine eye.
