When the mind has realization, one observes the purity of the precepts and attains the wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), the merit of a great seer.
Born from the seeds of that samādhi, it transcends all realms of samādhi; because it desires to cause them to grow and flourish, sentient beings rejoice and thereby attain ultimate wisdom.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Various people harbor different thoughts; As they draw near and stand before him, He discerns their diverse natures And reveals them to the Great Seer."
"One should be aware of that karma; by abandoning all dust-like hindrances, one fully realizes the observation of the mind—how excellent is this supreme among men!

He is such as he truly is, without craving or desire, and does not associate with such craving and desire. Furthermore, he has no ill will or intent to harm, and no delusion. He perceives those afflictions and is free from flattery, always maintaining gentleness. He does not praise himself, and his speech issues forth as wholesome instruction, free from conceptualization. Having removed the notion of hope, he is without a sense of "self" or "other. He does not injure others, having attained liberation for himself, remaining impartial toward all. Possessing a heart of compassion, he accomplishes everything he undertakes.

He does not lack compassion, yet he possesses a heart of pity; he is free from defiled thoughts, yet maintains a protective mind. Because he desires to deliver and protect sentient beings, he possesses the mind of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); because he is fully endowed with the precepts, he possesses the mind of wishlessness (*apranihita*); because his wisdom is moistening and nourishing, he possesses the mind of signlessness (*animitta*). He is neither stained by anything nor given to frivolous play, yet for the sake of the people of the world, he does not abandon such playful discourse. Avoiding all evil karma, he teaches the Dharma; his observance of the precepts is perfected without deficiency or leakage. His accomplishment in samādhi is unwavering; his accomplishment in wisdom has reached the further shore in every respect. Endowed with the ten powers, he is invincible; having attained the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), he is free from any timidity. Walking alone through the three realms, he lets out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
Thereupon, he spoke these verses:
"Just as this great ocean is vast, expansive, and most subtle,
So too are all the virtues of the Ten Powers, Which are observed by the wise."
Just as when the waves of this great ocean surge and stir,
a person standing on its far shore cannot fathom its merits. —
From the *Saṃgharakṣitasaṃyukta-sūtra*, Volume One.
*Saṃgharakṣa-saṃgīti-sūtra*, Middle Volume, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kapiśī during the Fu Qin dynasty, et al.
At that time, how did the World-Honored One distinguish the birth-city? It is what is called the exhaustion of birth and non-birth, the severance [of the cycle].

He crossed the moat of the blood-shore and the various wooden palisades; he was firmly attached by the delusion through which desire and lust proceed. Delusion served as his city, surrounded by the lack of shame and lack of remorse, its foundations unbroken and without leakage. The five hindrances were its gates, obscuring sentient beings. It was filled with various desires and the chariot of anger. Surrounded by countless diverse multitudes, he raised the banner of pride and blew the conch of darkness as he wandered east and west. With his body entangled by various false views, he maintained these characteristics and reflected thus with careful contemplation:

“The various gardens and groves of sentient beings are extremely subtle; the mind finds delight therein, and one reaches that place of pleasure, or perhaps reaches a place of famine. This is the path traveled by merchants seeking what they desire; having crossed over the realm, they proceed to that place where there is the fruit of liberation through gain. Encountering the calamities of intense heat, cold, wind, and rain, there is the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death. One belongs to birth and death as one heads toward all realms of existence, just like that boat drifting east and west with the current.
Within that state, one should form this thought: ‘Doubt is difficult to enter; one should neither join with it nor fight against it.’”

At that time, the World-Honored One, through samādhi, observed that such power is difficult to obstruct or destroy; he reached that realm where all states of death are completely extinguished, and wherein all that is auspicious is free from conditioned activity.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"In the land of birth there are manifold perceptions; Having already crossed over, one is delivered from the river.
Its moat is filled with blood, As deep as the bottomless sea."
"Hearing the sounds throughout the three periods of time, Surrounded by the city of folly,
When the World-Honored One observed them, He went forth to destroy them with expedient wisdom.
At that time, how did the World-Honored One subdue the hosts of Māra?

That is to say: they bathe in the pool of the eight liberations; through virtuous conduct, free from defilement and attachment, they gradually reach the gates of liberation; they dwell together with the supreme, excellent teachings; their fame is heard afar; they wear the garment of shame and remorse; they take emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness as their jeweled crown; they are fully endowed with the power of patience; their countenance is always serene and joyful, their face full and radiant; they manifest the Eightfold Noble Path; and they are perfumed by various fragrances and arrayed in diverse garments.

Having already realized that the fetters and latent tendencies are defilements, he mounts the chariot of the precepts, with right view guiding him forward, surrounded by merit. Using the power of wisdom to drive that chariot, his mindfulness is unwavering as he awakens those sentient beings through skillful means.

Throughout the three realms, those who hear their teaching are all pursued by their fundamental practice. Taking the foundations of mindfulness as armor, they grasp the banner of the Dharma in hand and brandish the sword of wisdom. Using wholesome thoughts as a fly-whisk, they blow that Dharma conch with the ten powers and fearlessness. Through the power of the supernormal faculties, they attain mastery over the three thousandfold world system; they skillfully distinguish the seven riches, and their four analytical eloquences are inexhaustible.

If the fetters and afflictions arise, one can immediately cause them to be extinguished; the merit of bestowing wealth and resources is incalculable, a hundred thousand million times greater, just like a great elephant adorning its body, gathering in sentient beings and establishing them in wholesome karma.
With a mind like a leaping lion, free from timidity, he opens the gates of the Dharma; at times manifesting terror, at times manifesting ferocity.

Internally free from anger, yet possessing great wealth and treasures, he appears like a rākṣasa demon baring its fangs and claws. Having such forms, he does not distinguish between his own kin; he may appear as a cat or a fox, or as a host of māras. He may have the head of a lion with the body of a tiger, or be a seven-step snake. Standing tall, he desires to cause harm, the fire of his wrath blazing intensely. Among these various transformations, some carry mountains or vomit fire; some are dogs full of arrogance; some have one body with two heads, or play with their tongues and glare with wide eyes; some have long bodies and short necks, or the form of a garuḍa.
Some hold swords and staves, or wheels and vajras; others let out lion-roars, desiring to harm people.

They manifest such monstrous transformations, some taking the form of yak-cows, while others take the form of kumbhāṇḍas holding great flaming torches in their hands. All are clad in armor, their eyes red with light emitting from them as they brandish great flames, seeking every opportunity to inflict injury.

Those rākṣasas all have two wings; various drum-sounds of many kinds fill the void of space. Like *yātudhāna* spirits, they wear such bells around their necks, or take the form of youths holding iron wheels. With their various evil deeds and diverse appearances, they are like the sea-god holding the sun and moon in his hands, yet they are subdued by the sword of wisdom.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"With fetters exhausted, there is no fear; One finds joy therein through the long night.
Various forms and shapes undergo transformation; Various colors are inexhaustible."
"Such transformations arise as the result of karma created in the past;
yet, by grasping the sword of wisdom in one's hand, one can immediately subdue them.
At that time, how did the World-Honored One cross the River of Ashes?

This refers to when crossing the Ashes River (*pāṃśunadī*): one eliminates longing and ill-will, contemplates that the river is entirely impure, and completely abandons all various perceptions. By taking those manifold [perceptions] as conditions until they are forever exhausted without remainder, what is observed is subtle and exquisite. At that time, one cannot cross the ocean of birth and death, which is difficult to traverse even through collective effort; these are all the karmic actions created in the past, cherished by the mind. With the two kinds of grass—*gaśa* and *jośa*—flowing with the current, one cuts off longing and removes the sorrow-tree at the riverbank where the grass abounds.

Such are the actions performed by this body: the flourishing trees and the various kinds of wailing; the hands grasping stones fashioned through hundreds of thousands of unwholesome deeds are likewise the product of unwholesome conduct. Just as those insects in the ocean seek a place of pleasure, they are turned back by desire and harmed within the field of existence.

With blazing anger, their eyes are like red copper; though they cultivate a mind of purity and are filled with thoughts of desire, they become a river of ashes and various steep, difficult pits and channels.

Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—all these outflows (*āsrava*) are like swords and spears spread across that ground. There is great darkness and no luster, as they follow the current up and down such a river.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having long sought to distance himself from the immeasurable cycles of birth and death throughout his bodhisattva career, gave rise to this thought:

"This River of Ashes is extremely perilous; its bed is strewn with thorns, and it is utterly dark and devoid of light. As these multitudes of people follow the current therein, I shall now cut off its flow."

Having made such a vow, he sought skillful means; taking the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) as his guide for the world, he further applied skillful means to fully master the stage of the prohibitions (*śīla-bhūmi*) and established himself therein. Observing the four directions through the Four Noble Truths, he attained definitive discernment and, like a mountain of untainted vision (*anāsrava-darśana*), sat firm upon the shore of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Having already stood upon the shore of that birth-and-death, and having fully distinguished the wholesome karma, equal karma, equal skillful means, the *samādhi* of delight, and the Eightfold Noble Path, they desire to reach the other shore by the power of their spiritual feet (*ṛddhipāda*). With the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) free from fear, they abide in the state of *nirvāṇa*, dwelling in liberation, dhyāna, and *samādhi*. There, amidst the flourishing profusion of various flowers, those who do not emerge into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) possess awakened knowledge and discernment.

At that time, for those who uphold the sūtras, the World-Honored One is the seal of Dīpaṃkara Buddha; he is named Anuttarapuṣpa-vibhāsa-anuvyañjana Buddha, born into that lineage, and is capable of preaching the Dharma.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Though possessing power that knows no limit, One should harbor a heart of fear;
The River of Ashes is deep and bottomless, Yet the foolish take delight in wandering there."

"At that time, by the power of the World-Honored One, he delivered those who were drowning; having already reached the place of peace and security, he expounded its essentials for the sake of humanity.

The great merchant’s original vows were fulfilled; his disposition was gentle and mild, and he adorned himself with various merits. Adapting to the times to transform others, he observed the roots of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) among the classes of sentient beings. Having attained wisdom, he subdued those evil fetters and led them toward the good. His timely wisdom was perfected, and he skillfully observed the faculties (*indriya*), which are eternally subtle and wondrous. Relying well upon that wisdom, he was skilled in the wisdom of inquiry, perfected in respectful patience, and adept at explaining the meaning of the foremost Dharma. He was perfectly accomplished in the eloquence of explaining the Dharma and its meaning, perfected in the ultimate wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya*), and perfected in the analytical knowledge of the Dharma (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).

What is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*) refers to the thorough discernment of various kinds of sounds within the collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*). This eloquence regarding meaning is excellent, just as these collections of names, phrases, and phonemes are all made to lead toward what is wholesome.

He is skilled in the eloquence of sounds and resonance; he is endowed with these three types of eloquence and possesses the liberation of samādhi. He is skillful in turning toward the Path and knows the minds of others well. Having accomplished that wisdom, he remains unshakable even when receiving a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). First inquiring into their meaning, he expounds the Dharma without obstruction, leading them toward the single path of wisdom. They all achieve accomplishment, achieving the accomplishment of prophecy, and accomplishing the wisdom of non-abiding as they skillfully enter into all dharmas.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“There exists the jewel of manifest wisdom, And the eloquence that explains all meanings;
In its serenity, there is none equal to the Buddha, And in its merit, there is no peer.”
"The fundamental departure of the mind is without coming; how could one cause it to become pure wisdom?
To rescue beings from worldly karma, one opens the nectar for the world.
At that time, how did the World-Honored One preach the Dharma?

That is to say, whatever was previously sought is entirely fulfilled; for them, he expounds the meaning of the virtue of liberation, which is true and not false, complete in its flavor and excellence.

According to the appropriate occasion, he gradually provides the corresponding meanings, analyzing them all in the interim so that the preceding and following parts are mutually consistent. He teaches various and manifold realms according to their wishes, in accordance with the capacity of each individual.
The meaning of all dharmas possesses courageous intent; there are various transformations of wisdom that bear fruit, and the discernment of the dharma-realm is without limit.

That which is enacted by the All-Knowing One gives rise to such dharmas without any dependence; having removed all longing, one awakens to the practice of the dharma-activities and does not praise oneself. One preaches the Dharma to sentient beings to resolve the root and branches of their afflictions, accomplishing the three bases of mindfulness without harboring expectations. Gathering those multitudes, they marvel at what has never been before, receiving offerings and respect from devas and humans, and dwelling well in that state.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“As that Dharma of eternal cessation, Proclaimed by the mouth of the Most Victorious One;
Well-expounded and firm in practice, Wisdom and the like are immeasurable.”
That is the taste of ambrosia; externally, one does not receive dust or defilement.
Having refined away all taints and impurities, there is likewise no affliction of mixed evils.

Being free from filth and corruption, having removed the nature of delusion, the mind is pure. By relinquishing external matters, one shall attain the Buddha-eye. With the mind unattached and free from wounds, having transcended the mental faculty and not creating the past, one rests therein. All things are entirely level and upright; the mind does not waver, and one attains the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Practicing austerities with a single body, he performs those practices without any notion of a self in the body; among the śrāvakas, he may hear sounds with the divine ear.

Having nothing to grasp, he gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds within the mundane world; he does not consider various conditioned activities to be a burden, and for the sake of sentient beings, he personally recognizes countless matters of past lives, just as one now enjoys all forms of sensory activity.

Or, observing forms with the divine eye, one’s manifold perceptions likewise do not waver; all fetters have been extinguished and what is non-beneficial has been manifested. Because of the vow regarding suffering, one does not create expectations, but rests in purity.

That wisdom does not abide firmly; the desire for the sphere of consciousness has already been exhausted. He causes the meaning of parinirvāṇa to circulate throughout the world, relying inwardly upon himself.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"The mind is free from delusion, Tranquil and devoid of all conditioned activities."
The mental karma awakened by the Buddha—therefore I take refuge in him.
For those people he teaches the Dharma, which is pure and free from blemish;
he wanders among the pleasure groves and various secluded places of study.

At that time, the World-Honored One was called a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Based on that field of merit, there is something hoped for, just as one relies on barley to call it a barley field or a rice field; that Buddha, the World-Honored One, is likewise so called because he is a field of merit. For this reason, he is named "Merit" (*Puṇya*).

Having accomplished hundreds of thousands of practices, this field of merit has perfected the karma of contemplation born from the faculty of wisdom and has reached the further shore. Relying upon that, he preaches the Dharma; free from notions of arising and ceasing, and devoid of the mind of "self" and "other," he eliminates the view of annihilation. With equal vision and equal resolve, he is free from the notion of such views; with equal resolve, he utters sublime words. His body is equally virtuous and free from evil; his speech is likewise unstained. Having equally perfected his body, he is free from ailment; with equal vision, he gives rise to [right understanding], and through equal speech, he accomplishes his livelihood. Because of the fruit of joy, all his actions at all times are utterly subtle and unsurpassed, making him the foremost among the great assemblies.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Merit is the foremost field, purified through incalculable eons;
The fool does not observe it, and thus falls into blindness and darkness.”
"Those who possess good faith, who receive offerings and are able to consume them for their own extinction, now dwell in peace;
they shall surely return to the place of ultimate security.

He spoke thus of the appearance of that which is most rare in the world, as extraordinary and marvelous as the *udumbara* flower. Bearing the burdens of all labors, he marveled at this unprecedented event, appearing in the midst of the world with such diligent effort. This unprecedented appearance in the world is most marvelous and without equal.

The Great Way arises and does not depend upon pratyekabuddhas; such an arising occurs in both equal and unequal places, just as when the sun rises, it shines everywhere without discriminating between pits and channels.

There is such great wisdom that shines forth, born from the most pure field of merit; thus increasing the assembly of devas, it arises in this world through the power of virtuous conduct, benefiting all classes of sentient beings by manifesting instructions and admonitions, so that the darkness of ignorance is forever extinguished without remainder.
Wishing to manifest the Path and liberate beings from birth and death, each depending upon the other, just as all sentient beings with form are fully adorned;

at that time, sentient beings were profoundly moistened, and the foremost assembly attained realization corresponding to liberation. Because the tracks of the Path had ceased all evils, he contemplated the various classes of sentient beings and the flavor of the Dharma, constructing bridges to ferry those people across.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Whosoever among the classes of sentient beings Contemplates the Tathāgata,
They all give rise to a heart of joy And immediately attain liberation from worldly afflictions."
"The foremost and most subtle merit is to delight one's circle of kinsmen, set out upon the path to Nirvāṇa, and attain liberation in stillness.
At that time, the World-Honored One possessed this liberation; because his mind was not associated with the hindrances of sensual desire, it is called "liberation."

That diligence is also free from indolence; the roots thus produced are repeatedly cultivated until they are pure and flawless, their merit being immeasurable. One does not sever the conditions for the discernment of the realm of liberation, nor does one give rise to the notion of phenomena; one's vows are fulfilled, and there is no heart of envy.

All defilements are forever exhausted and all fetters of dust are transcended. By means of wisdom, one does not abide in birth and death, yet neither does one abandon them. Through the discernment of wisdom and liberation, it is like the autumn moon illuminating the darkness, causing light to pervade even the most obscure places;
it is like flowing water that moistens all trees, which then bloom with flowers according to the season;
it is like the swift current of a river where foam swirls along with the water, filling every place it reaches as it flows.
The World-Honored One is likewise thus, possessing the swift current of liberation in *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The Buddha can extinguish all evils; Liberation is the most sublime.”
Dispelling darkness and manifesting illumination, like the moon shining brightly among the stars,
it is no different by day or night; eternally abiding and unmoving,
having attained the Dharma of liberation, wisdom shines forth upon that.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed this knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Having distinguished this knowledge of exhaustion, he thought, "I have known it; suffering and its origin have been eliminated. Taking exhaustion as his realization, he practiced the Path and uttered this exclamation: "The karmic formations previously created have treated that illness; lust, anger, and pride have been thoroughly exhausted at their source. Through equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*), lustful desire has been extinguished. This is the wisdom of Nirvana, which is true and not false."

For example, suppose there is a person who undergoes manifold sufferings and afflictions with no one able to deliver them; that person, moreover, cannot be cured because the root source of their manifest illness has not been addressed. They then form this thought: "The objective realm is subtle and wondrous. Thus, they practice all that arises therein, removing the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and severing all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

It is like a powerful man who plants the roots of various diseases such that none can withstand them; as long as he has not yet conceived the intention for skillful means, they cannot be cured. Such are the afflictions of lust, anger, and delusion, which are brought to joy through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

It is like a person who constantly fears dangerous and difficult places, where there are various kinds of suffering, afflictions, and diseases. If such a person sees a bathing pool that is pure and free from dust and filth, with cool breezes blowing on both sides of the pool, fish and dragons sporting therein so that the bottom of the water is visible, and the sky being clear and cloudless; and if within it are filled with *utpala* and *kumuda* flowers, their branches, leaves, blossoms, and fruits all growing within the water, and various such subtle and wondrous trees are born amidst them—then whoever sees this will harbor a heart of joy.

However, this person, within that bathing pool, has their suffering and afflictions removed, as well as hunger and thirst; having attained such joy, they have accomplished what was to be done. At the bottom of that bathing pool, a subtle breeze arises; observing this moment, they may either sit or lie down there.
That Blessed One is likewise thus: having completely eliminated all previously created lust, anger, and delusion, he manifests such a bathing pool at the source of birth and death. Why is this?
Regarding all sentient beings born within the three realms, they have fully accomplished the rescue from their suffering and distress, acting as a bridge for them;
furthermore, through equal vision, they are like a pure bathing pool of coolness, remaining forever unmoved by the various samādhis;
and with equal resolve, they are like fish and dragons.
His equal liberation possesses a peerless complexion;
his equal skillful means is like the *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, which one never tires of beholding;

his equal mindfulness and wisdom are like heavy clouds. He does not concern himself with worldly samādhis, yet he is surrounded by a great assembly. Just as one who reaches that most beloved bathing pool experiences great joy, so too, when he bathes or drinks from the bathing pool of the Dharma, all lust, anger, and ignorance are forever eliminated without remainder; likewise, there are no further afflictions, nor hunger or thirst, for he has accomplished such a Dharma.

Furthermore, by means of this Dharma, he bestows gifts upon sentient beings until they reach the state of Nirvana; having accomplished what was to be done, he is free from fear. Arriving at the secure place of liberation, he contemplates the bliss of reaching the realm of Nirvana without remainder, and further causes sentient beings to share in these wholesome dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, remained seated without moving.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Whatever deeds are performed day and night, I desire to bring peace to all sentient beings."
Ultimately harboring joy, one has no manifold sufferings.
How much more so while dwelling long in this world, where various afflictions constantly press upon oneself—
how could one not attain that path beyond the mundane through the wisdom that exhausts suffering?

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). As for this knowledge of non-arising: "I have known suffering and shall not seek its exhaustion again; I have abandoned the origin of suffering and shall not seek its removal again; I have realized the cessation of suffering and shall not seek its realization again; I have cultivated the path and shall not seek its cultivation again. For this reason, it is called the knowledge of non-arising.

Therefore, regarding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), that wisdom brings about the great merit and the great task of the arising and ceasing of the fundamental and derivative [phenomena]. It is like sowing grain seeds and irrigating them at the proper times; through corresponding conditions, they gradually grow, flourishing according to the seasons, or at times not arising at all.
The World-Honored One is likewise: when the seed of consciousness is burned by the fire of wisdom, each is made to correspond with its own nature to eliminate the source of birth and death.

In the sphere of consciousness, there is no desire, nor is there permanence; all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) have been exhausted. Within this interval, the mental defilements that arise are inconceivable, and what the mind has created is not created again.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"Those who give rise to the knowledge of non-arising are protected by all Buddhas;
they realize the root of suffering, which gives rise to all afflictions and calamities."
"That wisdom is without timidity, pure and without blemish;
sitting upon that seat of enlightenment, it is a mind without arising or ceasing.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the precepts, causing all the villages, cities, and people to fully uphold the prohibitive precepts. Those who had transgressed were no longer associated with those [transgressions]; their evil minds were extinguished and made to correspond with those [precepts], corresponding with the ten wholesome actions, so as to purify sentient beings until they all shared the same merit.

Having thus accomplished these manifold virtues, he possesses such merit within the assembly that there is no longer any distracted thought. Within this state, he exerts himself with vigor so that all his previous vows may attain their fruition; he causes those who are not joyful to become joyful, and for those who have already attained joy through the merits they previously cultivated under various Buddhas, he causes them to practice even more deeply.

It is unprecedented that one has appeared in the world to subdue the non-Buddhists; through the merit of liberation, he brings peace and security to all who possess a sense of shame and modesty. Because he is already established in dignified conduct and etiquette, he has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) within this very life and severed their root; having further exhausted the remaining outflows, they shall not arise again. Being in accord with the Path, he speaks thus:
"May the holy life (*brahmacarya*) endure for a long time, so that gods and humans may attain peace and security."
They received and recited all those words of instruction, and the bhikṣus avoided whatever offenses they had committed.
Having spoken thus, they provided complete protection, just as a peacock guards its feathers or a yak protects its tail.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata has established the prohibitive precepts And manifested them for the sake of the Dharma;
To practice them with the highest joy Is like gladly wearing a celestial crown.”
"If there were anyone dwelling therein who attained the intent of this samādhi, none could transgress it, just as the ocean does not overstep its shores.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a subtle and wondrous head—firm, solid, and without flaw—which one could never tire of beholding; it was indestructible like a rounded canopy. Observing the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*, it was peerless; no one could see its crown, nor could anyone grasp its appearance.
He possessed exquisite eyebrows and hair, which were well-grown and well-proportioned; his hair was fine, blue-black, and most sublime.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"When Śakra, Brahmā, and the people of the world, All gathered to behold him at birth,"
All stand beneath him, yet none can see the crown of his head.
Having never given rise to contempt or arrogance, he has become a Lion of the Śākyas;
through the retribution of this practice, he has attained this mark of the protuberance upon the head (uṣṇīṣa).

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such subtle and wondrous hair, which grew from the crown of his head; each strand was soft and fine, without any irregularity or disorder. Each was of equal length, curling to the right in spiral patterns, fully endowed with all marks and dwelling in perfect stability.

Such physical forms are exceedingly soft, subtle, and brilliantly radiant; their light shines through with no equal. They are like the fibers of a lotus stalk, which are extremely soft and subtle—nothing can cross over them, nor can they be destroyed.

Those who behold him with their eyes all obtain peace and security; his merit is foremost. Various excellent fragrances permeate him, for he is fully endowed with all manner of practices. Possessing such signs, he fulfills the conduct that is to be practiced and attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Soft and fine, neither long nor short, His hair is the color of deep blue-black;
The Tathāgata’s countenance is pure and clear, Like the bright moon appearing in a clear night sky."
Various fragrances spread afar; upon smelling them, they are all distinguished.
A subtle and gentle breeze carries the scent, like that of *rocanaka* sandalwood.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a forehead: it was as firm as vajra, perfectly level and smooth without a wrinkle, and square. All who beheld it felt joy and were never satiated; it was neither stained nor discolored, with no spots of white or black. It was fully developed through his past deeds, without deficiency or flaw; those who saw it rejoiced, free from any harmful intent.

The eyes are pure and without blemish; all who behold them find every auspiciousness. Only after accomplishing hundreds of thousands of countless practices does one obtain the forehead of a Tathāgata.
At that time, he spoke this verse:
"Subtle and exceedingly pure, Completely liberated from all evil deeds;
The Buddha’s brow is inconceivable, Like an elephant's tusk submerged in water."
“The teachings he proclaims are such that the Tathāgata’s brow is peerless; like the purity of space, all who see it rejoice.

At that time, the Tathāgata possessed the mark between his eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which was most brilliantly radiant and situated in the center of his face. It was the color of cow’s milk, exceedingly soft and fine, like white silk gauze or the color of fresh snow. It was as white as the newly risen sun or the *kumuda* flower, incomparably pure. Like the autumn moon, it was extremely clear, bright, and pure; curling to the right, it was neither too high nor too low, entirely free from any obstruction.
Those who behold its form shall be free from all ailments.
It is as long as a cubit, of an exceedingly subtle and inconceivable color; having emitted light, it returns once more to its original place.
All are produced by past practices, such as this subtle and wondrous mark between the eyebrows of the Tathāgata, as he teaches the Dharma amidst the great assembly.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Created by hundreds of various practices, The mark between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows..."
This is a fertile field of merit, and also the fruition of past practices.
Neither coarse nor fine, its right-turning color is subtle and wondrous;
its protruding mark is equal in height to an elbow, unseen by none throughout the three periods of time.
The mark between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows is pure and free from all blemish;
like Mount Sumeru, it is the foremost among all mountains.
Sovereign over all dharmas, he is able to purify the multitudes of sentient beings.
Such is the mark of the full face, yet none surpasses the mark between the eyebrows.
That form is produced by the practice of conduct; its liberation is beyond compare.
Having extinguished the fires of mental defilement, all sentient beings share in that purity.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a subtle, wondrous, and pure eye, like the color of that hundred-petaled flower; each petal was distinct, and there was no shadow it did not illuminate. It was like the color of the *utpala* or blue *vaidūrya* flower in the void; the lashes were exceedingly white, no different from those of a king of geese, being supremely white, peerless, and foremost.

He beholds all the lands in the four directions and sees within them all the various forms of beings; he discerns them all, seeing that they possess no desire nor are they violent, and they have no anger nor are they associated with anger.

Observing the virtuous and non-virtuous deeds within those buddha-fields, they are also able to perceive all subtle matters; furthermore, they possess no fear or alarm. Cultivating loving-kindness, they attain compassion and do not look askance; toward all sentient beings, they cultivate sympathetic joy without ever feeling satiated. By guarding all wholesome dharmas and discerning each dharma individually, they pervade all buddha-fields.
He thus forms this understanding and contemplation that there is no evil and no indolence.
Thereupon, he speaks this verse:
"The eye is pure and exceedingly subtle; Nothing whatsoever can obstruct it."
Created by a hundred merits, he then becomes a Tathāgata.
His wholesome dharmas are utterly pure, and he is free from all afflictions;
his facial complexion is like that of a celestial king—this is the appearance of the nectar of immortality.
The characteristics of the Dharma are also complete, and there are no afflictions or sufferings;
it is like that bright mirror, in which the reflection of a face appears.
Beholding those dwelling places of sentient beings, one gazes upon them without ever feeling satiated.
"Only then did he attain perfect enlightenment and proclaim the Dharma of ambrosia. At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a subtle and wondrous nose;

throughout his past lives over countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he gave rise to these various forms of wisdom and distinguished them all. In the realm of birth and death, he extracted the thorns of emotional attachment, desiring to ferry beings to the other shore and to uproot all thorns of craving. For the sake of the people of the world, he diligently practiced such asceticism to bestow benefits upon others, or delivered them through the precepts—all of which were accomplished in his former lives. Possessing every excellence and free from all impurity, he healed their wounds.

Just as a mass of gold possesses the most supreme and brilliant color, so too for one who wishes to reach that state, the mind’s aspiration must be free from deceit; therein one manifests all essential practices through their application.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Subtle and free from all impurity, The Tathāgata’s nose is foremost;
It is like the beak of a parrot; Therefore, I take refuge in it."
Upon his face, he is the one whom all sentient beings revere;
his nose is so wondrous that it resembles a latāpṛṣṭha flower or a parrot.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such teeth: they were without gaps or flaws, even and level without variation in height, like the color of white snow or a conch shell, and also like the color of the kumuda flower.

He possesses this subtle and wondrous form, endowed with the most pure conduct; he is radiant, entirely liberated from all unwholesome deeds, and as firm and indestructible as a vajra. The Tathāgata has forty teeth, four in both the upper and lower jaws, and upon each tooth is the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata’s teeth are even and straight; His preaching of the Dharma is most subtle and wondrous.
Without flaw, without gap, and without falling away, They are just like those tilaka flowers.”
"The eyes are pure and most subtle; their excellent color is unchanging.
This is the virtue of the Śākyas: they possess forty even teeth.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a broad and long tongue that it was never false; its excellent color was indestructible, like the *aśoka* flower, and like a lotus petal, it was exceedingly soft, delicate, and smooth. Furthermore, he was free from coarse speech and harsh words; having removed the afflictions of lust, anger, and delusion, he dwelt in a state of tranquility, delighting in joy and fully accomplishing the precepts.

There is no one whom he does not deliver through his preaching; by means of the wisdom of the Dharma, he rescues those who are impoverished and brings about liberation from attachment to perceptions and from lust, anger, and ignorance—all of which were produced by his past practices. The Tathāgata’s tongue-organ completely covers his face; how truly marvelous and extraordinary!
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
“The deeds produced by a hundred blessings— The Tathāgata’s tongue is foremost among them;
His teeth and lips are all perfectly even and upright, Constantly emitting the Dharma of ambrosia.”
"If one obtains various flavors, whether exquisite or unrefined, one can discern every flavor, following them in sequence without losing their order.

At that time, the Tathāgata gave such instruction, speaking of wholesome conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava*). His voice was free from coarseness; his speech was fully endowed with merit, possessing immeasurable qualities. Regarding the practices of the permanent and the impermanent, his resolve was without timidity. It was profoundly deep, without bottom, and foremost among all things. The teachings he spoke were never tedious; their meanings corresponded to one another, manifesting the original *pratītyasamutpāda*. He skillfully discerned the dharmas and, through skillful means, taught and transformed sentient beings according to the times. Free from anger, he adorned his own person and found joy in the tranquility of the mind.

He makes offerings to the wise and extols their reputations in accordance with their respective qualities; just as great birds delight in deep pools, he rescues all those who encounter hundreds of thousands of afflictions, causing all classes of sentient beings to attain complete joy.

Having crossed to the other shore beyond birth, old age, sickness, and death, they attain the most supreme practice free from longing; with minds untainted by fetters, they manifest all virtuous deeds and achieve unprecedented practices. Like crossing water by boat, they are without fear; they deliver all beings from birth and death, extolling the virtues of dhyāna. Their merit is subtle and wondrous, their lifespan enduring, as they extinguish the mind and intellect to reach the realm of nirvāṇa. Attaining the Dharma of ambrosia, they extinguish the source of all birth and death, instructing others on good and evil so that those who hear them harbor no fear, like light that cannot be obscured.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"By manifesting the guidance of the Dharma, He honors the conduct of the Buddhas;
Through the power and force of patience, He is like that flower in full bloom."
"Satiated by the taste of nectar, those who are blind and ignorant cannot cross over;
yet those who can eat this nectar shall attain passage across the realm of birth and death. At that time, the World-Honored One produced such a resonance;

the merit of what he spoke was free from any coarseness, like the voice of the *hṛdbhī* bird—extremely subtle and exquisite. His voice reached the four quarters, and as the teaching was transmitted from one to another, it possessed such power and majesty among the classes of sentient beings. It did not go outside the assembly, yet all heard the pure sound; all of this was produced by his past practices, like the Brahma-voice or the cry of a sorrowful phoenix.

At that time, one hears five kinds of sounds that are profound and bottomless; all these teachings subdue the hosts of outsiders, just as that dragon changed its original habits. In ancient times there was such a form, most wonderful and without timidity; if one observes it with the eye and knows it, there is no attachment. The cessation of the mind corresponds to the flavor [of liberation]; repeatedly ceasing the mind without satiety, yet not being in contradiction, and not corresponding with anger—these are all brought about by the merit of the retribution of practice; therefore, it is called the "delight of the śramaṇa."

There is such a mind; based on that mind, there are these five kinds [of joy]: having previously heard the sound of flowing water and having heard it, one rejoices; how much more so now, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching which increases and benefits the roots of goodness—how could one not rejoice and increase liberation upon hearing this resonance?
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"The resonance of his voice is gentle and beautiful; The Buddha’s sound brings peace and joy to the mind.
Come, O Subduer, and listen to the teaching; His merit is beyond measure."

"Those who hear the sound of his voice, Which arises from his past conduct, Are already able to realize it; He has subdued five hundred peacocks. At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a face:

exceedingly pure and free from blemish, supremely upright and peerless, with beautiful eyes one never tires of beholding, long-dangling ears, lips like vermilion fire, a complexion like genuine gold, and teeth that were extremely white, subtle, and infinite in their perfection—flat, full, without spot or stain, without scar or blemish, and without sorrow or affliction. All who beheld him rejoiced; his merit was immeasurable, and he possessed a supreme fragrance. His original deeds were like the full moon, utterly pure and free from blemish, most honored and foremost.

If he sits in the full lotus posture and preaches the Dharma to the great assembly, those seated before and behind him all see his face; if he rises from meditation, he first preaches the Dharma to the assembly.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"All rejoice with joy, desiring to behold the form of the Tathāgata;
having now seen the Tathāgata, he is like the full moon."
"The foremost bliss of gain is none other than the assembly of the Tathāgata;
like the fullness of the moon in the third or fifth month, the bliss of the Tathāgata is described as equal [to that].

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a head: well-born, firm, perfectly symmetrical and peerless, without unevenness, and in harmony with his own physical marks. Its color was supreme, resembling the inexhaustible power of the eight arms of Nārāyaṇa; its golden hue was similar to that place [of radiance], and those marks were most subtle, of excellent color and exquisite beauty, entirely free from all obstruction.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Perfectly fulfilled and most subtle, Gradually proceeding by way of that practice,
The Tathāgata possesses such a head— The peerless banner of the Śākya clan."
"Nothing can harm him who has resolved his mind upon the Tathāgata; among all classes of beings in the three realms, they shall praise the virtues of that Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such arms: well-born and peerless like Mount Sumeru; his shoulders were likewise sublime, with no equal, neither too high nor too low, and exceedingly soft and delicate. They were as unharmed and supple as the king of *sāla* trees, and as fine and non-coarse as the *campaka* flower. The soft hairs that grew there were of an intensely blue color, each curling to the right, exceedingly soft and delicate. All who beheld them obtained joy. With these most subtle hands, he extended them to subdue the realm of Māra and to bear witness for me.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Just as the Śirīṣa tree Subdues all hosts of Māras,
Like unto a vajra-pestle, Therefore I take refuge in the Buddha."
"Acting as a guide for the three realms, illuminated by the light of the Dharma, his mind is immeasurable; I take refuge before the Most Victorious One.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such hands: exceedingly soft, well-formed, and peerless; neither decayed nor marred, without flaw or leakage, they were perfectly full, like the heights of a great mountain.

His hands bear the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel; his fingers are joined by a web-like membrane; his nails are exceedingly white and pure like the radiance of the sun; and like blue lotus flowers, they are all fully blossomed with petals that are soft and delicate.
When he preaches the Dharma, there are no sentient beings who hear it and do not attain liberation; his speech is always timely.

Regarding what was originally created, he is born with light that shines through his palms and brings about liberation. If they encounter his compassion, they follow the light and all attain deliverance.

Skillfully discerning sentient beings so that they distance themselves from evil and draw near to the good, he teaches the Dharma to them. In his place of birth, he attains loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; desiring to eliminate unwholesome conduct and cultivate all wholesome conduct, he addresses sentient beings, saying:
"All things are suffering; do not accept those defilements, but grow weary of and seek to transcend birth and death."
To cause sentient beings to attain purity and inspire hope, and to eliminate their delusions, when he sat in meditation, all the hosts of Māras flocked to his location.

They came on various vehicles—mules, donkeys, camels, elephants, horses, and yaks—and in the forms of birds, beasts, lions, dogs, pigs, and sheep; or they took the shape of horses with heads of various creatures, wearing swords, drawing bows, and grasping arrows; or they struck bells and beat drums, assuming every form of a māra host, desiring to come and harm the Three Buddhas.

At that time, the World-Honored One pressed the earth with his finger; this ground was most excellent, with its mountains, forests, cities, walls, springs, bathing pools, and various sources of water. All these bathing pools were filled with precious jewels, some contained within golden bowls. When a strong man struck those bowls, sounds issued forth, and as he stroked the Dharma-wheel with his hand, it was most wondrous and beyond compare; thereupon, he prostrated himself.
The Buddha then spoke this verse:
"The foremost pure karma, Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma—
The Tathāgata’s hand is subtle and wondrous, Exceedingly marvelous and beyond compare."
With his hand he should stroke and turn it; the place where the Wheel of Dharma stands is one, yet its location cannot be seen, nor can any who test it be seen.
When he turns the Wheel of Dharma, he does so according to the needs of sentient beings.
"By turning this wheel of Dharma, sentient beings shall obtain peace and security.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a body: it was perfectly upright and without flaw, perfected in the observance of the precepts; like the chest of a lion, it was encircled by marks of merit, with upper and lower parts in harmonious proportion, and its color was like that of an *utpala* flower, neither faded nor decayed.

When walking, his gait is profound, turning to the right, neither too high nor too low; his skin and hair are extremely soft and subtle, all curling to the right, being of a peerless and double-refined subtlety. He is like the *campaka* flower, exceedingly fragrant; he is neither too young nor too old, possessing nothing that does not correspond to him. He is free from association with anger; his faculties are complete, such as have never before existed in the world. He is gradually firm and most subtle, with a vajra-body that is neither lax nor rigid, skillfully discerning sentient beings.
All who see him give rise to a heart of joy, never tiring of gazing upon him.

His halo extends seven feet, like Mount Anavatapta; amidst the great assembly, he is like a king of elephants among a herd of elephants, the most preeminent of all, and like King Nārāyaṇa, whom none can harm.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Having practiced for a hundred kalpas, I have become the most eminent among men;
Now I have attained this physical body, And now there is none equal to me."
Because lust, anger, and delusion have been extinguished, all evils have forever ceased;
therefore, I now bow my head, that I too may be so in the future.
Should lust, anger, or delusion arise, one is able to extinguish them immediately.
"Now, observing the Buddha’s countenance, his body is free from all afflictions and ailments.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such thighs as these: they were symmetrical from top to bottom, well-formed, subtle and peerless, with no unevenness, bringing joy to all and being perfectly proportioned to his body.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“His thighs are pure and exquisite, Peerless and beyond compare;
Whoever beholds them Is free from all blemish.”
"Subtle and delicate hairs grow [upon his calves], well-settled like gold;
never again shall he undergo other realms of existence. Behold this most wondrous form!

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such calves: thus formed, they were rounded and gradually tapered, proportionate to his body, like the calves of a deer; their excellent radiance was pure and peerless.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata’s calves are subtle and wondrous, and their color is beyond compare;
one should contemplate all these marks, each one difficult to measure.”
"One should realize him thus: he is praised by all the world;
even after his parinirvāṇa, one should therefore take refuge in the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such feet: his gait was composed and steady, remaining firm and unmoving; they were not wavering, being exceedingly subtle and exquisite; his toes were long and endowed with the marks of a hundred merits—having performed such ascetic practices, he subsequently attained them.

He went to the site of enlightenment for the sake of worldly beings, desiring to deliver them. Those who hear his voice are like that Dragon King Sunetra, who remains unmoving; regarding the merit performed by that Samyaksaṃbuddha, it is a hundred-thousandfold greater than ordinary merit. His ornaments are subtle and wondrous, and his radiant light is peerless. Because he possesses such merit from this point onward, he prostrates and speaks these verses: "Your loving-kindness cannot be harmed;
I now pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, and also pay homage to the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. The Tathāgata has liberated the multitudes."
"Those who have attained this faith before that Most Victorious One, Whose white parts are exceedingly subtle and smooth, Therefore, I take refuge in the Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such wheels: they were perfectly round, free from impurity, and devoid of coarseness; they were profoundly deep with a thousand spokes, their resonance gentle and harmonious. His body was fully endowed with all faculties, lacking nothing. He had performed great karmic deeds regarding the four directions for the sake of the Holy Wheel-Turning King, his realm being complete. Second, he possessed a mind free from cowardice. Third, it was as if a wheel had blocked the moon with its hand so that no light remained. Fourth, when the wheel was released, there was great radiance, like a springtime free from dust, where neither clouds nor particles exist within the void.

At that time, in the middle of the night, when there were no afflictions or lunar eclipses, the moon emitted a great light; this is also like that: the Wheel-Turning Sage King originally lacked the marks of a Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"A human life lasts a hundred years, yet its moments are constantly passing away;
possessing such marks of a noble wheel, he is like a lotus flower in full bloom."
Just as Mount Sumeru is peerless and without equal,
so too is that which results from planting merit— the practice cultivated by the Tathāgata.
Now, having come from those palaces of the Śākya clan, he has arrived to announce his presence.
Praised by all the devas, the Tathāgata should turn the wheel of Dharma.
If one can awaken to this and observe those few locations,
seeing that each possesses its own single mind, there is none who can surpass the Buddha.
“His resolve and nature are exceedingly firm; he emits light that shines everywhere through all things.
Wherever the solar orb shines, he universally delivers all classes of sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded with such a gait: first raising his right foot, he stepped upon the ground neither too slowly nor too quickly; his stride was level and upright, neither abrupt nor violent, just like that of an elephant king and no different. His walking was steadfast, and the World-Honored One’s body did not waver, like Nārāyaṇa.

At that time, among the World-Honored One’s assembly, those who were high became low, and those who were low became high; all small doors naturally became wide and spacious. The Tathāgata’s body never bent or stretched, for in his previous lives he had been free from pride and arrogance.

All musical instruments sounded spontaneously without being struck, and all wriggling creatures attained peace and security, for in his previous lives he had practiced a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“He possesses great divine wondrousness; Fearless, he has these virtues.
Dwelling there, he receives an auspicious form, And destroys those who are stubborn and fierce.”
"He has already abandoned pride, awakening to that which is to be awakened by himself.
Subtle and free from craving, he dwells receiving the fruits of his practice.

At that time, the World-Honored One displayed such traces: the thousand-spoked wheel-mark appeared with supreme subtlety; his faculties were complete and his complexion was most marvelous and peerless. He was the foremost among men, inspiring all manner of joy—the result of the merit cultivated through hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

He is free from coarseness and violence; he has eliminated lust, anger, and delusion. His original conduct is without hypocrisy or flattery and is devoid of all evils. He does not associate with delusion nor perform deluded actions; such is his reputation.

His character and nature are upright and straightforward; in all he does, he harbors no expectations and entertains no doubts. His mind has extinguished all attachments, having eliminated longing so that his conduct is free from deficiency or leakage. His mind makes no distinction between self and other, and his merits are fully perfected. Having accomplished the ten powers, he removes all afflictions.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"The Most Victorious One possesses these virtues, Accomplished through various modes of practice;
Discerning the karma of the stages of practice, He illuminates all like the rising sun."
"That wheel, hidden in the earth, now appears; it is that which the mind observes.
You should take refuge in the Buddha yourself, and thus seal the earth.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with such a cause and condition; because he had cultivated past practices and felt compassion for those sentient beings, he manifested such a smile.

At that time, when the World-Honored One smiled, there was this foremost, supple, most pure, and subtle [experience] heard by the ears; seeing the Buddha’s smile, free from dust and defilement, pure and without blemish, one realizes that his original practice has been without false speech. It is like the various fragrances of the *utpala* and *campaka* flowers; the nectar-like words manifest various radiances, and the foremost, most subtle mind is able to discern them.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s body was the color of gold; like a high mountain, he circumambulated those three times and ascended to the Akaniṣṭha realm. There, in the celestial palaces, all those who had attained faith received the Tathāgata’s instructions without any transgression or loss, and as they passed them on to one another, they rejoiced in the Tathāgata. This was due to the original deeds performed by the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“In various colors, blue and yellow, The mouth proclaims the light of the prohibitions and precepts.
The Tathāgata’s body emerges from the essential path, Worshipped by devas and humans.”
“The mark between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, Incomparable due to three causes and conditions, Reaches as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, And comes to the place where the Tathāgata dwells.
At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such radiance; all of it was produced by his past practices.
Behind his body there is this light; it is a most wondrous and excellent light of liberation, the foremost of all.

His body emits radiance, bringing joy to all who see it. Various luminous ornaments adorn his person, such that no dust, smoke, or Rāhu the Asura can obstruct it. He is liberated from the five fetters and has eliminated all delusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the nectar of immortality, enabling those sentient beings to encounter this flavor; his natural supernormal powers were inconceivable.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"The body is well-liberated, Nothing can obstruct or destroy it."
The One of Ten Powers possesses this light, which the ignorant do not perceive.
The Tathāgata has supernormal powers, manifesting himself equally for all sentient beings;
his great radiance eclipses the brilliance of the sun. Therefore, I take refuge in this light.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such robes; he wore them at appropriate times, neither too high nor too low. Having extinguished the source of birth and death, no weeds or filth adhered to him. His clothing was harmonious with his surroundings, and wherever he went, all were filled with joy. Such was the fruit [of his merit]; therefore, Venerable Nanda’s robes were always bright and clean. Furthermore, when the bhikṣus stood by the side of the World-Honored One wearing their saṃghāṭī robes, none could soil the Tathāgata’s garments.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda marveled at what he had never before experienced and went to inform the World-Honored One, wishing to learn the method for putting on robes.
The World-Honored One said to him,
"How is it, Nanda, that the Tathāgata has not appeared in the world throughout the long night?"
"How can one eliminate the defilements of lust, anger, and delusion in sentient beings so that they are forever exhausted without remainder?
Then, following his instruction, if one were to practice accordingly to achieve this, even the Sīlavant wind could not move this robe, nor could dust or grime stain it.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The robes worn by the Tathāgata Spontaneously cover his physical form;
Just as a lotus is unsullied by impurity, So too is this robe.”
"If the Svalāṇa wind should arise, its power and force are difficult to restrain;
yet one might wish to move the Tathāgata’s robe—who could surpass the One of Ten Powers?

At that time, the World-Honored One thus sought alms from the houses of the noble and eminent, not discriminating between the lowly and the base, visiting them all without exception. He maintained no wrong livelihood: he did not stoop to eat, nor did he rely on astrology, divination, or fortune-telling for his food; he did not accept invitations to meals sent by messengers, nor did he observe the four directions for alms; he did not eat through the use of incantations or illusions, nor did he depend on the fruits of agricultural labor for his sustenance.
He begs for food in order to provide relief to others, without expectation and without attachment to the meal.

At that time, the World-Honored One has no further craving or attachment toward food; observing such karma, he accepts the food without greed or clinging. Free from lust, anger, and delusion, and without confusion, he eliminates the deluded mind and completely abandons all thoughts of attachment, remaining dissociated from them. Having abandoned those sensual desires that cannot be thwarted, he constantly delights in them by taking meditation as his sustenance. Furthermore, he is without the notion of self; he has utterly relinquished suffering and departed from what is unwholesome in the present.
This body must inevitably perish; knowing this, one should abandon the three matters, becoming pure and free from lust, anger, and delusion. Why, then, eat?

It is because one wishes to demonstrate that this body lacks solidity, thereby nourishing its illness so that the fires [of passion] do not arise. Having completely cast away all things and produced no disordered thoughts, one manifests the nectar of immortality and cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Thus, though pain decays and perishes, one does not create new pain.

For this reason, the World-Honored One accepts their offerings of faith and partakes of the fruit thereof; he desires that the retribution produced by his own body may bring peace and security, and protect the people of the world.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Going from place to place and house to house to beg, I desire to cause the True Dharma to prevail."
In those garden groves, like six-legged bees tasting nectar, they do not discriminate between the fine and the foul;
they give rise to neither good nor evil thoughts.
They cannot be thwarted or destroyed, for their minds desire the flavor of liberation.

At that time, the World-Honored One had such resting places as mountain crags, caves, and open-air seats; groves, the sides of gardens, and springs where various flowers and fruits flourished in abundance—places of incomparable bliss and solitude where he sought liberation.

Dwelling therein, they are liberated from all evils and free from the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-nīvaraṇa*). In places where ordinary people do not go, they are without fear; having departed from attachment to form, they constantly delight in tranquility. They preach the Dharma to sentient beings, as is extensively explained in the sūtras.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"The trees bear flowers and fruit; Behold the garden of Mānava!
Delighting in solitude and tranquility, The lush green flowers are all in full bloom."
"Seeking liberation therein, one should therefore rely upon that place;
when going to dwell in seclusion, there shall be no sound and no distracting thoughts.

At that time, the World-Honored One spread grass upon the ground—it was free from dust and impurity, unadorned, extremely fine, soft, smooth, well-grown, and exquisite; seeing its reflection, one could gaze at it without weariness, observing it all as being neither high nor low.
Reflecting thus, [he saw that] name-and-form and the six sense bases depend upon one another, appearing there without end.

Alternatively, he might spread grass upon the ground; because he has subdued those [defilements] many times, he sits upon the spread grass free from thoughts of desire. Using grass as a mat, he is likewise free from fetters and afflictions, being entirely pure.

The merits cultivated by the Buddhas of antiquity were likewise not grasped; through non-attachment, they realized the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They turned [the wheel of Dharma] extensively, and no afflictions or fetters (*saṃyojana*) arose within them. Their robes were neatly arranged without disorder, and for those sentient beings upon whom they relied, there were no hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); thus they attained samādhi and the supernormal powers.

He lay on his right side upon the ground and did not sleep for long; soon rising, he practiced the Way through walking meditation. Because of the samādhi of non-discursive thought, he lay on his right side; because he wished to subdue his adversaries, he ascended the lion throne. Wearing five kinds of fine silks, he manifested colors that were not real; appearing in the form and appearance of a śramaṇa, he practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) without any attachment, relying on the minds of sentient beings seeking liberation.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
“Rootless are the virtuous beings; The merit of the Śākya clan— The wholesome deeds performed by the mind, The mind itself fully awakens to them.”
“Excellent is the meaning of the Great Dharma; none can surpass it.
Now, within the assembly of the Tathāgata, he uses grass to eliminate craving.

At that time, how did the World-Honored One awaken to the faculties? That is to say, he realized that in the past he cultivated such faculties and their corresponding flavors; through the Path, these faculties arose, yet they were subject to subjugation by the inverted tendencies of desire and flowed along with the stream in accordance with birth and death.
These faculties give rise to impure conduct while depending on other conditions; these faculties are greedily attached to the world and deeply clinging to pleasure;
these faculties give rise to various powers and forces such that all fetters and latent tendencies blaze intensely;
these faculties drive the body through the cycle of rebirth without ceasing; these faculties do not accomplish the Great Purpose. This...
The various faculties are deluded as they traverse all sensory objects; these faculties are like being wounded by swords and spears;
these faculties are afflicted with suffering; these faculties are like festering sores from which the fetters and latent tendencies leak;
these faculties are like a disease, devoid of strength and vigor; they possess no satiety and seek incessantly without ceasing.
These faculties do not cease and repeatedly give rise to fetters; these faculties are like poisonous medicine, failing to sever the root of suffering;
these faculties have not been trained and are associated with all manner of evils;
these faculties do not conceal themselves from the sword-thorns of sensory objects and are bound by them; these faculties lack protection and are devoid of the essential flavor of the Dharma.
These sense-faculties are devoid of a mind, yet they rush toward their respective objects.

When these faculties do not practice cultivation, they are ignited by the fire of desire, and the objects of perception continue to increase. These faculties, beset by various afflictions, wander among external objects, and thus the entire body and mind experience suffering.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"When the faculties are full within their respective spheres, And one is led astray by evil,
that mind is constantly ablaze, Just like a glowing ball of hot iron."
"The Tathāgata’s teaching is excellent; it leads to the place of peace and security.
Since there are no afflictions of the sense faculties, how much less could there be objective realms?
At that time, how did the World-Honored One awaken to and know the mind?

That which is called "arising in dependence on objects" leads to growth and increase; this mind is distracted and unstable, like a swift wind; this mind never tires of its objects and brings about calamity through evil; this mind wanders afar like a dream; this mind greedily clings to objects like a monkey; this mind naturally engages in various attachments, like a peacock that constantly looks at its own reflection with its wings spread; this mind runs toward distant thoughts of wealth and enterprise; this mind gives rise to the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), like a mirage that one tires of seeking but can never attain; this mind is difficult to control, for it does not abide within its objects; this mind is like a king who always possesses sovereign power.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"Supremely profound and wondrous, The mind is known to have no root;
Yakṣas and gandharvas, Even throughout the three times, cannot awaken to it."
He attained such mastery that he spontaneously had this thought:
"In this world there is no illumination; I shall act as the light of the Dharma.
At that time, how did the World-Honored One manifest his awakening so as to bring enlightenment to the world?
That which is called the world lacking any reliance, being greedily attached to one's own body; this world where the mind has no refuge, being greedily attached to sensory objects;
this world where evil karma arises based on various false views; this world created spontaneously by itself;
this world falling into the flow of the wrong paths and wandering toward evil destinies; this world dwelling in the miserable realms is just like...
O monkey, in this world there is no illumination, for it is shrouded by the veil of the five aggregates;
in this world there is blinding darkness, for the eye of wisdom does not arise; in this world there is hunger and thirst, for craving knows no satiety;
in this world there is blazing fire, for one is bound by various fetters; in this world there is little flavor, like a bee gathering nectar from flowers; in this world there is no place of refuge.
This world is subject to decay; it wanders afar upon the wheel of saṃsāra; it is bound within the cycle of birth and death;
the manifold afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death arrive here; this world is not excellent and must inevitably perish;
this world offers no refuge and is oppressed by suffering; this world was not created by oneself and must surely be abandoned.
Depart! This world is a mechanism of successive dependencies; the various activities of this world will lead one toward evil states.
This world appears like an illusion manifesting forms and images; it produces nothing beneficial for others and is a vessel of decay.
This world is frivolous, its basis is unestablished, and it is difficult to awaken to, being devoid of any true realm.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Sentient beings encounter suffering and affliction; Contemplating the world, one finds no true world therein.
Seeking the Way through wisdom, One should draw near to that state.”
"Gradually increasing from small beginnings, though one desires to cherish one's life, this [body] will inevitably perish; therefore, its cessation is bliss.
How does one cross over the mire in this life?
It is like the lotus seeds in that pond, which sprout within them and gradually grow larger.

This is also thus: all five flavors die, yet through the station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) they take birth, surrounded by the formations of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), formed by wind and fire, irrigated by the water of pride (*māna*), and receiving death while sprouting forth within.
Just as those sprouts arise, so it is with this: because sprouts arise, there is neither annihilation nor permanence.
Just as one previously observed those sprouts, so it is with this: because those sentient beings are bound and attached, there is neither annihilation nor permanence.

Just as that earth is blown by the wind, so it is with this; just as the four great elements are firm yet undergo all manner of suffering and affliction, so it is with this; therefore, everything is spontaneous.
It is like a naturally occurring, indestructible lotus producing sprouts; therefore, all things are not natural, for they are practiced through a single principle.
It is like those external four great elements which, once blown by the wind, do not create these four great elements again.
This is also like that; therefore, all [phenomena] should be relinquished.
Just as there are conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) arising from that, so it is with this; thus, those phenomena are like that sprout.
It is similar to the seed of a tree; this case is likewise. The marks of a Great Man cannot be destroyed, for they are produced by such a nature.
It is just as when the sprout of a lotus seed grows; therefore, these marks are infinite and yet not something that has arisen.
Just as when that sprout arises, it has no place from which it comes, so it is with this; therefore, there is neither coming nor going.
Just as when it departs, there is no place where it stays, so it is with this; therefore, there is no place of abiding.
Just as those sprouts grow together, gradually flourishing and eventually blossoming, so it is with this: there is neither high nor low.
Just as those lotus sprouts will inevitably continue to grow, so too shall this.
This is also like that: what was originally created as a sprout gradually grows and increases within the womb.
Just as those lotus flowers with their lush leaves are exceedingly lovely and desirable, so too are these various conditioned activities exceedingly lovely and worthy of veneration.

Just as that fruit is about to ripen, so it is with this: when the seeds are about to ripen, the hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and the five sense faculties shall all be cast off; the six sense organs will decline and waste away, and the mental faculty will dissolve, abandoning this body.

Just as that flower is certain to ripen fully, and just as the sunlight possesses a color and fragrance that are most subtle and wondrous, and the range of the king of bees is most lovely and worthy of reverence, so too it is with this: at the moment of initial birth, when the four great elements are illumined by the sunlight and the courageous embryo awakens, its qualities are analogous to those; therefore, pride and the rest all rely upon one another, being most lovely and worthy of reverence.

Those who are hungry and thirsty, and those caught in the cycle of birth and death, claim that desire is pleasure; such foolish people harbor these inverted perceptions. It is just like this: at all times and seasons, one cannot escape old age and death.

Just as at that time of year, when the seasons lack power and vigor, being scorched by hot winds, all things are cast away; flowers and fruits fall apart and have no basis for remaining; there are neither bees nor fresh colors, and none who delight in them—so it is with this: life gradually diminishes until one has no power or vigor within this existence. Who can remain with their life intact?

Both internally and externally, all things are subject to decay; the vigor of youth is lost and one must inevitably pass away. There is no stem or joint, no teeth or hair; there is no seeing, no hearing, no taste, and no fragrance. There is no smoothness of touch, nor any further sensory pleasure. The body is ruined and all pride is utterly eliminated. There is no relish for flavors, and the mind is no longer ardent; having transcended the realm of form, the skin becomes slack and the face wrinkled, devoid of youthful vigor. Once this old age has arrived, one does not love the various decaying forms, yet men and women are harmed by them and remain attached to them.

Just as that which is withered and decayed has no fragrance and must eventually disperse, so too is this: when the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exhausted, one shall be carried toward the cemetery.

Just as the seeds of a lotus flower, after ripening, again produce sprouts, so too is this characteristic: one repeatedly undergoes existence (*bhava*). One should regard the various classes of sentient beings as being like those withered and ruined flower stalks.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Therefore, one should abandon existence, And likewise contemplate this flower;
Just as that which is born from a womb, One should earnestly seek its cessation."
"If one wishes to seek the sprout of life, one must know that joy lies in emptiness and non-existence;
if one wishes to reach that state, one should seek it from within one's own mind.
