What is the meaning of the World-Honored One being called "the Ocean"?

That which is called the foremost ferrying of sentient beings to the other shore consists of contemplating immeasurable increases in merit, possessing pure and flawless great wisdom, and being liberated from a mind of resentment.

First, he attains liberation; through skillful contemplation, he never departs from the roots of goodness. His fame spreads afar and his wisdom reaches everywhere. Like a tree in full bloom, various fragrances waft far and wide. He discerns the seven factors of enlightenment (sapta-sambodhyaṅga) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Having crossed over, his wisdom is perfected with a hundredfold merits. He constantly enters samādhi without distracted intent, exhorting and assisting sentient beings to give rise to wholesome minds. He is able to accomplish all manner of samādhis and is the foremost among those in training and those beyond training.

He manifests aspiration toward the Dharma without ever becoming weary; his speech is impartial, upright, and gentle; he is pure and flawless, free from lust, anger, and delusion, and possesses the foremost merit among the great assembly.

Universally compassionate toward all, he brings them peace, happiness, and rest; he instructs others regarding the spheres of experience with constant mindfulness and reverence, his merit being inexhaustible.

At that time, throughout ninety-one kalpas, the World-Honored One gradually perfected these virtues; he awakened to all profoundly deep karmic actions and desired to cause all living beings to share in a single flavor. He preached the Dharma without missing the proper timing, always remaining in accord with them. Possessing the ten powers as precious jewels, he was endowed with every kind of treasure; relying on the four fearlessnesses, he took up residence within the four great elements. For the sake of those sentient beings, he made no distinction between the noble and the lowly; having transcended the eight worldly dharmas, he harbored no thoughts of increase or decrease.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Therefore, one should seek deliverance, Diligently relying upon the boat of the Path.
The ocean of the Tathāgata is immeasurable; For this reason, I prostrate to the Buddha."
"Having already crossed over to that place, where merit and blessings are immeasurable,
and having experienced these joys and sorrows, one should seek the place of peace and security. What is the Tathāgata’s boat?

This refers to the skillful cultivation of firm karmic fruition; practicing all virtues without transgression or omission, with all practices complete and all evils forever exhausted; binding the body with the foremost nectar of the precepts; being free from the notions of annihilation or permanence; having already abided in rest and attained that Path; always delighting in patience and not giving rise to anger; discerning the five faculties and attaining equal vision without divergent thoughts; and being fully endowed with various pure liberations and the three samādhis of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.

Constantly harboring a sense of shame and remorse, they deliver others from hesitation; through various practices such as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the formless samādhis, they discern them all without limit. Contemplating the impurities of the body, the foremost patience and wisdom are ever present before them; regarding the perceptions of desire as entirely impure, they constantly mindfully remain detached, manifesting the Vajra Samādhi.

With immeasurable skillful means, he desires to deliver sentient beings; his precious jewel of awakened mind is in accord with wisdom. He practices the essential path that transcends the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet intentionally undergoes rebirth in a womb to deliver sentient beings. His conduct throughout the three periods of time is complete and indestructible; he takes no pleasure in any worldly things and contemplates all phenomena with the desire to relinquish them.

With such a mind free from increase or decrease, one is able to deliver all sentient beings; using the ship of the ten powers, one delivers sentient beings through the long night to the other shore. Constantly maintaining this contemplation, one does not regard oneself as the foremost among the śrāvakas.

Entering the Samādhi of Universal Observation, one performs various contemplations; one serves and makes offerings with silk banners, flowers, and canopies. Taking the three samādhis as the Buddha-seal, one anoints the body with cool sandalwood. With the five supernormal powers, one sees through all things and various fragrances spread afar. Taking the four fearlessnesses as conch shells, one possesses bells and drums complete and without flaw. Desiring to transcend the sea of birth and death through impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, one subdues the hosts of Māra, causing them all to be shattered and destroyed.

Exhausting the sphere of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they do not grasp at any conceptualization of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) through discrimination; they deliver those who have not yet crossed over.

Having attained the cessation of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)—a state free from suffering and pleasure—they reach *nirvāṇa*. Riding the chariot of merit for the sake of the fourfold assembly, they cause them all to rejoice and leap for joy beyond measure. Using the ten powers as a ship, they carry sentient beings with their virtuous body, speech, and mind, enabling them all to reach the place of all-pervading ambrosial *nirvāṇa*.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Through ascetic practices over countless eons, He fashioned a vessel of merit and virtue;
To lead others to the secure and peaceful realms of happy rebirths, He acts as a protector for the three periods of time."
"With that heart of joy, one swiftly crosses to the far shore of birth and death;
all things shall surely come to an end, and all shall possess this bliss.

At that time, the Tathāgata possessed such qualities as these: namely, the practice of the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables, complete and without deficiency; conduct free from leakage or defilement; skillfully guarding all precepts so that his reputation spread afar; being revered and honored by all classes of sentient beings, enabling them to find a place of peaceful rest and bringing joy to their hearts.

Having practiced the path of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the way for countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). With the illumination of wisdom, they dispel the darkness of ignorance and extinguish all sufferings as they move among the multitudes. They have fully accomplished the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the courageous mind; they utterly destroy the three thousandfold world-systems, yet out of compassion they protect those who have not yet crossed over, their wisdom remaining indestructible.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the light of the sun; he was fully endowed with untainted conduct and rode upon the chariot of the Great Vehicle. He steered it with fearlessness like the wind blowing a sail; his mindfulness-chariot appeared before him in perfect correspondence with all things. With equanimity, he was fully possessed of everything therein; through the samādhi of equanimity, he contemplated all classes of sentient beings. He was accompanied by a retinue complete throughout the three periods of time, who all received and upheld the intent of his teaching. Free from desire, anger, delusion, and pride, he had abandoned all fetters and afflictions. The multitudes of devas and humans made offerings of flowers, and there were no five hindrances. Through the treasury of faith, he caused all beings to clearly perceive and know [the truth]; free from dust and defilement, his various fetters and afflictions were unimpeded. In this way, the World-Honored One is the radiance of the sun.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Having fully perfected a hundredfold wisdom, He is without deficiency among the assembly;
Having manifested the light of the three periods of time, Therefore, I prostrate to the Light.”

Having practiced for countless hundreds of kalpas, extinguishing the darkness of ignorance and delusion, you have already crossed over to this shore; we shall prostrate ourselves before the Sun of Wisdom.
What is the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Lotus?

That which is accomplished through the foremost merit, attaining liberation from the three realms of existence; possessing faith toward sentient beings, with pure and equal wisdom pervading everywhere; crossing to the other shore by the power of diligence; extinguishing the clouds and mists of the world while fully attaining the bliss of dhyāna; and recollecting liberation, free from all manifold conceptualizations.

By contemplating the breath, he observes those various defilements and afflictions without divergent thoughts; with equal vision, he fulfills and accomplishes them all, perceiving them completely. With the fragrance of his precepts, his scent wafts far and wide; with pure radiance, he transforms the classes of sentient beings, just as a swarm of bees distinguishes their many kinds of sounds. Having thoroughly understood the three realms of existence, he attains equal liberation; all sentient beings come to have hope in him, and through various skillful means, he desires to bring them peace and security. He never tires of this most wondrous contemplation; his faculties are without defect or leakage. Among the assembly of those who have stilled their minds, the afflictions of lust, anger, delusion, and pride no longer blaze forth; being supremely pure and supple, he attains deliverance.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Born of purity, An incomparable flower for offering,
Endowed with countless merits, Subtle, wondrous, and most supreme."
Desiring the bliss of rest, may sentient beings attain purity;
having already been able to awaken to that, they are said to possess the voice of constancy.
What they themselves praise and extol accords with the world.
Subtle and supreme in form, with exquisite fragrance most wondrous;
the highest among men, praised and extolled by the world—
I now prostrate myself in homage to the Great Seer, the Unattached One.

At that time, the Omniscient One possessed such clouds as these: namely, the practices cultivated over ninety-one kalpas; his contemplation of impurity; that which was established by his supernormal power and his teaching were without discrepancy; he had exhausted all craving and affection and was free from sorrow; he had reached the ultimate state through various samādhis; for the sake of all sentient beings with great compassion, he caused them to attain the merit of the hundred blessings; he caused them to obtain rest and contemplate that [truth] through mental observation; and toward the multitudes of humans, asuras, and spirits, he practiced loving-kindness throughout the three periods of time, causing them all to attain pure shade and coolness, the gates of liberation, and the essential place.

Furthermore, with the light of wisdom, they wash those pure multitudes of people, ensuring that even the lowliest men and women attain goodness. Wandering among them, they cause them to attain the various karmas of patience (*kṣānti*), to obtain the profound Dharma and the Dharma of virtuous beings, and to plant roots of goodness. Seeing sentient beings hungry and parched for the flavor of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), and grieving that they have not attained liberation, they employ the methods of practice to cause them to realize that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, suffering, and empty, and that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*), and that Nirvana is the supreme bliss. They impartially transcend this duality of suffering and pleasure, becoming fully proficient in the complete expression of language; amidst various assemblies, they extol the wholesome Dharma and plant the roots of liberation, completely abandoning the dharmas of lust, anger, ignorance, and arrogance.

With a resolve as unshakable as the vajra, he delivers others from the afflictions of toil and suffering; among the masses of others, he causes them to receive the True Dharma. To all who are terrified, his omniscience inspires universal compassion; he bestows all things with total detachment. Therefore, I prostrate and pay homage to him who rains down ambrosia.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Merit issues forth illuminating light; The cloud of the Ten Powers is peerless.
One should give rise to a heart of joy, As he proclaims the nectar that quenches thirst.”

"Having attained fearlessness, he is a cloud of omniscience; having already subdued external [opponents], he therefore partakes of the nectar. At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a fire:

namely, all those seeking the path among the classes of people sought joy and happiness; they had attained liberation through the four immeasurable minds and were already crossed over; they were endowed with the ultimate truth and conformed to wisdom; they possessed the supernatural power of the *sarvatraga-samādhi*; they were fully equipped with various reputations and the powers of the faculties; they had already attained this power of profound meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) in countless hundreds of thousands of ways; they had mastery over all dharmas through these faculties and precepts; as the most honored in the three periods of time, they attained fearlessness through the majestic spirit of the ten powers; this is the foremost liberation, attaining the foremost radiance and the foremost emptiness and stillness.

Possessing such virtues, he manifests the profound Dharma; he instructs those classes of sentient beings to practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) so as to subdue all anger, speaking with gentle words that cause no injury and extinguish all fetters (*saṃyojana*). Having well-cultivated his practice among the fourfold assembly—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—he thus points out the retribution of suffering.

His merit is infinitely vast; having perfected wisdom, he has set out toward the gateway of Nirvana and attained the foremost honor and respect. His grace extends to all sentient beings; therefore, I prostrate and pay homage to the Buddha-fire.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"The fire that can burn away grasses and trees has no limit;
The fire of the Buddha is the most sublime of all. Therefore, one should pay homage with joined palms."
"The Buddha's fire has been extinguished; suffering and pleasure no longer arise.
Yet there remain residual merits, which spread throughout the world.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such a garden-villa, perfected by the most gentle precepts. In that place, there were no five hindrances, nor stones, sand, or impurities, nor barren hills. He had attained complete mastery over the root of all dharmas; with great compassion, pure and free from defilement, he dwelt in supreme joy, having reached that state through equal deliverance.

Possessing such meritorious reflections, their various practices are pure and wholesome; through the power of their exertion, they establish the roots of goodness and remain unshakable in their dharma-patience. Free from doubt and other such views, they are fully endowed with the Eightfold Noble Path. They receive all manner of offerings and possess incalculable hundreds of thousands of practices, including immeasurable precepts and samādhis. They are fully endowed with the Ten Powers and are entirely without uncertainty.

The aggregates, hindrances, and liberations are purified; their vows have reached fruition, and branches and leaves flourish, thereupon producing flowers and fruit. Hundreds of various samādhi-forests grow, all of them luxuriant. With right view and no false views, they delight in the body through the meditations and formless attainments. They constantly extend kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings. Within this state, they discern the seven factors of enlightenment; with the mind stilled, they realize the foremost fruit. Encircled by a sense of shame and remorse, they are ever mindful of giving. Because they seek the essential way of deliverance, there arises this cool cloud. By means of power, they uproot all fetters and latent tendencies; possessing such valor, they desire liberation. Their merit is indestructible, and they gather excellent awakening therein. Having removed the lust, anger, and delusion of those sentient beings, they attain fearlessness.

Just as those such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Kātyāyanaputra, Aniruddha, Nandi, Gavāmpati, Nanda, and Revata are the peerless kings of the śrāvakas within that śrāvaka grove—possessing pure bathing pools and all manner of virtues spread abroad, praised throughout the three times—I therefore prostrate myself and pay homage at their crowns.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Skillfully establishing protection throughout the three periods of time, for the sake of all living beings,
his body is adorned with the flowers of the mind of enlightenment, and the fruit of liberation is perfected.”
"Among the assembly of śrāvakas, the King is born with merit and free from defilement;
one should seek that place of bliss, and one will surely attain the state of peace.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such emptiness (*śūnyatā*): because his mind was of a single color, pervading boundlessly, it was called "empty"; he had severed all desires and attachments, abiding nowhere at all; through the retribution of wisdom, all things were moistened and nourished; he was free from all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and also free from all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

By means of the love of samādhi, one crosses over all defilements; through skillful emergence from the essentials, one attains liberation. With the pure moon-like excellent light, one focuses the mind on a single lifetime’s practice through immeasurable merit. Cultivating the Brahma-conduct of a single lifetime, one constantly harbors joy; the eye of wisdom is pure and its sphere is pure. Because all fetters and latent tendencies are severed, there is no attachment; because great compassion has been attained, there is nowhere to be found; because the mind is discerning, various accomplishments are achieved; and because one has received offerings, one is not stained by fetters.

Relying on that mind, he does not defile his heart with the pure or the impure; surrounded by various birds—the assembly of śrāvakas—he is exceedingly subtle and inexhaustible because he is fully endowed with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; surrounded by the host of stars—the forest of *samādhi*—he is difficult to match as he subdues external adversaries through the True Dharma.
One should contemplate in this way: just as a person who has attained ultimate joy in their practice will certainly have no doubt or regression to their former state.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Joyful in mind and full of love, Free from the defilement of fetters."
Though there be various forms, he is able to discern them all.
Having attained equanimity of mind, though others wish to praise him,
he has already reached the further shore and possesses no heart of delight.

At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such wheels: he was fully endowed with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), and the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), all of which were without deficiency and served as his own adornment. He was supreme in the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). His body was well-adorned by the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and his excellent oral teachings spread far and wide. Through the seven factors of awakening, he attained liberation through equal vision.

Through the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā, they are free from delusion and craving; having already transcended those states through samādhi, they attain fearlessness and roar the lion’s roar without dread. Possessing unimpeded eloquence, they gain faith and joy; with diligence free from indolence, they transcend all realms and attain the liberation of wisdom.

Wandering through the realms of Māra, he is free from desire and attachment; endowed with all virtues, he extinguishes all evil destinies. The fruits of the Three Vehicles are subtle and wondrous, most excellently accomplished. He extinguishes the hosts of Māra so that the three desires are forever ended; all sorrows, anxieties, and afflictions are forever exhausted without remainder. There is no craving, no five hindrances, and no defilement; relying on the exhaustion of that body, he abandons them all. Having removed doubt, he is free from delusion; possessing applied and sustained thought, yet without arrogance. Arising in accordance with the occasion, he is without inversion; having forever eliminated false views, he possesses majestic power. With joy, he extinguishes the fetters and subdues the hosts of Māra.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"Receiving offerings from all people, He delivers the various classes of sentient beings;
Providing protection for those who have no protector, He turns the wheel of Dharma before Māra."
"That wheel has no equal; praised by gods and humans, it already possesses such renown; it is the most supreme.
At that time, for what reason did the World-Honored One subdue that Māra with a vajra?

At that time, the World-Honored One mounted the chariot of the prohibitive precepts and donned the armor of the great vow; possessing the power of patience, he took the great cloud as his pure banner and canopy. With no fetters or latent tendencies, he maintained the embrace of desirelessness and upheld right view. Through the four dhyānas, he attained liberation from craving and pride, becoming pure. His equanimity of mind and equanimity of speech were both entirely purified.

Adorned with eloquence, wisdom, and the power of the supernormal faculties, he maintains his own resolve with firm liberation, free from lust, anger, and delusion. With the light of awakening and liberation blazing brightly, he is fully endowed with all virtues and devoid of the three cravings. Having transcended all fetters, his power and momentum are indestructible; he has reached the ocean of Nirvana, free from all worldly afflictions.

By means of the vajra of wisdom and further through the activity of wisdom, one extinguishes all evil destinies; through the ten powers, liberations, and four fearlessnesses, one subdues [all adversaries]; the practices originally cultivated remain unimpaired; all various forms and images are fully accomplished; and one extinguishes the hosts of Māras without any attachment.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"From various sources come fears; With a mind of adamantine diligence, He subdues those hosts of Māra And all other defilements and fetters."
"Those who possess birth and perception, whose fetters and afflictions are forever exhausted—
because they practice this samādhi, they take refuge in the Muni.
At that time, how does the World-Honored One rain down the rain of the Dharma?

This is what is called turning the wheel of the deathless, extolling this Dharma among the eight classes of beings. The virtuous practices cultivated over a hundred kalpas become firm through compassion; such is the purity of the Dharma, steadfast in the noble ones, abiding in the contemplation of renunciation, and possessing great majestic power and non-attachment.

Furthermore, by the power of patience and wisdom, he made all the gates of liberation firm and secure; following his original vows, he returned with various kinds of precious jewels and necklaces. Employing skillful means, he dwelt in a subtle and wondrous place to the east, beneath a *pāṭala* tree that was most perfectly upright. The heavens filled the void as he sat facing the east in contemplation.

At that time, the Buddha was most excellent; there were also those in the midst who scattered flowers in such joyful celebration and offered praise. Observing this moment, when the assembly of *śrāvakas* heard of such virtues, as well as the various *ṛṣis*, they attained the foremost mastery of mind regarding those Buddhas of the past: the Most Victorious Banner (*Jinastambha*), Lotus Fame (*Padmaśrī*), and Lamp-Light (*Dīpaṃkara*). As for the *Anupūrva* Buddhas, within that great assembly, their minds attained the highest sovereignty.

At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the Omniscient One, was greeted with joy by the assembly of devas; all these were created by the Original Buddha. Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King attains sovereign mastery over his realm, so too does the World-Honored One attain sovereign mastery within his own untainted dharmas.

Just as the Wheel-Turning Sage King has sovereign mastery over his realm and is able to completely sever all disputes among the various classes of sentient beings, so too is the Buddha, the World-Honored One; among the śrāvakas, he is able to completely sever all doubts regarding the Dharma that any sentient beings may have.

Just as that Wheel-Turning Sage King is able to bestow all manner of wealth and treasures upon those who lack them, so too is the Buddha; to those who are destitute of the jewels of the noble ones, he bestows the gift of the seven riches.
Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King shows the True Dharma to beings of external paths, so too does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, guide sentient beings to the path of Nirvana.

Just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, all those confined in prisons are completely released, so too it is with the Buddha, the World-Honored One; when he appears in the world, he completely releases [beings] from the prison of birth and death.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The Dharma King is supreme; among all honored ones, none surpass the Buddha.
Out of compassion for those classes of sentient beings, the Buddha protects them throughout the three realms.”
"One who is worthy of service and reverence, who desires to deliver those not yet delivered—
such a person of merit is a Buddha who awakens those who are unawakened.
At that time, in which city was the World-Honored One?

This refers to the four noble wisdoms of right contemplation. Within that ground of ethical discipline and meditative concentration, one practices the signless and unconditioned. Taking wisdom as the city wall, the three samādhis as the defensive ramparts, the gates of liberation as the inner chambers, right view as the streets and alleys, mindfulness as the walls, the foundations of mindfulness as the moats, the five faculties as the hall, and dhyāna as the inner room; using shame and remorse as one’s own private screen, one points out the path. Traveling by means of the supernormal powers, one remains unobstructed; adorning oneself with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment, taking the fruits of the truths as one’s practice, and delighting in the supreme state of the noble ones, one provides instruction in ultimate peace and delivers all beings across.

Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana possess immeasurable and wholesome perceptions; they constantly travel about teaching and transforming others, fully perfecting their virtues, and all that they have realized is accomplished. They bathe in that bathing pool, using the precepts as unguents; they adorn their bodies with eloquence and wisdom as their Dharma robes; they take the three samādhis as food and the flavor of the Dharma as drink, being fully endowed with the seven jewels.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly of both those in training and those beyond training. He desired to lead that multitude to nirvana and the state of fearlessness, from which there is no regression; he was free from desire toward sentient beings, had attained fearlessness, was fully endowed with the power of the Dharma, had perfected the aggregates and sense bases, and was unattached to worldly defilements.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"All evils have been stilled; They are restrained by the Great Seer, Bringing them to purity, As taught by the One of Ten Powers."
Within those cities and fortresses of the Śākyas, they are constantly fearful of birth, old age, and sickness;
that they do not reach the place of Nirvāṇa is entirely due to the suffering of sentient beings.
— *Saṃgharakṣita-saṃgīta-sūtra*, Middle Volume.
*Saṃgharakṣa-saṃgīti-sūtra*, Scroll II, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kaśmīra and others during the Fu Qin dynasty.
At that time, how did the World-Honored One speak of the path-traces? When he spoke of those path-traces, it was as follows:
The great road of a king is called the royal road; the path of the constellations is called the stellar path. This track is likewise:

that which leads to nirvāṇa is called the path to nirvāṇa. That is the locus of right view, where right intention, right speech, and right livelihood are without deviation; right effort is without deficiency or omission; right mindfulness is immeasurable; and right concentration is such that its form does not change.

Conditioned by those various forms, there is no sensual desire and no defilement; the fetters are forever prevented from arising. There is no attachment to form nor any thorns; because one seeks to extinguish craving, there is no mire. Because one seeks to eliminate wrong views, right view is fully realized; because one equally extinguishes the fetters, they never arise again.

Because that is the subtle and wondrous fruit, it manifests various meanings; because it seeks to eliminate longing, it is free from manifold conceptualizations; because it seeks to attain the bliss of the essential path of deliverance, it accomplishes various fruits; because it is the essential state of non-attachment, it equally transcends name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Because one traverses therein, it is called the Path, which is singular and without duality. All reach that station of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); the object-condition is one, and the practitioner’s own mental vow is called the single entrance.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through his foremost eloquence, realized the Path; because he had attained self-awakening, he was indestructible. His deeds were supreme and free from distracted thoughts, and having already obtained the fruits of all wholesome roots, he was able to awaken those sentient beings. He then preached this Path to lead them to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The classes of sentient beings who have arisen, The Dharma of the Path and the nectar-like Dharma— The Buddha possesses these merits; He is the most supreme in the world.”
"I have now attained for myself, The complete purity of the precepts;
I must speak of this for the sake of others, Therefore, I prostrate with joined palms.

At that time, the World-Honored One knew that Aṅgulimāla was ready to be transformed. At that moment, there were no words from any evil associates; having awakened to this, he proceeded along that path where only one person remained, the road drenched in flowing blood, and everyone witnessed crows and vultures devouring [the corpses] everywhere.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla moved like a swift wind; whenever he raised his foot, the herds of deer and the flocks of birds were all terrified and fled.

Then, while Aṅgulimāla was in the Śāla Grove, looking around in every direction, he saw nothing at all except for the World-Honored One, whose countenance was peerlessly upright and of a purple-gold hue. With skillful deportment, his waist did not lean or bend; his body was exceedingly supple and his gait was dignified and orderly. Exerting all his strength and power, he pursued the Tathāgata from behind.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not alter his original course, nor could he overtake them.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One transformed this ground into pits, ditches, and thornbushes; for this reason, they were unable to catch up with him.
Some say that because he stepped upon the earth with his feet, for this reason he could not reach the World-Honored One.
Others say that he manifested formless great elements, which cannot be grasped by visual consciousness.
Some may say that the Buddha’s merit is inconceivable.

Yet, although Aṅgulimāla’s strength was like that of a wild elephant such that none could withstand him, the Buddha’s majestic power is nonetheless inconceivable; even ten billion Nārāyaṇas, like divine dragons, could not come near the Tathāgata.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla uttered this exclamation:
"I behold what has never been seen before!
He then addressed the World-Honored One:
"This intention is most marvelous and extraordinary," he thought,
and thus he was free from anger and harmful intent.
He reflected as follows:
"Whose grace is this? This must surely be a divine being.
Just as this beauty has returned to me in such an evil age, it is like finding profit during a famine, or like the arising of a feeling of love."
"However, I am unable to reach it; this must surely be a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
For now, I shall rest, as I am utterly exhausted.
Thus he spoke from afar to the World-Honored One.
“For the sake of my body, you who are rare to see or hear of in this world, I now behold your virtue myself; I pray that you will remain for a short while.
The World-Honored One replied:
"You yourself do not abide, yet you say that I abide.
Thereupon, Aṅgulimāla addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The śramaṇa himself does not abide; though I abide, he says I do not abide."
"How is it that I do not abide?
I pray that the Blessed One will explain this in full.
At that time, the Blessed One said:

"If there were no evil, one would abide [in peace]; by upholding the precepts, one protects people for their long-term benefit, as did the disciples of Kāśyapa. Therefore, you do not abide [in such virtue].
His past conduct had involved few evils, yet he was forever stained by blood flowing from his body. He then untied his sword, cast it aside to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Teacher is now my protector; having encountered this holy Master, I seek to become his disciple and shall not transgress the Teacher’s prohibitions and precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu! he said, and then spoke this verse:
"Just as that great ocean water Also gives rise to flames of smoke and fire."
Those who have not yet been subdued should now receive my transformation.
There are also those well-subdued, pure and having attained liberation;
they too shall become my disciples, thus no longer undergoing existence.
"Those who behold him are all struck with fear, as are the various yakṣas and spirits;
yet this most excellent one enters even those abodes of the spirits.

At that time, hearing these words of the Khara-piśāca, the Āḷavaka spirit was filled with a blazing rage, his complexion changed, and the fire of anger rose within him so that his eyes became like red copper. His voice thundered like a clap of lightning, and with countless outbursts of fury, he shook his head, bit his lips, and convulsed his body, then spoke these words:
"I have never seen any among the people of this world who could come to my dwelling," he thought, harboring such doubt:
"For what reason has that person come to me?"
Then those spirits named Vāta, with Likhita and Pīṭha as their leaders—these two being virtuous and detached—caused them to speak to that great spirit, saying: "Do not speak such words!

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, can subdue those who have not yet been subdued; he can establish sentient beings in the attainment of the Unsurpassed Way, and cause all forms of living beings to be protected."
"Such an incompatible field of merit as this, you now address with coarse words and evil speech that do not accord with it.
At that time, his rage intensified, doubling what it had been before. Then the Aravāḍa ghost panted with breath like the flames of fire;

his gaze was extremely malevolent, and he immediately abandoned that ghost realm. Enveloped by wrath, his body became pitch black and his complexion changed, no longer resembling its usual state. Four fangs protruded from his mouth, and his hair turned yellow like gold, with the upper and lower strands interlaced. His form was stained with human blood, all of it wet and not yet dry. He wore lion skins, elephant skins, and yak-tail cowhide. Great flower garlands were like blazing fires. Holding swords and blades in his hands, he struck the ground as he walked, shattering mountain peaks, displacing forest ranges, and uprooting trees.

He raised great clouds to shroud the great radiance, sprinkled water into the void with a voice like the roll of thunder, and arrived at his dwelling place intending to harm the World-Honored One; all manner of trees were completely incinerated and their colors changed, as he held a wheel in his hand amidst thunder and lightning bolts.
Thus, with malice, he observed the Tathāgata, performing various transformations in an attempt to find an opening against him.
At that time, the Buddha spoke this verse:
“Though sentient beings harbor thoughts of fear, my resolve remains unshakable.”
Now that I have attained the Dharma of liberation, I am free from any heart of fear;
dwelling amidst fire, I do not fear the fire, nor do I fear water.
How could those who harbor evil intentions ever be able to harm me?

At that time, having heard the words of the World-Honored One, the Ālambā ghost immediately stilled its mind and was unable to cause destruction. Fearing that place where no human could go, it then sent down hail and rain upon the Tathāgata; yet none fell to the ground, each dispersing elsewhere, and even those that did fall upon the body of the Tathāgata all transformed into celestial *mandārava* flowers.
At that time, the King of the Ghost Spirits, beholding this power and majesty, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; he then conceived a heart of joy and addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"Come forth quickly!"
“Śramaṇa! Then the World-Honored One went out.
At that time, wishing to test the World-Honored One, the ghost spoke these words:
"Go back, śramaṇa! However,
the World-Honored One, being free from any heart of resentment, immediately entered that place.
Thus it was repeated three times, as explained at length in the sūtra.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Neither Śakra nor the Brahmā devas Are able to move a single hair."
How much less could you, with your present strength, possibly harm me?
Now, abandon your anger; if you have any doubts, ask them at once.
Whatever hesitations you may have, I shall resolve them for you point by point.
At that time, the ghost asked this question:
"What is supreme among humans?
The full explanation is as set forth in the Sūtra.
At that time, in this very life, he felt great joy toward the Tathāgata and spoke these verses:
"Never before have I seen anyone like this śramaṇa;
who could abandon the great ocean to seek the water in a cow’s footprint?"
For the sake of my body, he then spoke these words:
"Who would not partake of this flavor? Who would abandon the nectar and depart?
Like that strong man who was being swept away and drowned by the water, he cried out.
Having already uprooted the place of calamity and distress, they dwell securely on the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Their sublime form is beyond compare; it is that which the wise behold.
Whatever its meaning may be, they are able to expound this Dharma in its entirety.
"From this day forth, we take refuge in the Buddha; the Triple Gem is most venerable.
Therefore, those who offer prayers shall all attain deliverance.

Thus, the great deity of the five lands within the realm of Yamaka, who dwells in the city of Rājagṛha, protects the people with his great power. Carriages are abundant and the land is fertile; sages and virtuous people all reside therein, peerless among men. Their food is like nectar, and these three matters are sublime, free from all affliction—just as Nandana Garden is the foremost among the celestial realms.

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was peerless. Devadatta constantly harbored malice toward the World-Honored One without ceasing, and his conduct was contrary to the Dharma. Driven by this hatred, he ascended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—a place where the gardens were flourishing, the trees were lush, and the springs were pure—and grasping a stone with his hand, he intended to hurl it at the Tathāgata, and immediately released it.
At that time, although that rock was devoid of sentient thought, it was still able to hold itself as it gradually descended toward the ground.

Devadatta harbored such malicious intent that various classes of spirits and deities sought to support the rock so that it would not fall. The yakṣa Kumbhīra dwelt on Vulture Peak; when the rock was about to fall by its own power, he conceived this thought:

"Although this is an evil deed, we yakṣas ought to accomplish this matter with these very bodies of ours, so that the World-Honored One may experience hundreds of thousands of joys, if I am able to perform this task."
Then he spoke this verse:
"My mind is pure and without blemish; I have given rise to manifold meanings.
Now that I am departing from this body, No one can harm the Most Victorious One."

At that time, Devadatta released a stone toward the Tathāgata. Then, from atop the mountain, a spirit caught the stone with its hand; however, a fragment of the stone fell upon the Tathāgata, causing blood to flow from his toes as a retribution for this act. Devadatta shall undergo immeasurable suffering and, due to this karmic fruit, he is destined to enter hell.

At that time, when the stone fell to the ground, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven scattered flowers as an offering through the liberation of space; the flowers scattered then filled the void. In that Hall of Transformation where the Trāyastriṃśa gods dwell, there is the Pārijāta tree; the Buddha’s radiance shone far upon it, illuminating all sentient beings with compassion free from pride.
At that time, while the Brahmin Pāṭikāputra reviled the World-Honored One with five hundred accusations, the bhikṣus Śāriputra, Mañjuśrī, and others praised the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata felt no distress if he were reviled, nor did he feel joy if he were praised.
He then spoke this verse:
"Though undergoing suffering, his mind does not waver; He remains as peaceful and luminous as an immovable mountain."
His tranquil mind is most firm; thus he bows his hands to the divine immortals.
For the sake of other sentient beings, his merit is immeasurable;
like a father’s love for his child, who would not bow their hands in reverence?

Thus have I heard: The World-Honored One was staying within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha. At that time, the World-Honored One, endowed with immeasurable merit, dressed in his robes and took up his bowl at the proper hour. Surrounded by a great assembly, his faculties were perfectly composed; observing himself, he was free from all agitation. His gait was measured and dignified, neither hurried nor violent, as he led a multitude of countless bhikṣus toward that place.

At that time, the King of Magadha had an elephant named Dhanapāla, whose physical appearance was exceedingly handsome, with three protuberances on its head and a voice so clear and resonant that it was difficult to restrain its will wherever it turned. Upon hearing a strange sound, it would become enraged; upon seeing its own reflection, it would likewise become enraged. No one could stand before it, and it acted according to its desires. Even when engaged in battle, its strength was neither impaired nor diminished.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered that city, which was fully equipped with defensive towers, battlements, and parapets; it was teeming with people, some of whom were sorrowful and others joyful, fearing harm to the Tathāgata yet desiring to draw near to him.
At that time, Devadatta made the elephant cub drunk and released it.
Having released the elephant, Devadatta then spoke this verse:
"I claim for myself great strength, As well as the ten powers of the body."
“Today the assembly has gathered; all shall here attain extinction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, free from fear, spoke this verse:
“There are a thousand Airāvaṇas, yet none can overcome me.”
"How much less this tiny insect, which seeks to harm the Supreme among Men?
At that time, being free from all conceptual thought, I spoke this verse:
"The power and majesty of desirelessness—yet sentient beings possess minds of desire."
"Having eliminated this desire for retribution, I shall likewise harbor no disordered thoughts.
Furthermore, he spoke this verse:
"Though I have now broken it, this great elephant is exceedingly firm."
"I have now subdued him; he is unsurpassed in all the world.

At that time, Dantapāla gazed intently at the Tathāgata’s form; his complexion was exceedingly dark. Seeing the elephant with its tail raised and its body square and imposing, all who beheld it were struck with terror, yet the elephant ran toward the Tathāgata.

At that time, the bhikṣus, having received the power of the Tathāgata’s grace and following his instructions, were to avoid this wicked elephant; they each fled far away from the Tathāgata’s presence. Only the Venerable Ānanda remained behind the Tathāgata, for throughout countless lifetimes he had always been joined with the Tathāgata; he neither spared his own life nor would he abandon the Tathāgata.

At that time, the elephant Dhanapāla was consumed by a fierce blaze of hatred that enveloped his body as he sought to harm the Tathāgata; however, the fire of his hatred gradually subsided, as described at length in the sūtra.

At that time, his hand possessed wheel-marks (*cakrāṅka*) that were exceedingly subtle and peerless. Then the Tathāgata raised his hand and placed it upon the elephant’s head; with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, free from any thought of malice, the elephant heard the Tathāgata’s words and immediately shed tears. It bowed its head and face at the Tathāgata’s feet, licking them with its tongue, and could not move away.
At that time, the elephant was seized by this fear; its body lost all strength and vigor, and it could no longer control its excrement and urine.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, through this noble and holy means, spoke this verse:
"Free from desire and pride, The World-Honored One is without such defilements."
"At that time, having given rise to a heart of compassion, you shall surely be reborn in a celestial realm.

At that moment, the World-Honored One, with this voice, felt redoubled joy; with a serene and pleasant countenance, he placed his forehead and nose against the Tathāgata’s feet and returned to his own country.
The multitude of people, seeing this unprecedented event—the elephant having been subdued—were filled with joy and free from fear; all of them conceived faith and delight in the Tathāgata.
At that time, he spoke this verse:
"As a mountain cannot be moved, how much more so can one overcome anger?
By conquering those enemies, one is like the Elapattra dragon."
Possessing such virtues, with power and majesty beyond compare,
the Lion among Men, the Great Teacher— all shall come to pay him homage.
Such beings as these possess no heart of delusion.
His name is venerated throughout the three realms; his awakened mind has no equal.
Even among such classes of sentient beings, those afflicted by the malady of anger find their dispositions entirely stilled; his steadfastness is renowned far and wide.
"Adorned with wisdom, the mind is pure and free from attachment;
the ten powers are fully perfected—for this reason, one should prostrate.

At that time, the King was like the moon in the sky, free from all dust; his mental activities were stilled and all his tasks were accomplished. The seven seers were likewise adorned as if with necklaces, yet they were without any defilement. Like the star Elapatra, they were adorned by their very nature, and wherever they went, clouds followed behind them, their bodies graced by various kinds of ornaments.

Having heard this, he proceeded like that divine elephant roaming at will; he had no doubt regarding the precious treasures, and while the fourfold army and the people surrounded him, he raised a torch upon the elephant and held it with its trunk.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the city of Rājagṛha. Desiring to see the Tathāgata, [the king] went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that moment, the World-Honored One saw that King Bimbisāra had emerged for a brief interval, surrounded by an incalculable multitude. The king then thought to himself:
"I have come from afar; I ought to protect myself."
Having formed this thought, he addressed Jīvaka; upon seeing [the King], he spoke these words: "Will you not restore me to life?

At that moment, King [Bimbisāra’s] countenance became incomparably handsome and surpassed all others; flowers and fruits flourished, and there was no dust at all. Endowed with the three qualities, his voice was like that of a king of bees—sweet and excellent. In that park, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, he came from afar wishing to see the Tathāgata. Having seen him, he looked back repeatedly at Jīvaka and said to him:
"What is that object which occupies the center?
Then Jīvaka addressed the king, saying:
"This is called the *uṣṇīṣa*."
Then the king asked again:
"Is this spontaneous, or is it not spontaneous?"
Jīva addressed the king, saying, "The fruits that are produced are sown from previous causes; they are not created in the present.
The king replied:
"Furthermore, by what fruits is one established as a bodhisattva?
"By that which was originally born, that which was originally conceived, the conduct originally performed, and the body originally formed."
The full details are as set forth in the sutra.
At that time, the king spoke these verses:
"Just like the bright light of the sun, there may be various kinds [of radiance];"
The uṣṇīṣa on his crown is unsurpassed, let alone his other marks;
his countenance is serene and joyful, and the Muni is free from timidity.
Having emitted this radiance, it illuminates the lands throughout the ten directions.
Then the king went to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha said to Jīvaka,
"Why did you speak in such a manner?
Jīvaka replied to the king:
"Thus, the Heavenly King who is able to subdue pride attains a noble and exalted station, while those who are proud are born in a lowly place.
At that time, the King himself became still and reflected upon these words, then spoke thus:
"This is a field of merit; should I practice this deed?"
"How can I, who am so noble and honored, pay homage to him?
He is without finery, while I am now clad in royal robes and a celestial crown.

Although that man is upright and his mind is at rest, and though he is endowed with all the marks of excellence without any ugliness, those marks of his are exceedingly subtle and immovable, like a mountain."

He then went to the gate; with a heart filled with joy, his hair stood on end. Because of his mind directed toward the renunciation of the world, he manifested the signs of desirelessness. He prostrated himself at the feet of the World-Honored One and spoke thus:

"Just as the World-Honored One possesses such a physical form and has attained the perfection of a rightly directed mind, may the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus likewise cause me, Prince Udāyibhadra, to become so as well."
He then inquired about this matter and, rejoicing in these words, also spoke this verse:
"Just as the ocean has no limit, And its waters move when stirred by the wind, The Holy One is immovable; Now I behold the Supreme among Men."
"Śakra comes to pay homage, as do the hosts of Brahmā deities;
I too shall now show them respect and take refuge in the World-Honored One.

At that time, the brahmin Jātiśronī, like a pure white flower, mounted a horse-drawn carriage and, surrounded by his disciples, departed from Śrāvastī. Desiring to test the Tathāgata, he traveled by carriage as far as it could go, then alighted and entered the park on foot. There he engaged the Tathāgata in a gradual discussion of the Dharma and sat to one side.

At that time, in the place where the World-Honored One resided, nothing was seen to exist; yet the Rūpa-kāya of the Tathāgata appeared exceedingly subtle and wondrous, peerless and without any timidity, possessing the marks of a Wheel-Turning Sage King. Beholding this body, one perceives such dharmas through the eye: just as the Dharma of the World-Honored One is profound and subtle, so too is the Brahma-conduct (brahmacarya) without fixed location, yet it possesses such great merit, praised and proclaimed by the wise. Lustful desires possess neither solidity nor essence, yet they are not false.
At that time, the brahmin asked this question:
"How is it, Venerable One, do you yourself know that you practice the holy life?
Or do you not practice the holy life?"
"Is it that the faculties have been established thus from the very beginning?
It is difficult to measure this.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:

"If one speaks in such a manner, it is neither deficient nor incomplete; it is not without power, nor is it devoid of manifold practices; it is utterly pure, free from blemish, and constitutes the cultivation of the holy life."
"If someone were to say to us, 'This is what was said,' what would the meaning of this be?
This is explained at length as in the Sūtra.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśronī again questioned the World-Honored One:
"What is meant by 'deficiency'?
What is meant by 'outflow'?
What is meant by 'activity'?"
"How is it that one is not without power?
How is it that among all practices, this Brahma-faring is supremely pure and peerless?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied:

"Thereupon, the brahmin should practice this: seeking the further delight of sensual desires, or when there is a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) who personally experiences pleasure and pain, he contemplates the eye and forms. Thus, the practitioner of the holy life should initially seek the holy life. If he gives rise to conceptual attachment toward them, it is called a 'deficiency' (*chidda*); if he calculates their numerical aggregates, it is called an 'outflow' (*āsava*). That which is cognized by the mind is not without power; though there is no defilement, the mind runs wild therein and gives rise to impure thoughts. Because these are the defilements of the holy life, it is therefore called 'the holy life' (*brahmacarya*)."
As explained at length in the sūtra:

"O Brahmin, when I observe this heap of impurities covered by skin, I discern the body within it; since my craving for physical form has been exhausted, how could I still regard the eye or contemplate the objects of the eye?"
"However, O Brahmin, when I observe that contact is also without volitional formations, how could there be contact?

One becomes stained by desire for contact and experiences its smoothness. Yet, O Brahmin, when I observe that all things are impermanent, how could one who desires not have a mind free from attachment?"

O Brahmin, regarding these phenomena, I do not even observe them; since I distinguish between both men and women, how could I give rise to thoughts of desire for a woman and run toward or become attached to her?
Furthermore, O Brahmin, if one has no thought of male desire, nor is associated with the thought of female, yet still gives rise to the thought of desire— just as that Brahmin,
having attained the bliss of liberation through certain limits, when would he ever recall his original karmic actions?

Thereafter, certain Brahmins of ignoble birth, desiring to be delivered from suffering and distress, left the household life to study the Path. They cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) with this vow, yet for seven reasons they were not in accord with the holy life; they were neither free from taints nor possessed of manifold practices.
As explained at length in the sūtras:
"Furthermore, O Brahmin, if there are sentient beings who possess distracted perceptions and are not free from craving and desire, how should one regard such classes of sentient beings?"
All those who harbor pure perceptions regarding this body, and whose desires for this foul-smelling vessel within are not yet exhausted—
just as when a Brahmin mixes water with milk, such that there is both this milk and this mixture, so too is this conjoined craving and desire.
One should examine it thus: the tendons and bones are joined together, and within lies putrid filth; what is there to be craved?
It is like a Brahmin who first places a sweet taste in the mouth of an infant, only to have the child drink bitterness afterward.

This is also like this: when the conditions assemble and the thought of desire arises, one is able to endure the various hundreds of kinds of characteristics of the suffering of desire. It is just as when a newly dead calf is examined; seeing its skin and milk, one observes that many new calves have died. Taking the skin and fermenting it with grass, one fashions it into the shape of a living calf and places it before its mother.
Because the mother believes her child is alive, her milk does not fail.

This case is also like this: when one transcends the realms of death and so forth, yet perceives their appearances and gives rise to thoughts of attachment, it is like a hungry and thirsty Brahmin who dreams of eating sweet delicacies and drinks, thereby leaping for joy; however, that person has actually eaten nothing.

This is also like that: foolish people who are greedily attached to sensual desires are no different from those in a dream; they give rise to thoughts through their associations, yet such persons truly possess no inclination toward wholesome conduct, whether they be men or women, or whatever various transformations they may undergo.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"This is not the true Dharma; how can one crave desire and anger?
O Brahmin, you should observe well: the root of suffering is difficult to uproot."
"Approaching the Path is most essential; one should sever the mind of craving and desire.
Through the Noble Eightfold Path, you shall reach the place of ultimate goodness.
At that time, the five men encountered the Tathāgata, and having seen him, they said to one another:

"This person has come here, yet the purpose for which he originally set out remains unfulfilled; whatever he has seen and heard extensively, and whatever he has conceived in his mind, he lacks restraint and caution, and through various diligent and painful practices, he remains deluded and has not accomplished the Way."
The full account is as set forth in the sūtra.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I pity these deluded people who have established their own restrictive rules; those who hold such restrictions lack a heart of reverence toward the Tathāgata."

At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the place where those people were and sat upon a pure ground. He bound himself [in meditation] to investigate from what [afflictions] they arose, desiring to treat their illness.
Then the Buddha said to the five men: "Why do you speak such words?"
They went on almsround together and taught him the profound Dharma.
At that time, the five men did not accept his instruction, perceiving this Dharma as extremely painful.
Then they said to the World-Honored One:

"In the past, you practiced the Way with diligent austerity for six years, eating but one sesame seed and one grain of rice a day, yet you still did not attain the Way; how much less now, when you follow the whims of your own mind and mouth to speak of having attained it?"
"Eating sweet delicacies and fine foods, and wearing robes of precious jewels, they nourish their bodies according to their every desire.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed them, saying:
"Monks, how is it that you perceive any change or alteration in the Tathāgata’s complexion?"
"The faculties and mind are tranquil, and his countenance is upright and handsome; is his present appearance not different from his former features?
That realm has passed away. He replied:
"Now he is so handsome that there is none to compare with him.
The World-Honored One replied,
"If one had not originally attained this ambrosia, who would have attained ambrosia within these three thousand worlds?"

I have also heard that the devas and asuras obtain ambrosia within the great ocean at the base of Mount Sumeru. This is likewise so: within these three thousand worlds, one obtains the flavor of the ambrosia of wisdom through a courageous mind.

This is most marvelous and extraordinary, never before seen in the world. The practice cultivated over hundreds of thousands of kalpas—stilling the mind—is the most sublime; it is the profound flavor of liberation and mastery, far removed from name-and-form. For the sake of those sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma; he endures great toil without ever shrinking back. Because of all the fetters, he does not give rise to worldly afflictions; desiring to open the heart-mind of wisdom, he dwells in the mother’s womb, and through this cycle of birth and death, he brings its ultimate origin to an end.

Because there is no cessation, it is inexhaustible; because it is eternal, the Dharma is never diminished; because there is no sorrow or grief, it is blissful; because one seeks to extinguish the fetters, one creates no new karma; and because one has been praised by the assembly of great seers and perfected all qualities, yet my practice has been diligent and arduous for the sake of all living beings, I shall now preach the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s halo extended seven feet, his countenance was like Mount Anavatapta, and he was revered by the three periods of time. All-Knowing as he was, he spoke without any obstruction:
"Such, O bhikṣu, is called the root of suffering; it brings about the attainment of non-abiding nirvāṇa."
The details are as explained in the sūtra.
Praised by gods and humans, his radiance was inexhaustible; at that time, the sun was obscured and did not appear.

Furthermore, these people—some wearing exquisite garments, others wearing celestial robes—approached the Tathāgata, all adorned with various celestial crowns of differing colors, or with necklaces falling to the ground, for they were parched with hunger and thirst for the ambrosia of the World-Honored One.
At that time, he spoke this verse:
“The World-Honored One is likewise unborn, Bringing benefit to the multitudes of devas and humans;
Like tasting the flavor of ambrosia, One shall never again suffer the affliction of hunger or thirst.”
"Today, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, at the time of his birth, was praised by the world;
he shall now drink the flavor of the profound Dharma and has already reached the realm of liberation.
At that time, as he thus observed with various modes of conduct the Noble Truth of Suffering, [he considered]: "From what does the suffering of the initial conception in the womb arise?"
To dwell forever in darkness without seeing the light of a lamp is, for this reason, the most grievous form of birth.

Contemplating these marks of suffering, one sees that birth is long-term suffering; being incapable of bearing it, it is the suffering of karma over a long duration; there is the suffering of striving with physical strength to accomplish tasks while harboring expectations;
and there is the suffering of the mind never being satisfied, failing to obtain what one seeks.
Not fulfilling one's hopes while protecting [them] is suffering;
employing various skillful means with the desire to prevent their loss while protecting them, yet seeing them gradually wear away, is suffering;
when various afflictions all arrive, even though one has already attained the further shore, it is difficult to avoid the suffering of internal and external disputes.
When kinsmen and wealth are all dispersed, the sorrow of recollecting them is difficult to forget;
not being free from craving and desire, there is the suffering of the various fetters and afflictions.
Desire is the greatest suffering because it has not yet been extinguished.
Hatred is suffering because unwholesome deeds are not extinguished;
delusion is the greatest suffering because there is no illumination;
pride is suffering because the mind is inflamed.
Arrogance is suffering, for it lacks the sense of nobility and humility;
friendship is suffering, for the mind cannot bear separation;
craving is the greatest suffering, for one is never satiated by its relish.
Greed and envy are suffering, for the mind finds no liberation;
lack of precepts is suffering, because of subsequent regret;
one's own views are suffering, because the True Dharma is not seen.
Yet there are all the fetters; taking form itself as suffering, having nothing to rely upon as suffering, and seeking retribution as suffering;

that which is composed of trees, grasses, and the four great elements, bound together by mutual attachment to give rise to various causes and conditions, is the suffering of the internal four great elements;
and the various transformations and anomalies, as well as the aggregates (*skandhas*), are suffering.
Because they are subject to nature, the sense bases (*āyatana*) are suffering;
because one cannot be separated from their support, the objects (*viṣaya*) are suffering;
because they draw forth external forms, painful sensations are suffering.
Because it consumes the physical form, pleasant sensation is suffering;
because it arises from suffering, neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation is suffering;
because it arises from sensory objects, perception is the foremost suffering.
Because sentient beings engage in conditioned activities, consciousness is the foremost suffering;
arising in dependence upon those activities, old age consists in the weakening and impairment of the sense faculties, and is thus the foremost suffering;
when the four great elements no longer function in harmony, death is the foremost suffering.
Furthermore, receiving a different form is suffering through association with what one hates;
being separated from those one is fond of and not obtaining what one desires is the greatest suffering, indeed a most grievous suffering.
To state it in brief: the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Constantly bearing heavy burdens to the destinations they go toward: in hell, suffering consists of the burning and scorching of their physical forms;
among animals, suffering consists of devouring one another;
among hungry ghosts, suffering consists of hunger and thirst afflicting their bodies.
The human realm is suffering, characterized by various unwholesome actions;
the celestial realms are suffering, for when merit is exhausted one must inevitably fall, descending according to those realms into the three evil destinies; thus, the desire realm is suffering.
Ensnared by craving and attachment, there is likewise no wisdom in the realm of form or the formless realm; all are entirely suffering.
Thus, one is oppressed by these three types of suffering and is completely encompassed by them.
At that time, because of the activities of body and mind, one may create suffering through even a single action; all such created actions result entirely in suffering.
Thus, these manifold sufferings have no end as long as their causal conditions are not exhausted. One should realize that form is thus: it is the doing of the foolish.

However, the Srotāpanna has thoroughly exhausted its source; the Sakṛdāgāmin has a slight remainder, no more than the thickness of a hair; the Anāgāmin should eliminate it; and upon reaching the Arhat, it is forever exhausted without remainder, appearing as a brilliant illumination for the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, acting as a great protector for all classes of sentient beings, spoke this verse:
"Through countless hundreds of practices, They constantly create karma of suffering and affliction;
Because they harbor this difficulty regarding form, This realization is manifest in the present."
"That which is truly impermanent, understand it to be fundamentally and entirely empty;
established by the nature of things (*dharmatā*), one should always awaken to this for oneself.
At such a time, how could suffering arise again?"

That which is called the realm of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-viṣaya*) is the perfection of the five sense faculties. If one understands that this realm of specific characteristics involves the process of cognitive transformation (*parivṛtti*), it is therefore utterly pure; yet it is not perceived by the ignorant, as it does not correspond to their [dualistic] wisdom.
Furthermore, there are those of sharp faculties whom the foolish call blind and ignorant.

The World-Honored One and the śrāvakas, through their original cultivated practices, have wisdom and roots of goodness that naturally accord with one another; they observe the Noble Truth of Suffering exactly as it was practiced.
How should one contemplate this suffering of birth and death?

One should know that the Noble Truth of Suffering is entirely impermanent, and holding fast to it without abandoning it, all should together give rise to such a mind: to contemplate suffering as suffering is the most sublime.

Contemplating emptiness within suffering, one first attains the subtle and sublime equanimity that transcends that state; when contemplating emptiness within suffering, all such things are phenomena subject to dispersal, and one naturally observes them in this way.
Contemplating non-self within suffering, that wisdom is accomplished through faith.

At the outset, there is this supreme dharma (*mūrdha*) which brings great benefit; repeatedly seeking skillful means and the merit of equalizing wisdom, one remains free from expectation. The forest of samādhi is without deficiency or leakage; external objects are forever exhausted and there is no attachment. By means of conceptual reflection, the dust of defilement is removed.

All objective realms are suffering, yet they cannot cause ruin; having eliminated craving for existence, one is neither fearful nor violent, but with a serene countenance, observes the realms within oneself.

Manifesting light therein, they give rise to the great lamp of illumination throughout the three periods of time; wishing to destroy those fetters and rescue beings from the evil realms, they maintain no sense of self or other for the sake of the multitudes and remain free from indolence. Having attained the flavor of the nectar of immortality, they discern its chapters and, in order to equally deliver others from birth and death, they circulate through the four spheres of existence.

Desiring to illuminate those sentient beings, he diligently practices asceticism, exhausting all possibilities; yet there is no fixed location and no inversion. One who has eliminated such inversions is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"When there is clarity amidst suffering, Pure and immeasurable mindfulness,
Tasteless yet exceedingly brilliant— This is what people praise."
With such wisdom as this, they find delight in the resonance of sounds;
observing the ten powers of the Buddha, they protect the various classes of sentient beings.
Possessing the vision of the prohibitions and precepts, they receive the growth and benefit bestowed by the Tathāgata.
With a resolve as firm as a diamond, he discerns that all things are empty.
Having uprooted the very foundation of craving, he is likewise free from all suffering and affliction.
One should prostrate with a tranquil mind to this most supreme being, who has no equal.
"How should one contemplate the Blessed One?

It is by means of such untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that he perceives the power and majesty of the site of the place of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). For the sake of the world, he contemplates the light of the world; he thoroughly observes all the ascetic practices he cultivated therein. Toward each and every sentient being, he contemplates a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, desiring to bring peace and security to them amidst their immeasurable toil and suffering."

Contemplating such ascetic practices within various spheres of experience, he observes them for himself; amidst the great assembly, he contemplates the Tathāgata preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma, observing the distribution of its meaning and the mastery of the Dharma. If his Dharma-eye is pure, he further contemplates that Dharma-body as being devoid of any notion of a sentient being. Even when performing such contemplations, he does not speak of prohibitive precepts.
I have heard that there was once a venerable one named Upavāsa, who had a disciple named Pāmaka. He traveled to the realm of Mathurā and took up residence there.
When he arrived, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded as described at length in the Sūtra.
Having never seen such a person before and not understanding his deportment, he entered the village of courtesans.
When those courtesans saw this bhikṣu—young, handsome, and free from dust—they were filled with joy upon seeing him, and their lustful desires blazed up intensely.

Then that bhikṣu entered a brothel; observing such fetters and afflictions, he did not wish to create further bonds. Thus, through this method of purifying liberation, he swiftly attained the fruit of this dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke these words and recited this verse:
“Desire is like that poisonous drug; desire is an impure practice;
desire ruins one’s virtuous beauty and causes people to fall into the evil realms.”
Having spoken thus, he withdrew and departed.
That man’s lustful intent was so intense that, for the sake of that bhikṣu, he performed a *caṇḍālī* incantation and explained its meaning to that *caṇḍālī*.

At that time, the Caṇḍālī adorned this woman and manifested a village settlement. She brought a bhikṣu there and said, "Observe this place; it is no different from the palace of Śakra Devānām-indra. The summer hall is lofty and vast, beyond compare. Within that summer hall are countless varieties of finely adorned bedding. Upon the place where one lies are embroidered rugs and cushions. Behold this site, strewn all around with various flowers and perfumes, and growing at its borders are various blue lotuses and fragrant orchids."
Having made such an observation, he performed this binding incantation and said to the bhikṣu:
"This is extremely subtle and wonderful; we may enjoy it together.
Then the bhikṣu Patamarṣi replied:
"I have observed all of this, and I shall observe the rest as well.
The Caṇḍāla asked, "What is that 'rest'?"
The almsbowl replied silently:
“I now observe the fruit of my actions: desiring that which is most supreme is suffering;
in the end, I shall enter hell and undergo the torment of the boiling cauldrons.”
At that time, the Caṇḍālī replied:
"Stop, stop, Bhikṣu!
Do not speak such words to me."
The bhikṣu Pātra remained silent and replied, "These words are the delusions of a fool seeking to bewitch me; I do not associate with you.
When the Caṇḍālī saw this, she immediately created a great pit of fire, free from any dust or smoke.
Then the bhikṣu Pāṭalaka replied,
“I have already seen this fire pit. The Caṇḍāla replied:
"If one does not wish to associate with women, it would be better to die by entering this fire pit.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:

"Although this fire is terrifying, those who avoid the fire yet associate with desire find that desire is more fierce than a great fire. If one commits an act of desire, one will later suffer immeasurable retribution; it would be better for me to enter this fire pit today rather than commit such desire."
Yet my teacher’s supernormal powers are peerless; how could I ever contravene his instruction?
For this reason, I shall enter the fire pit and die, rather than live by violating my desire for purity.
Now that I have renounced both matters,
how could I establish prohibitive precepts for the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and then violate them myself?
For this reason, I shall enter the fire pit and die.
Having reflected thus, he wished to take his saṃghāṭī robe and alms bowl to give them to that person.
At that time, the caṇḍāla replied,
"What use have you for these robes and bowl?"
The Bhikṣu Patamkara replied:
"Now, to all these fellow practitioners who hold my robes and bowl as an offering,
and to all those gathered here, convey my words to them:"
“The bhikṣu named Pāṭalaka, having encountered this place of calamity,
now casts himself into a pit of fire to die, rather than accept those sensual desires.
Thus it was that both of them left the household life to study the Path, as is explained at length in the Sūtra.
At that time, he further spoke this verse:
"Though the worldly cultivation of goodness be slight, If one contemplates and remembers it without forgetting,
One will not be subject to those desires, For the sake of delivering all sentient beings."
How much more so when the Ambrosia is opened—O World-Honored One, the most wondrous of all!
How should one cultivate merit?
That wisdom arises in accordance with the occasion.
At that time, how does the World-Honored One circulate and come and go while being aware of the origin of arising?
It is said that regarding these words there are two kinds of winds: those of physical form and merit, and those perceived by the mind; these are called the two winds.
That wind of physical form gives rise to various thoughts of craving.
What is perceived by the mind is like a flower in full bloom, fresh, bright, and pure.
Just as that wind perceives the excellence of the deeds of liberation, so too is this mind like snow turning into water.
Grasping at internal and external objects, a cool breeze arises; one perceives that intention, which maintains immeasurable non-destruction.
There are six objective mechanisms, externally driven by the four great elements and bound by the power of the four great elements and the faculties.

A gentle wind arises within him, and gradually wisdom is born; it is just as when he lifts his feet, all of which is due to the virtue of his fundamental practice. He does not lose the characteristics of what was originally performed; as the ankle bones move back and forth, fire arises from them, and as all the bones bend, extend, contract, and relax, the tendons and veins gradually loosen as he harbors his aspirations.
Furthermore, whether looking or gazing, with eyes open or closed, the internal contact of the sense faculties gradually intensifies as it follows their coming and going.
