Moreover, whether eating, chewing, bending, stretching, or contracting, all these are produced by the physical form; likewise, other mental formations depend on the wind of warmth for their removal, while the wind of inversion also blows them away.

The sounds produced by the lips and teeth are all phenomena created from seeds within the original intention; yet wherever that wind resides, it possesses excellence and contains these words, possessing such sounds as these, where it speaks thus:
"If one does not perform merit, how can one not be bound?"
I have said this: "There is this mechanism;

externally there is decay and ruin, and internally there are the various formations (*saṃskāra*). When these do not arise, there is exhaustion, and there is nourishment. It is like a wise chariot being mounted here; by depending on such noble and exalted dharmas, one depends on and relies upon those perceptions of time that are inverted."
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"This is most marvelous and extraordinary— The wisdom that realizes emptiness and non-existence.
Dependent upon one another in succession, The mechanical device is the most essential."
Nor does it touch that mind; though body and mind depend upon one another, and such manifold things exist, they are delusive illusions and subtle.
At that time, for the sake of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), how is the holy life not disturbed?

Not following others' teachings, he wanders alone without companion; among humans, his meritorious deportment is most subtle and exquisite. He is unattached to any sentient beings, and no one can equal the deeds he performs. Sentient beings are immeasurable, yet he relies upon all subtle and wondrous Dharmas. Because the Dharma is spontaneous (*svabhāva*), the All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is indestructible. Having perfected the essential path, whatever he seeks to accomplish will certainly bear fruit without doubt.
Endowed with all virtues and surrounded by śrāvakas, he gives rise to all merit and all that is subtle and wondrous.

At that time, the World-Honored One was the most supreme among those with exquisite physical forms; having accomplished all virtues, he dispelled the darkness and was unattached to the world. Unattached to the three periods of time, he cast off all fetters and attained great compassion. His mind was free from distracted thoughts; having already crossed over the place of sorrow and fear to reach the state of peace and security, he had long subdued his own mind and spontaneously bestowed [this teaching] upon others.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"The holy life is most sublime; The merit of loving-kindness is perfected.
If others hear this teaching, Both devas and humans shall pay homage."
"In the True Dharma there is no duality, and that bliss is likewise without duality;
one will surely become a noble sage (ārya). Therefore, I prostrate to the Sage.

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha), possesses the most subtle and wondrous stage of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi). He has eliminated all fetters and afflictions (saṃyojana) and is free from attachment. He cannot be burned by fire, and his realization surpasses the wind. Furthermore, he excels in merit and fearlessness; having perfected the great assembly, he bears the heavy burden of the multitude. His profound correspondence with reality is inconceivable.

Just as a lion has no timid or weak mind and his countenance is serene and joyful, he has cultivated non-attachment for the sake of those outside the teachings; like a lotus, he remains unstained. Because he relies on the assembly, he brings about its own transformation; he can accomplish whatever his mind desires. Because he has uprooted all fetters (*saṃyojana*), he is the most excellent among the assembly. It is excellent to undergo various births through manifold manifestations; it is excellent to seek one's own welfare within all forms of birth.

One should prostrate to the supreme field of merit; among those who protect the people, the King is foremost. Not forming such views, his meaning is exceedingly profound. Abandoning all defiled dharmas, the Moon is most excellent. Discerning all phenomena, Vaiśravaṇa is foremost. With a clear and penetrating resonance, the Lion’s Roar is foremost. For those wishing to plant seeds in a fertile field, there is the higher training (*adhiśikṣā*). Abandoning all fields of worldly activity, Śakra Devendra is foremost. Among all the merits of the world, he is foremost; manifesting the path to Nirvāṇa, he is likewise supreme. Out of compassion, he protects all sentient beings; liberating them from all bonds is wondrous.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“The merits of the Tathāgata are universally and entirely complete;
dwelling in the house of the Śākya clan, he is like the ocean gathering all manner of treasures.”
"And the remaining Buddhas and their assemblies, filling the three worlds—if you wish to seek the further shore, you should receive it from the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the lion among men, was filled with the color of joy for the sake of all-encompassing wisdom; his throat possessed incomparable merit, and the merits of his Buddha-dharma were endowed with the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*). He moved with profound composure, having abandoned coarse and vulgar speech; his body was upright and his mind correct, fully endowed with manifold wisdom. His eyes were the pure roots and sprouts [of enlightenment]; he discerned all dharmas and extolled their virtues. His knowledge of the unknown was like a rain of nectar, impossible to obstruct or destroy; endowed with the ten powers, his valor surpassed all others. Having realized the destination of all things, he went forth to rescue and deliver them.

His great compassion, meditative liberation, and the four immeasurables were never lacking; moreover, he ate his food with the contemplation of it as being like the taste of excrement, free from the flavor of craving, and having attained fearlessness, he subdued those hosts.

It was just as when the lion, king of deer, lets out a roar; those who hear the sound all flee toward the four quarters—the valley-dwellers to the valleys and the cave-dwellers to the caves—while the birds fly into the void.

This is also like that: if they hear the sound of impermanence, these ordinary worldlings and long-lived beings all harbor fear; they all flee from the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), just as when that nāga-elephant hears the roar of a lion, it involuntarily voids its bowels or breaks its tether and runs away.
It is likewise with the long-lived devas of the form realm; hearing the teaching on impermanence, they remain attached to their pleasures, each harboring this heart of craving and attachment.

At that time, the World-Honored One was the lion-deer king; his mind was entirely free from fear, he had realized the fruit of the Path and would never regress. All who beheld him rejoiced in his subtle and wondrous samatha-vipaśyanā, knowing that his merit was beyond all delusion or ignorance.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Just as that lion’s roar Startles all who hear it,
So by discerning phenomena with wisdom, Their various distinct names are revealed."
"In the face of the terrors of birth and death, the Buddha’s virtues are beyond measure;
therefore, I prostrate to the Lion, the King of Kings among lions.
At that time, the World-Honored One was a bull elephant among men, fully endowed with all wisdom, his every limb and joint in perfect proportion to his head.

That which is called the head of wisdom arises from wisdom; mindfulness is its head, and it relies upon *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as its belly. Through rest and liberation, it is spontaneously perfected without a teacher’s instruction. Taking the faculty of faith as its sublime Dharma and binding itself with the power of faith, it possesses such strength as to protect purity as its tusks, thereby eliminating the evil realms. With shame and remorse as its attendants and the excellence of the body as its ears, the Buddha-body is fulfilled and free from malice. Cultivating the holy life to its ultimate source, one seeks skillful means with courageous non-retrogression; among all things in the world, there is nothing subtle or wondrous that can surpass these merits.

Like Mount Sumeru, he practices and cultivates dhyāna like a sharp blade; his awakened mind is sovereign, serene in the seven stations. He contemplates all phenomena as impermanent, suffering, empty, and entirely without self; with nirvāṇa as cessation and purity, that which he upholds is like ambrosia. Possessing the power and majesty of the ten strengths, all who behold him rejoice.

By destroying the conduct of pride and arrogance, he takes as his objective support the fruit of liberation. That nectar is free from calculation and attachment; it is produced by his original intention. He partakes of the fruit of the nectar of liberation; like nectar, he receives offerings and sustenance, yet removes all impurities and filth. Even when taking food, he does not store it away, having well subdued himself throughout ninety-one kalpas.
At that time, he possessed this concentrated mind, free from all disturbances.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"Harmonious and joyful, free from all disturbances, With an extremely pure and settled mind."
I bow my head to the one of immeasurable virtue, the elephant-king among men.
That being possesses virtue; he has destroyed all perceptions of form.
His eye is pure and free from blemish; I bow my head to the most supreme Awakened One.

That Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses such merits; he has thus awakened to them through self-realization, which is so profound, extremely subtle, and incomparable, within which he has personally realized all dharmas.

Furthermore, suppose someone were to slander me, saying: "He may have a nature of sound that corresponds [to his words], yet there is something remaining; for instance, it is as if someone were to say: 'There are certain other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are intelligent and wise, whether they dwell among the gods, or among the Māra-devas of the desire realm, or among the sublime ones of the Brahmā-realm and the form realm,' and who speak the Dharma in such a manner. I do not perceive any such characteristic in them, nor is there any causal basis for it.
As it has been stated: "If one does not perceive their marks, how could even a Perfectly Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha) speak in such a way?

It is by perceiving them that he teaches the Dharma; having attained the state of peace, he dwells in joy; as a Perfectly Enlightened One, he has reached the state of fearlessness, as well as other states of non-attachment," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
That is the most sublime, unattached, and immovable state; it is nameless and manifold. Therein, the Brahma Wheel of Dharma shall be turned.
That Brahma, the World-Honored One, turns this Dharma, namely the Noble Eightfold Path. Wherein shall it be turned?

Or they may say: "He turns the wheel of Dharma within this assembly; he roars the lion's roar within this assembly. He does not turn the wheel in an empty place, nor is there any fear in his roaring the lion's roar within this assembly."
Furthermore, it is said:
"In order to subdue that assembly, this is the first ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).
As for the second, regarding the fact that 'all outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted,' what is the meaning of this?"

Regarding what is called the "obstruction of outflows" (*āsrava-āvaraṇa*) wherein there are various fears, if one further possesses the perfection of knowledge through abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna-sampanna*),
what is the meaning of these second and third dharmas of the path taught by me?
That which is called "such a reality" is sought for its sake; he speaks thus: "This creates the internal sense bases; this is the third and fourth [link] wherein there is bondage."
There are ten matters practiced by people that cause them to have no fear when among the assembly, yet lack a heart of reverence.

Because they thus lack dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), they harbor fear within the great assembly. Furthermore, even if one possesses a heart of reverence, is intelligent and discerning, and maintains such dignified deportment, they may still harbor fear.

Although he possesses a mind of reverence toward the assembly and feels no fear toward them, he remains ignorant of their meaning; thus, despite his service, offerings, and reverent heart, he does not practice repeatedly, and even when he does practice, it is not for long, and therein he still harbors a sense of fear.
Although one has practiced for a long time therein, the mind is not swift; thus, there is still fear within it.
Although the mind may be swift, one does not yet approach [the goal]; thus, there is still a heart of fear within it.
Although they associate with them, they do not rely on them in truth; within that [association], there is still a mind of fear.
Although their minds incline toward the wholesome, they themselves lack this wholesomeness; therefore, amidst those crowds, they have a mind of fear.
"Even if one possesses this intention universally, yet lacks skillful means (*upāya*), one will still harbor a heart of fear amidst the assembly.

When that Blessed One was a bodhisattva, he served the teachers and the multitude—the essential jewel-banner of the triple world. From the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha until the attainment of *samyaksaṃbuddha* over many kalpas, his mind was utterly pure and free from blemish; there was nothing obscure that it did not illuminate. Due to those conditions of awakening-intention (*bodhicitta*), such forms and types [of manifestations] were produced, and through the accomplishment of what he did for the sake of that Path, he performed practices for ninety-one kalpas.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having received his name, gave rise to such wisdom and attained Buddhahood; his mind was in perfect accord with wisdom and fully awakened. Relying on that benevolent intention, he accomplished all things and his mind was entirely unattached. He was foremost in being undefiled and harbored no fear.

Therefore, the World-Honored One thus abides eternally and constantly enters samādhi; he possesses excellence in that wisdom and excellence throughout countless ages. Making such an observation, he never hesitates when faced with difficult questions, and his words are free from any deficiency in phrasing.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"His body is like that of the lion king; Desiring to cross over that garden grove, The various beasts are all struck with terror, Each fleeing hither and thither."
"Thus being unattached, the Great Assembly manifests valor;
taking no pleasure in the source of birth and death, they deliver devas and humans by means of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One observed all worlds as being like grass and trees, wondering: "How should this be tested?"
The initial seeds consist of five elements, just like external plants and trees; what five kinds are there in this case?
Furthermore, it is said:
"How do those trees lean against one another?"

The various fetters that arise are abandoned through the Truth of Suffering; externally, there are also five kinds of formations that arise, and observing those produced from the ground of suffering, one sees that they all arise in dependence upon the external.
Regarding how it arises internally, some say:
"One performs this contemplation regarding the internal bases of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and so forth; thus, when abiding externally, it arises according to its respective seed."
Regarding this, it is said:
"Just as the sun and moon appear without light, these depend upon one another;
so too, that which is spoken arises depending on the external."
"What is the meaning of this? He replied:
"At present, they do not depend on food; they are soaked by water, cooked by fire, established within the physical form, or moved by wind."

Just as one perceives all that occurs when trees growing from the earth sway back and forth with the wind, so too does one recognize and know when the body is touched by the winds or when there is something heard by the ears.
He said, "It is the subtle and smooth; it depends on the external and is firm. Is he not possessed of wisdom?
Such is his distracted thought.
If it arises from external fruits, one should thoroughly observe both external conditions and the internal."
Within this, it is said:
"Is it not the case that all things are non-conceptualized forms?
One does not form such a view; rather, one contemplates all such objects just as one observes the four great elements.
Alternatively, one may observe that from a single cause, visual consciousness arises as various effects, with consciousness as the primary factor; therefore, it is subject to disintegration.
Regarding this, it is said:

"Externally, too, there are those that produce various effects, such as a form that is half-blue and half-yellow, or like a tree from which a single root produces various kinds of fruit, which may not exist in autumn or may arise according to the season."

This tree of birth and death is likewise: the body is its root, while the faculties are its branches and leaves; it is like the realm of samādhi. Therefore, the fruit of giving consciousness is supreme.
Thus one should understand: using the eye as a metaphor for that tree, if the eye-consciousness apprehends a form, how could its root—namely, the present form—be established?

That which is called "contemplation as it has been taught" is indeed sublime when contemplated; it manifests in such a way that it further manifests, meaning that the seeds produced gradually grow and increase, and from their arising, the fruit is realized. Just as they wither in due course, that fruit does not exist without causes and conditions, yet this fruit exists.
Regarding what is called "being defiled by the impurities of the mind," it is therein stated:
"Visual consciousness cognizes everything. It is therein stated:
"In the interim, it is not as when that form conditions the arising of its fruit;
likewise, conditioned by mental consciousness, there is this tree of birth and death, with visual consciousness as its primary element."
Regarding this, it is said:
"Just as the embryo gradually grows and visual consciousness arises therein, so too does visual consciousness exist.
Regarding this, it is said:
"One does not die in the interval of visual consciousness, nor is there a body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), yet the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is not something produced.
For what reason?

Whether it be that external [objects] do not depend on the fruit of the faculty as their basis, or whether they are like the fruit of a reflection—how can one say in this case that [the eye-faculty] is equal to all the body-faculties?"

Because in the past they did not rely on rootless [plants], yet the roots of grass and fruit are subject to decay; furthermore, this is an object of knowledge: externally there are no sentient beings, yet internally there are sentient beings.
Regarding this, it is said:
"How can there be fruit from mental conceptions?
It is just like external flowers and fruits; this kind of fruit is likewise. For this reason, whether it be a sentient being or a shared conception, within it there is truly no obstruction."
"How should mindfulness be maintained?
Regarding this, it is said:
"What is the meaning of this?"
Some may say: "In that place there is no abode.
To this, he replied:
"Just as there is no locus for that, so there is this purity; as there is no external destruction, so there is this causal condition.
Regarding this, it is said:
"That the four great elements possess supremacy, such that there is a fruit according to what they depend upon—that is not the case."

Furthermore, this is to be known: the karmic actions performed do not manifest externally; just as that which exists internally does not abide is called a "tree," whereas that which abides is not a tree.
Regarding this, it is said:
"How is it that this earth-element remains indestructible?
This earth-element also possesses a subtle quality; if one relies upon it, its characteristic of solidity can be known when it is blown by the wind, and this case is likewise so.
However, one should observe that the medicinal herbs, trees, and forests outside are impermanent, subject to interruption, and associated with decay;
the same applies to the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self of causes and conditions.

Yet, the external is empty and non-existent; sentient beings are likewise so. Just as there is no self when observing the internal, how much less could there be anything created within, or any thoughts harbored within?
All those are external, just as damp wood sprouts immediately when sown; this is also like that.

That which is taught by the faculty of mind is like the body and mind moving back and forth and revolving in dependence upon the *dharma*; these all have no basis, just as life-span, warmth, vitality, and consciousness; this is also like that, having neither beginning nor end.
Observing their dispositions and inclinations, as well as external trees and grasses—
which are truly empty and bear no fruit— one should discern the nature of phenomena.
Since they are already subject to decay and ruin, one should contemplate the body and all things accordingly.
He destroyed those fetters of worldly toil, and his five faculties were forever extinguished.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having grown weary in body from diligently practicing asceticism, found delight in that park and grove. He served the sacrificial fire without ceasing; surrounded by a multitude, his *saṃghāṭī* robe was worn, and his hair and nails were long. His faculties were fully matured, and he had inwardly subdued lust. Whether walking back and forth or observing, he knew all things. Delighting in secluded places, his fame spread far and wide, and thus he attained great compassion.

There is none whose virtue equals that of the Honored One; he is the object of offerings for devas and humans, a great field of merit. With increased reverence and prostrations, he delivers all who encounter distress and calamity. He delivers them from birth and death, manifesting the characteristics of the Dharma and manifesting joy. He protects them as if they were his own father, no different. His meritorious acts of offering are as immovable as a mountain. Rejoicing and leaping with joy, desiring to observe the Tathāgata and wishing to dwell alone in a secluded place, he went to where the World-Honored One was. Because of his delight in the extraordinary Dharma, he bowed his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to praise the virtue of having few desires, addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:

"Kāśyapa, you are now old and your form is mature; you no longer possess the vigor of youth. Elder, your body is no longer capable of much; it has gradually declined and wasted away, and your former flourishing spirit is exhausted and will not return."

The patched robes you wear are extremely heavy; considering your current physical condition, your body cannot endure such weight. As you have reached an advanced age, you should accept the robes offered by those who are wealthy and wish to give.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, conceiving thoughts regarding all phenomena with a heart of reverence for the Tathāgata, rose from his seat, knelt on both knees, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Birth and death are long and far-reaching; their meanings are all unreal. Experiencing this pleasure and pain, the mind is constantly filled with sorrow and anxiety."

Even those who are noble, honorable, and wealthy do not wish to go to such a person's home; for he himself dwells as an araṇyaka and praises the virtues of the araṇyaka life, and he himself possesses few desires and praises the virtues of having few desires.

However, the World-Honored One and the devas bear witness that in this present life, whether I possess strength or lack it, I am able to carry [the burden] upon my head; how much more so now, when my body is free from lust, anger, and delusion, when pride has been entirely exhausted, and when I have attained all that is pure and flawless—having departed from the world and no longer corresponding with worldly things. How could I now discard these coarse robes?
At that time, the World-Honored One asked, "What is this?
It was explained in detail as in the sūtra.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied:

"One dwells in a secluded place for two reasons: either to praise the virtues of seclusion, or because one desires to attain joy within this present life and acts as a lamp and manifestation of such virtues for the sake of future generations; it is for these reasons that one practices such diligent asceticism."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Mahākāśyapa!"
"One should always delight in dwelling in seclusion.
This is explained at length as in the sūtras. Thereupon, this verse was spoken:
"What sovereign mastery has he attained, that his disciples practice asceticism,
pure and free from all afflictions, as bright as the moon among the stars?
Now, being without doubt, he possesses such great virtue."
"One should firmly uphold the True Dharma and purify all defilements.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, relying upon the profound and boundless [wisdom] whose knowledge was as limitless as the great ocean, was capable of debating with and subduing all non-Buddhist scholars; he extolled the wholesome Dharma without contradicting their intentions, had attained liberation from sensual desire, and had exhausted the very roots of the destinies of birth and death as known by his mind. He then went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at His feet, and said to the World-Honored One:

"I have established such principles, all of which are firm and stable. While those various non-Buddhists and heterodox teachers abide in their respective places, I have now come to this place desiring to partake of the nectar to eliminate all fetters, my mind being free from attachment."
"In my presence, the World-Honored One has spoken this meaning for my sake; it shall remove my affliction and distress.

Having spoken these words, all ordinary persons were filled with sorrow, and those who were still in training were likewise filled with sorrow; yet those free from doubt all desired to hear [the further teaching].
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected for a moment and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"These practices are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, who always delighted in secluded places and took joy in the Dharma, prostrated himself before the Dharma, circumambulated it three times, and then, straightening his body and gazing at the form of the Tathāgata, he went to the village of Nālada, spread grass upon the ground, and entered the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*.
Having entered that samādhi—the skillful means by which the Tathāgata abides—he attained parinirvāṇa therein.

At that time, the novice Saṃtuta (also known as Śun-tu) constantly provided for the Venerable Śāriputra with whatever was required; he turned the sublime wheel of Dharma, performed the Buddha’s work, and was the greatest among the śrāvakas. All people in the world made offerings to him, and they offered their gifts at the site of the Tathāgata’s body: his relics, his alms bowl, and his three dharma-robes, which he then entrusted to the Venerable Ānanda.
Having arrived, he spoke these words:
"The teacher for whom I served has now passed into parinirvāṇa.
Venerable Ānanda then asked the novice Saṃputta:
“Who is your teacher? What is his name?
“The teacher I serve is named Upatissa; that venerable one has now entered parinirvāṇa. This is the venerable Śāriputra.”

At that time, when the Venerable Ānanda heard these words, he was immediately filled with sorrow. He entered the city of delusion, and his mind became so bewildered regarding those relics that he lost all awareness. Standing there for a moment in grief and agitation, he took the novice Saṃgharakṣita and went to the place where the World-Honored One was, reporting everything to the World-Honored One exactly as it had been said:
"Today my body is not as it used to be; this is because I have heard that the Venerable Śāriputra has attained parinirvāṇa."
The full explanation is as given in the Sūtra.
The Blessed One said:
"Does that person depart with a body of ethical discipline?"
"And do you also take away the dharmas realized by me?
That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness.
This is explained at length as in the sūtra.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Conditioned formations cannot be maintained for long; they must all eventually decay and perish. Ānanda!"
In the practice of impermanence, there is nothing that exists eternally, nor is there any failure to observe wholesome conduct.
Ānanda! Conduct has no basis upon which to rely.
Ānanda! One gives rise to the contact of suffering and harbors perverted perceptions. Ānanda!
Practicing non-self, one does not attain mastery.
Ānanda! Practicing that which is difficult to relinquish, one constantly receives the teaching of existence.
Ānanda! All conditioned formations that involve harm are entirely empty and quiescent. Ānanda!
"You should remain far removed from such conduct that gives rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the novice Saṃtha:
"Hand these relics to me and place them in my hand."
At that time, the śrāmaṇera Sundara immediately offered it to the Tathāgata. Then the World-Honored One extended his golden arm—extremely soft and delicate—and received it.

At the moment the World-Honored One accepted the relics, they were utterly pure and free from blemish; those who beheld them with joyful hearts were all filled with delight, as the relics rested within the darkness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!

You should pay homage to these relics of Śāriputra. He praised himself, saying that his fame was spread far and wide; among the śrāvakas, he was the most honored and most sublime, with only one remaining."
All those have already passed away; yet all living beings who desire this bliss manifest supernormal powers to remove defilement.
Furthermore, that luminosity of theirs pervades everywhere; if such form were to exist, one should pay homage to that wisdom.

He possessed a renowned name that could fill all worlds; these are his relics, which attained mastery over the body within the three realms and were perfumed with sublime fragrances. Therefore, one should prostrate and pay homage to such merit, which manifests as a multitude of virtues like a lamp for the world; one should train for liberation in order to reach that state.

At that time, the World-Honored One also relinquished his life-span; at that moment, the earth shook violently, thunder and lightning flashed from all four directions, and the various devas filled the void with musical performances. A great radiance shone everywhere, illuminating all things, while clouds and mists covered the sky so that the fires lost their light. Such words were spread abroad: "The All-Knowing One shall now enter parinirvāṇa."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat early in the morning, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the feet of the World-Honored One, stood to one side, and asked the World-Honored One:
"What is the cause and condition for this great shaking of the earth?"
The World-Honored One’s mind remained unmoved, and he spoke these words:
“Ānanda, it is for eight causes and conditions that the earth undergoes a great trembling.”
He spoke again to the Venerable Ānanda:
"When a foremost disciple enters parinirvāṇa, or when the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, such a portentous sign as this occurs."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does the World-Honored One also relinquish his life-span this day?
The World-Honored One replied:
“In this way, Ānanda, I too shall relinquish my life-span.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda threw himself to the ground; as described at length in the sūtra, he addressed the World-Honored One:

"I have personally heard from the Tathāgata and have received, upheld, and recited [this teaching]: that there are bhikṣus who, having cultivated the four dhyānas and the bases of psychic power, can abide for a kalpa or even for incalculable kalpas."
The details are as explained in the sūtra.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s mind remained unshaken, and he uttered these words of instruction, saying:
"What do you think, Ānanda?"
“Did I not tell you this repeatedly?

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, whose word was never in vain, remained silent. Like a ship wrecked in the great ocean with no means of reaching the other shore, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“Since the time of the World-Honored One Suśānta, throughout the realms of all those Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the people were entirely long-lived and accomplished. Today, the realm of the Tathāgata’s practice is one of extreme hardship; though his diligent giving and generosity are without limit, the lifespan of sentient beings today is so very short that the root of their transformation has not yet been fully realized.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"How is it that the world is now peaceful, abundant, and free from fear, terror, and hardship?

There is a Dharma King who has appeared in the world, a Wheel-Turning Sage King who governs and transforms by means of the Dharma; the trees, medicinal herbs, and grasses are beyond counting, and all those imprisoned and confined in jails are made to be liberated."
Furthermore, in an era of tumultuous upheaval, he is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King, causing all those imprisoned and confined in jails to be liberated and spared from suffering and calamity.
"How does one show kindness toward those sentient beings? How is it that one shows kindness toward sentient beings?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"The foremost Dharma King, who transcends all men, is most essential in being able to liberate those who encounter calamity and suffering from their distress."

“Just as, Ānanda, in an age of great peace there is a Wheel-Turning Sage King, so it was when the Buddha Suvarṇaprabhāsa was in the world; just as those confined and imprisoned in a jail are all delivered and liberated.”

Ānanda! Just as my lifespan today is extremely short as I appear in the world, those sentient beings are born during a kalpa of swords and blades; the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of that evil kalpa are thick, and they have not yet been able to abandon those fetters. Among those sentient beings, such evils arise from various wrong views, resulting in the fetter of wrong view; because of unrighteous desire, there is the fetter of desire. Because the times are so evil, those who can be taught are few; yet, if one diligently cultivates this practice among those people, [the result will be great].

Ānanda! When I had not yet attained the Way and was a monkey, I did not spare my own life so that all my fellow species might attain deliverance; there was not a single one among them who did not attain deliverance.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when I was formerly a lion, I delivered that many merchants from falling into those evil destinies and long cultivated that holy life.
At that time, Ānanda!
Wherever I went, there were none among the sentient beings who were not moistened by my grace. At that time, Ānanda!

I returned to a human body and moistened all the people within the realm of Magadha; furthermore, during my time as a blue jay, I delivered and liberated countless merchants; and later, as a great rishi, I delivered and liberated countless Brahmās.

When I was eight years old, I made this vow with the aspiration that my resolve would never regress; clad in garments of grass, I diligently practiced austerities and dwelt in those secluded places, fully maintaining all such practices.
"What do you think, Ānanda?
When it rains from the heavens in this deluded world, it is Śakra Devānām Indra who causes the rain to fall.
At that time, Ānanda!"
Before I was born, the people of the world cherished their only son.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
for the sake of even a single sentient being, I would undergo the sufferings of hell for the duration of an eon, enduring such afflictions on behalf of that being.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Regarding this body of mine, born of my parents, there is no enemy capable of harming it; such a thing can never happen.
This Vajra-samādhi distinguishes all various samādhis; if, after my parinirvāṇa, someone were to make offerings to my relics even as small as a mustard seed, the merit thereof would be limitless.
At that time, he spoke this verse:
"From the first moment of generating the resolve, my actions have been foremost;
having attained the highest rank among men, who could possibly be my equal?"
"If parents, wives, or children have attained mastery over the world,
though their remaining life may yet persist, when that life is exhausted,
they must be abandoned. Go now, Ānanda!"
"For the sake of the Tathāgata, go to those twin trees.
This was explained at length as in the sūtra.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the instruction from the Buddha, reflected thus:
"Has the World-Honored One truly entered parinirvāṇa today?
Thus he harbored sorrow and grief, yet did not disobey the Honored One’s instruction.

Immediately seized by alarm and fear, he went to that place; for all were pursued by the conditions of their past lives, and though he sought to state his grievances born of diligent suffering, he was again gripped by doubt:
"How should these words be spoken?
he then addressed the World-Honored One:
"What was to be done has been accomplished."

At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to that place; as he raised his foot to step upon the ground and was about to reach that spot, the Venerable Ānanda’s mind became intensely agitated, and this thought arose again within him:
"Is this a magical illusion or a dream?"
"Is this indeed so? Having reflected thus with such hesitation, he again rectified his mind, thinking: "This is called impermanence; sentient beings transmigrate and cannot escape this affliction."

At that time, as the World-Honored One gradually approached the space between those twin trees, the sky was filled with various devas; some performed music and dance with their complexions altered, while others wept and shed tears. Countless assemblies of *śrāvakas* looked longingly toward the Dharma and paid reverent homage to the Dharma.
At that time, he spoke this verse:
"This Honored One is the foremost and most sublime;
for the sake of those classes of sentient beings, this Dharma is likewise unsurpassed; now he shall enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the space between the twin trees and sat down. Thereupon, the devas in the space between the twin trees announced to one another, saying:
"In this age of chaos, the All-Knowing One shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"How can one abandon the multitude of beings and enter parinirvāṇa?
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
"For the sake of the profound meaning, One swiftly attains the flavor of the Deathless."
That Honored One possessed such power, yet now it shall all pass away.
Like that wheel of adamant, which was praised and extolled by the people—
even if that wheel might eventually break, this Honored One is difficult to destroy.

"In that interval, he fully cultivated the contemplation of impermanence; his power of diligence was indestructible. He realized that all who are young and strong are entirely impermanent, and even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise pass into parinirvāṇa—this affliction is truly painful and distressing."
Then he spoke this verse:
"Reflecting deeply upon that, one sees that forms and appearances undergo transformation;
bound by further craving, one undergoes all manner of suffering and affliction."
Among them, some recited this verse:
"Birth is suffering from the very beginning; When these aggregates (skandhas) exist, there is a name.

Among them, some spoke these verses: "From what does impermanence arise?

such is their nature—that the Buddhas do not abide eternally."
"What practice should we cultivate today?

This field of merit cannot be grasped, yet one should give rise to a heart of joy.

At that time, all the devas within the Śāla Grove prostrated themselves before the World-Honored One and rained down various kinds of *mandārava* flowers. Weeping with tears streaming down their faces, they spoke this verse:
“Those who have beheld the Tathāgata Are diligent day and night;
Now he desires to enter parinirvāṇa, And cast off this body of the four great elements.”
"Through diligent toil he perfected his virtue, never having transgressed the True Dharma;
having crossed the ocean of birth and death, he shall now cast off the aggregates and sense-bases.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“O bhikṣus! If you have any doubts, you may ask about them now; even such things as ‘how is it that all conditioned phenomena are neither pure nor permanent?
Venerable Aniruddha said:
“Has the Blessed One entered parinirvāṇa?

Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, standing behind the Tathāgata, observed the Tathāgata’s complexion, limbs, joints, and sinews; they were all firm and robust, capable of bearing heavy burdens, and likewise capable of expounding the subtle and wondrous Dharma. He then wept and spoke these words:
“Stainless and free from all blemish, The world has lost its protection.”
Like that purple-polished gold, he shall now depart, leaving the multitude behind.
Just as in this world, when the harvest season has already passed,
Śākyamuni of the Śākya clan enters the eternal stillness of non-conception.
Among them, some said, "Stop, stop! Do not speak such words.
At that time, harboring this vexation, he spoke thus:

"I recall that when the World-Honored One descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born into the world, I remembered those several tens of millions of devas who, by virtue of their own merit, all wore blue robes; they possessed majestic spiritual power, a strength that could not be thwarted or destroyed, and five hundred of them were non-retrogressive."
Furthermore, there were twelve great spirits and deities whom all who saw them were struck with terror; they wished to come and protect the Tathāgata. After reflecting for a moment, they spoke again:

"The joints and limbs of the Tathāgata have been gathered and all emit radiance. He has issued a command to us, and this message was delivered to the devas: 'The World-Protecting Deities have sent envoys here. Having received this word from him, we joyfully serve and make offerings to him, just as when he was in the womb; whether in dreams or while awake, we are never far from him."

We are deeply attached to the sentient beings of this world; we hold them in firm regard, perceiving in them both suffering and joy, perceiving them as our parents, and regarding all that is subtle and excellent in the world as supreme. We perceive those who protect the world as our brothers, and because they accept even small offerings of faith, we perceive them as fields of merit. Our minds are not inclined toward deviance, and thus we perceive them as our guides. Because they desire to ferry us across the current, we perceive them as boatmen. Because they are ungraspable, we cherish them as precious jewels. And because they have attained great compassion, we perceive them as world-protectors.
If my adamantine body were not shattered into a hundred pieces this day, or if there were one who could say that this body would surely attain the fruit—why is this so?
"In order to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada spoke these words: "How is this so?"

At that time, when the Prince rode out of the city in his carriage, his horse returned and for seven days refused to eat; it was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. How much more so should we, who serve him and receive the Tathāgata’s instructions?
Those who hear it and those who recite it shall all learn to deliver sentient beings without limit; furthermore, one should seek this ocean of rare treasures extensively.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada and two other noble beings spoke this verse:
“In the abode of the divine nāgas, The vajra emerges from the ocean;
How shall one provide protection For such a lion’s roar?”
At that time, reflecting thus, he further spoke these words:
"Just as that deep ocean, whose power none can surpass,
so too one who practices diligence in the world possesses great virtue that is boundless."
Thus the World-Honored One turned the Wheel of Dharma in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;
when he first turned this Dharma, it brought great benefit to sentient beings. During that very summer retreat, it was beneficial to the King of Magadha.
The second and third [turnings] were on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; the fifth was at Vaiśālī; and the sixth was at Makula.
For the sake of his mother Śuklā, the Mountain White [Buddha] appeared in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as the seventh; in the realm of ghosts and spirits as the eighth;
in the kingdom of Kośambī as the ninth; in Mount Citrakūṭa as the tenth; again in the realm of ghosts and spirits as the eleventh;
in a secluded place in Magadha as the twelfth; and returning once more to the realm of ghosts and spirits as the thirteenth.
The *Dhātu*: Chapter Fourteen, the place where the Buddha himself traveled, at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park;
Chapter Fifteen, in a village of the Śākya clan in Kapilavastu; Chapter Sixteen, returning to Kapilavastu;
Chapter Seventeen, Rājagṛha; Chapter Eighteen, again Rājagṛha; Chapter Nineteen...
In the nineteenth summer retreat he sat in the Śālavana mountain; in the twentieth, he sat in Rājagṛha;
in the twenty-first, he returned to the Śālavana mountain, where he remained within the realm of spirits and ghosts without visiting any other places for four consecutive summer retreats.
For nineteen years he did not travel to other places, but observed the summer retreat in Śrāvastī.
When the Tathāgata was observing his final summer retreat, he stayed for the rains at the village of Piṅgalā within the territory of Vaiśālī.

The World-Honored One has thus crossed the abyss of craving; he has fully accomplished all the acts of giving performed by past Buddhas and perfected those of sharp faculties. Having universally reached all practices and completely crossed over with a gentle disposition, he next crosses those of medium faculties, then those of dull faculties, gradually leading them to the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The World-Honored One gave exhaustive expositions for the sake of those of external paths;
at that time, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
“Because he wishes to deliver those of external paths, the Great Honored One is without equal;
having awakened himself, he delivers others, so that none remain submerged in this abyss.
He delivers them through various joys, and they gradually attain growth and benefit.”
Thereupon, they gave rise to joy, and all were delivered from that place.

Now, being pure and free from blemish, wherever they are born, they always encounter favorable circumstances; their own practice is perfected and they are free from all pride. Through various merits, they achieve complete accomplishment; because they correspond with those realms, they achieve success through diligent application. Because of their earnestness, their births are all accomplished so as to provide rescue and deliverance from suffering to the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Thus, one attains accomplishment: if born into a noble and honored household, one achieves success as a householder; because one’s physical form is subtle, one achieves success in kinship; because one’s undertakings are sufficient, one achieves success in the state of non-action; because there is a finite measure, all that is undertaken is accomplished; because various fetters and afflictions are severed, one achieves success in subduing them; because of the vows made regarding the karmic actions initiated, one achieves success in those vows; because various merits have been planted without ever transgressing, one achieves success in what is undertaken; one achieves success in majestic deportment; one achieves success in the precepts of all merits; one achieves success in the deportment that expounds the four foundations of mindfulness; one achieves success in the sphere of analytical instruction; one achieves success in gathering the assembly through the arousal of wisdom; and having already abandoned all states of existence, one achieves success in the perfection of the precepts.

Through wisdom, one focuses the mind and does not rely on the accomplishment of dhyāna-samādhi; through the wisdom that discerns those realms as they truly are, the accomplishment of wisdom is achieved; by severing all fetters and proclivities, the accomplishment of liberation is achieved; by severing all ignorance, the accomplishment of the vision and wisdom of liberation is achieved; by gathering all merits, all things are accomplished; having attained cessation, the accomplishment of śamatha and vipaśyanā is achieved. Therefore, I pay homage to the One of Ten Powers.
At that time, he spoke this verse:
"Form is inconceivable, awakened by the Buddha;
His name is extolled throughout the three periods of time; He is a divine sage who has reached the further shore."
"Having found rest within the world, forever extinguished and without arising or ceasing, possessing the foremost penetration of great wisdom, he has attained mastery over all.

Hearing that one hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the All-Knowing One’s vision was manifest in the world within the realm of Magadha at the city of Kuśāvatī, there was a king named Aśoka. His virtue was most majestic, no different from that of Śakra, the Lord of Devas; he possessed great majesty and power, was intelligent and wise, capable of engaging in debate with him, and regarded his subjects as his own children.
When he wished to sleep that night, he thought to himself:
"The wish I have now has been fulfilled; I have no further expectations. I shall protect the people."
What skillful means should now be employed, and what karma should be performed?
What matters should be undertaken so that all the people of the world may receive their merit?
Having reflected thus, he fell asleep that very night and heard this verse in a dream:
"Most profound and subtle, Honored by those of the three periods of time, The most excellent one has entered parinirvāṇa; You should widely distribute his relics."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately awoke from his startlement.
Having awakened, the king then uttered this praise:
"Excellent is that being; even after having attained parinirvāṇa..."
"What has been transmitted by the Śāri-devas, we shall now serve.
Having heard this oral tradition with their own ears, the Great King immediately summoned his ministers and assembled the great multitude, asking them regarding this matter:
"By what means should I provide relief and transform the people?"
The ministers and the people each presented their own statements:
some said they would make offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata, while others said they would perform sacrifices to the gods and spirits.
At that time, the king spoke as follows:

"You should protect this Dharma with words of utmost sincerity. Last night, in a dream, I heard these words: 'Contemplating these śarīras, I think they are most excellent. For the sake of this world, we ought to protect the people of the world; having ourselves obtained merit and enabled sentient beings to attain deliverance, the merit shall be immeasurable. You should practice dignified conduct and benevolent compassion, causing all to behold the illumination. Such were the words I heard within my dream."
Furthermore, he spoke this verse:
"If one hears that sound, one will personally realize it at the site of enlightenment;
he is the Lion of the Śākyas, whose śarīra should be venerated."
At that time, the king assembled the bhikṣus and again questioned them regarding this matter, saying:
"Bhikṣus, [explain] according to the teaching of the Dharma.
Then the king spoke further to those bhikṣus:
"What you noble ones have described as what I saw in my dream is indeed the result of the roots of merit I planted in previous lives.

At that time, on the eighth day, the king observed the eightfold precepts of the *poṣadha*, dressed in pure white garments, and sounded bells and drums; he performed various entertainments, playing the lute and the *vīṇā*, blowing conch shells, and burning all kinds of incense, desiring to obtain the *śarīra* relics from the city of Rājagṛha.

He heard that within that city there was a golden seal-scripture, and having already seen the form of that golden seal, he recalled his past life when he had given earth as a gift; upon hearing those signs, the bhikṣus said: "The King, after reflecting for a moment, spoke these words:
'This must surely yield a subtle and wondrous fruit.'"
"I wish to open the copper casket and see the contents within.

He immediately opened the casket and saw a golden certificate, upon which there was also writing. This certificate recorded that King Ajātaśatru had spoken of a King Aśoka; seeing this verification, he then read the inscription aloud for the sake of all sentient beings.

In the realm of Magadha there was the city of Rājagṛha. There lived a householder named Pāramitara, who had a son named Vijayamitra; the second family was that of Pauṣpadatta, who had a son named Pauṣkarasādi.

Those two sons of householders were playing with soil at the crossroads; while they were thus playing, the son of the householder Viśākhā-Maitrāyaṇī became filled with joy and, cupping his hands, offered some soil as a gift.
Furthermore, there are those who assist in this joy:
after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa at the age of one hundred, Viśayamitra shall appear in the world, owing to the merits of that land.
There was a king named Ajita, who emerged from among those of heterodox lineage.
When the king read these characters, he was filled with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, then addressed his ministers:
"Read this golden charter again; it is no different than what was above."
"He shall rule over all classes of people in this world; however, he will not praise or honor Vāsavadatta, but shall instead serve as that person's minister."
At that time, the king uttered this praise:
"Excellent, O great field of merit!
By making such a small offering, one gains great merit and the heart attains joy."
Some made this declaration:
"I shall take the relics of the seven stūpas and distribute them widely throughout the world.
At that time, King Śreṇika marveled at such unprecedented wisdom and joyfully took those relics.
From within the void, a divine voice was heard, reciting this verse:
"Generate a heart of joy; Virtuous merit is beyond measure.
One should widely disseminate one's merits And leave behind relics to transform sentient beings."
The Heavenly King rained down various kinds of flowers upon those relics.
At that time, the king erected eighty-four thousand stūpas, all of which were completed in a single day.
At that time, the king addressed his ministers, saying:

"He possessed such true and sublime teachings, praised by the world; yet now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, his relics have been distributed throughout the world, and he is free from all fetters."
The body is pure like gold and also like white snow; observing this ground, one never gives rise to evil, and it is the same for that [other] ground as well.

Having seen this ground, one protects it; the wisdom of the instructions is unshakable. It resides within a cave on a most precipitous high peak, immeasurable; how much more so when presiding over all.
"All stages are fields of merit; as the One Possessing the Ten Powers observes the various classes of sentient beings, the stūpas and temples they erect neither increase nor decrease.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s relics were of a single kind, yet each person formulated various different theories regarding them.
At that time, the king said:
"If even by this power of the countless Vajrasamādhis one must shatter one's own bones to attain rest,
how shall one ever cross over this?"
